sections.body:
Supervised learning fits a function from inputs to targets by minimizing a loss over training examples, hoping that low training error implies low error on data you haven't seen. That hope is the entire subject. It only works because real problems have structure, and because the model class you chose happens to match some of it.

Every loss function is a distributional assumption in disguise. Assume Gaussian noise around your prediction and maximum likelihood gives you mean squared error. Assume Bernoulli outputs and you get cross-entropy. Assume Laplace noise and you get mean absolute error, which is why MAE is the robust choice under heavy tails. Add a Gaussian prior on the weights and MAP estimation becomes L2 regularization. Knowing this chain lets you answer 'why this loss' with a reason rather than a convention.
sections.heading: What learning actually is

sections.body:
Expected error decomposes into bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is error from a hypothesis class too restrictive to represent the truth. Variance is how much the fitted function swings if you redraw the training set. Simple models are high-bias and low-variance; flexible models the reverse.

The practical use is diagnostic. High training error and high validation error means underfitting, so add capacity or better features. Low training error with high validation error means overfitting, so add regularization, augmentation, or data. A small persistent gap with still-improving validation loss is fine and not something to fix.

The incomplete part: in the overparameterized deep learning regime, test error follows a double-descent curve. It rises to a peak near the interpolation threshold, where the model is just barely able to fit the data and is forced into a brittle solution, then falls again as capacity grows. Parameter count is a poor proxy for effective capacity, because SGD is implicitly biased toward small-norm, flat interpolating solutions. Treat the tradeoff as a guide, not a law.
sections.heading: Bias, variance, and why the classic story is incomplete

sections.body:
Split three ways: train to fit parameters, validation to choose hyperparameters and architecture, test touched exactly once at the end. Every decision made by looking at a set is a form of fitting to it, so a test set consulted repeatedly stops estimating generalization.

Use k-fold cross-validation when data is scarce, because averaging held-out scores across folds lowers variance and the spread across folds tells you whether a difference between two models is real or noise. Stratify for imbalanced targets. For time series use forward-chaining splits, since random folds let the model peek at the future.

Accuracy misleads under class imbalance and asymmetric costs. With one percent positives, predicting negative always scores ninety-nine percent and catches nothing. Move to precision and recall at a chosen operating point, PR-AUC for ranking quality on the rare class, and ideally a cost matrix tied to the real decision so the threshold falls out of the economics rather than defaulting to 0.5.

ROC-AUC is the probability a random positive outranks a random negative. Its weakness is that false positive rate divides by a huge negative count, so thousands of false alarms barely move the curve. Precision-recall conditions on what you predicted positive and exposes exactly that.
sections.heading: Evaluation discipline

sections.body:
Data leakage means training saw information unavailable at prediction time, so offline metrics look excellent and production collapses. It is the single most common cause of a model that 'worked in the notebook'.

The classic vector is preprocessing fit before splitting: you standardize or target-encode on the full dataset, so test statistics bleed into training. Others are features computed from the future, near-duplicate rows straddling the split, and identifiers that proxy the label.

Defenses: wrap every transform in a pipeline fit only on the training fold, split by time for temporal problems and by entity when rows cluster per user, and get suspicious whenever one feature's importance looks too good to be true. That suspicion is a professional instinct worth cultivating.
sections.heading: Leakage: the bug that makes you look brilliant

sections.body:
A calibrated model's probabilities are literally trustworthy: of all cases scored 0.7, roughly seventy percent are positive. This matters whenever a downstream system consumes the number rather than the argmax, for expected-value thresholding, triage, or ensembling.

Measure with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error, not accuracy, because a model can rank perfectly and still be badly calibrated. Deep networks are systematically overconfident. Temperature scaling, a single parameter fit on held-out data, usually fixes most of it without changing the ranking at all. Isotonic regression is more flexible with more validation data. Note that resampling for class imbalance shifts your probabilities, so recalibrate afterward.
sections.heading: Calibration, and why it is separate from accuracy

sections.body:
Three distinct failures that are often conflated:

Covariate shift changes p(x) while the mapping holds. The model is still correct but is being asked about regions it saw rarely. Importance weighting or retraining on reweighted data can help.

Label shift changes the class priors, like disease prevalence rising. Since class-conditionals hold, you can correct it analytically by adjusting the prior or recalibrating.

Concept drift changes p(y|x) itself, because fraud tactics evolved or user taste moved. No reweighting of old data recovers this; you need fresh labels and retraining.

Operationally, monitor input feature distributions and prediction distributions continuously since those need no labels, then true error once labels land. That ordering tells you which of the three you're facing.
sections.heading: Drift, and what to do about each kind

sections.body:
Correlation is not causation, and feature importance is not a causal claim. A feature can be highly predictive because it shares a confounder with the target, or because it is a consequence of it. Acting on such a feature changes nothing. Impurity-based importance is also biased toward high-cardinality features, and correlated features split credit arbitrarily. If someone wants to act on a finding, insist on a causal framing: an experiment, a stated DAG with a defensible adjustment set, or an instrument.

No-free-lunch says that averaged uniformly over all possible target functions, no learner beats another. The takeaway isn't nihilism, it's that inductive bias is the product. Convolutions for translation-equivariant images, attention for content-based long-range dependencies, gradient-boosted trees for axis-aligned interactions in heterogeneous tabular data.

And the answer interviewers reward most: gradient-boosted trees are still the strongest default on tabular data, and a regularized linear model is a superb baseline that tells you whether the problem is hard at all. Deep learning earns its complexity when representation learning is the bottleneck.
sections.heading: Interview traps worth rehearsing

lessons.subtitle: The vocabulary every AI interview assumes you already have
lessons.title: ML Fundamentals

sections.body:
A composition of affine maps is another affine map, so a fifty-layer linear network has exactly the expressive power of one linear layer no matter how wide. The nonlinearity is what makes depth buy anything.

ReLU won because its derivative is exactly one on the positive side, so gradient flows undiminished through many layers, unlike sigmoid and tanh which saturate at both tails and multiply many near-zero derivatives into nothing. ReLU's cost is dead units: a neuron whose pre-activation is always negative receives zero gradient forever. Leaky ReLU, ELU, and GELU address this, and GELU is what transformers actually use because its smoothness helps optimization.
sections.heading: Depth needs nonlinearity

sections.body:
The forward pass computes and caches activations. The backward pass starts from the loss derivative and walks backward through the computation graph, multiplying by each node's local Jacobian.

The key efficiency property: it obtains gradients for all parameters in one backward pass costing roughly the same as a forward pass, whereas finite differences would need one forward pass per parameter. The cost is memory, since activations must be retained, which is exactly the tradeoff gradient checkpointing manages by recomputing instead of storing, cutting activation memory to about the square root of layer count for roughly thirty percent extra compute. It is mathematically exact, not an approximation.
sections.heading: Backpropagation is reverse-mode autodiff

sections.body:
Backprop multiplies Jacobians across layers. If their norms sit below one the product shrinks exponentially and early layers stop learning; above one it grows and you get NaN loss.

The fixes stack. Initialization sets the scale so activation variance is preserved through depth: Xavier uses roughly one over fan-in for symmetric activations, He uses two over fan-in for ReLU because ReLU zeroes half its inputs. Weights must be random, not constant, or every unit in a layer receives an identical gradient and symmetry never breaks.

Residual connections are the structural fix. With y = x + F(x), the Jacobian contains an identity term, so there is always an unattenuated path backward. Equally important, the identity mapping becomes free, so each block only learns a correction and adding depth cannot make the achievable function class worse. Every transformer block is a residual stream that attention and the MLP write into.

Gradient clipping by global norm, usually at 1.0, is essentially free insurance and standard in all LLM training.
sections.heading: Gradients that vanish and explode

sections.body:
BatchNorm standardizes each channel using mini-batch statistics, then applies a learned scale and shift. It speeds convergence, tolerates higher learning rates, and adds mild regularizing noise. But it couples examples within a batch, which degrades at small batch sizes, complicates distributed training, and requires running averages at inference, creating a train-versus-eval discrepancy.

LayerNorm normalizes across the feature dimension inside each token independently, so it is batch-size agnostic and behaves identically at train and test with no running statistics. That is why sequence models use it: sequence lengths vary so padding pollutes batch statistics, and at autoregressive inference you process one token at a time with no meaningful batch. RMSNorm simplifies further by dropping mean subtraction, saving compute at no quality cost, and pre-norm placement stabilizes very deep stacks.
sections.heading: Normalization: batch versus layer

sections.body:
The learning rate is the hyperparameter to tune first. Too high and updates overshoot local curvature, giving loss spikes or divergence; too low wastes compute and can settle in sharp minima that generalize worse. Standard practice is a range test to find the largest stable rate, then linear warmup followed by cosine decay.

Momentum keeps an exponentially averaged gradient, damping oscillation across ravines. Adam adds a second moment, the exponential average of squared gradients, and divides by its square root so each parameter gets its own effective step size, plus bias correction because both moments start at zero. Cost: two extra states per parameter, so three times the optimizer memory. Plain Adam's L2 penalty interacts badly with the adaptive denominator, which is why AdamW decouples weight decay and is the default for transformers.

Larger batches give lower-variance gradients supporting bigger steps, roughly the linear scaling rule, though square-root scaling fits Adam better. Warmup is required because a large step from random initialization is where the loss surface is worst-conditioned and Adam's second-moment estimate is least reliable. Past a critical batch size, doubling the batch stops reducing steps proportionally and you are burning compute for nothing.
sections.heading: Optimizers and the learning rate

sections.body:
Dropout zeroes units with probability p during training so no feature is load-bearing alone, approximately averaging over an exponential family of subnetworks. At inference it is disabled with activations rescaled, which frameworks handle via inverted dropout. Forgetting model.eval() is a classic bug that leaves dropout and batchnorm in training mode.

Transfer learning reuses pretrained representations so the target task needs far fewer labels. With a few hundred examples, freeze the backbone and train only a head, since full fine-tuning would overfit and destroy the features. With more data or a real domain gap, unfreeze at a much lower learning rate, often with layer-wise LR decay so general early features move less than task-specific later ones. Always run the frozen baseline first, because it is cheap and tells you how much headroom fine-tuning actually buys.

Knowledge distillation works because a teacher's softened distribution says this image is mostly a husky but somewhat a malamute and not at all a truck, encoding learned similarity structure that a one-hot label cannot. That is a lower-variance, more informative target, which is why a small student trained on it can beat the same architecture trained on hard labels.
sections.heading: Regularization and transfer

sections.body:
Data parallelism replicates the model and all-reduces gradients: simple, but every device holds full weights plus optimizer state, so it hits a memory wall. Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices, communicating every layer, so it needs NVLink-class bandwidth and stays inside a node. Pipeline parallelism assigns layer groups to devices and streams micro-batches, communicating only at boundaries but introducing bubble overhead. Frontier runs combine all three and add ZeRO or FSDP to shard optimizer state, gradients, and parameters.

Mixed precision runs matmuls in half precision with an fp32 master copy of weights. fp16's narrow exponent range makes typical gradients flush to zero, so loss scaling multiplies the loss before backprop and divides it back before the update. bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range at the cost of mantissa bits, needs no loss scaling, and is therefore the default for large model training.

When loss goes NaN, bisect cheapest first: check inputs and targets for inf/NaN and whether failure reproduces at the same step, which points to data rather than numerics; look for unsafe ops like log of zero or division without epsilon; read the gradient-norm history, since a spike over several steps means explosion while an instant jump means a bad op or input; and in mixed precision check whether the loss scaler is repeatedly overflowing.
sections.heading: Scaling and debugging

lessons.subtitle: Why depth works, how it breaks, and what the optimizer is really doing
lessons.title: Deep Learning

sections.body:
Each token projects into a query, a key, and a value. The query represents what this position is looking for, the key advertises what the position offers as a match target, and the value is the content retrieved. Dot each query against all keys, softmax into weights, output the weighted sum of values. Separating key from value matters because what makes a token a good match is not necessarily what you want to read from it.

Scaling by one over the square root of d_k is not cosmetic. With unit-variance components, a d_k-dimensional dot product has variance d_k, so scores grow with head dimension. Large logits saturate softmax toward one-hot, where the Jacobian is nearly zero and gradients vanish. The scaling keeps logits at unit scale independent of dimension.

Multiple heads exist because one softmax attention produces a single weighted average per position, which is a representational bottleneck. Splitting the model dimension into h heads lets them specialize: interpretability work finds heads tracking syntactic dependencies, resolving coreference, attending to the previous token, and induction heads implementing copy patterns. Since each head uses d_model/h dimensions, total cost is roughly unchanged.

The feed-forward sublayer is the other half of the block. Attention moves information between positions; the MLP does nonlinear computation at each position independently, expanding to about four times width and projecting back, often with a gated SwiGLU variant. It holds roughly two thirds of the parameters and is where interpretability work locates factual knowledge, which is consistent with mixture-of-experts routing at the MLP.
sections.heading: Attention as soft dictionary lookup

sections.body:
Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the inputs and the outputs shuffle identically, so the model sees a bag of tokens. Position must be injected.

Rotary embeddings (RoPE) are the modern answer. They rotate pairs of dimensions in queries and keys by an angle proportional to position, and because the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the angle difference, you get relative-position behavior from an absolute-position implementation with no extra parameters. Applied inside every attention layer rather than once at the input, so positional information does not have to survive the whole depth. Crucially it extends past the trained context length by rescaling the frequency base, which is what position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN do, making long-context adaptation a cheap fine-tune.

Causal masking sets scores for future positions to negative infinity. The reason it matters so much is efficiency: one forward pass over length n yields n training examples simultaneously, each predicting the next token from only its prefix. Distinguish this from padding masks, which hide meaningless positions, and from BERT's masked-language-model objective, which corrupts random tokens and reconstructs them bidirectionally.
sections.heading: Position and masking

sections.body:
Encoder-only (BERT) uses bidirectional attention with a masked-token objective, so every position sees full context. Excellent for classification, extraction, and embeddings; cannot generate autoregressively.

Decoder-only (GPT) uses causal attention with next-token prediction. That turned out to be the winning bet: the objective is dense, it scales cleanly, and prompting makes one model do nearly any task. It dominates today.

Encoder-decoder (T5, the original transformer) keeps a bidirectional encoder for the source and a causal decoder that cross-attends into it. Natural for transduction where input and output are distinct sequences, and still common in speech and multimodal setups.

For embeddings specifically, prefer an encoder-style or contrastively trained model over a raw decoder, because bidirectional context and a pooled objective produce better representations per parameter.
sections.heading: The three architectures

sections.body:
During decoding, keys and values for tokens already in context never change, since causal masking means they do not depend on anything later. So you compute them once and cache them; each new token projects only its own query, key, and value and attends over the cache. Without this, generation would be quadratic overall instead of linear.

The cost is memory: roughly two times layers times KV heads times head dimension times sequence length times batch size. At long context it dwarfs the weights, and that single fact drives most modern inference design.

Multi-query attention shares one KV head across all query heads, cutting the cache dramatically at some quality cost. Grouped-query attention is the pragmatic middle, with query heads grouped to share a smaller number of KV heads, capturing nearly all the memory win for almost no quality loss, which is why GQA is standard in modern open models.

PagedAttention manages the cache in fixed non-contiguous blocks like OS virtual memory, eliminating fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing. People also quantize the cache to int8 or fp8.
sections.heading: The KV cache is the center of inference

sections.body:
Prefill processes the entire prompt in one parallel pass. It has plenty of arithmetic per byte of weights loaded, so it is compute-bound, and it determines time-to-first-token, scaling with prompt length.

Decode produces one token per forward pass, streaming all weights plus the growing KV cache to compute a single token. Arithmetic intensity is terrible, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound, and it determines inter-token latency.

Everything about serving follows from that split. Batching is transformative for decode because one weight load amortizes across many sequences, but does little for prefill which is already saturated. Continuous batching schedules per decoding step, evicting finished sequences and admitting queued ones so the batch stays full, which can multiply throughput several times over static batching. Chunked prefill stops one huge prompt from stalling everyone's token stream. Quantization and GQA help decode by cutting bytes moved; FlashAttention and better kernels help prefill.

FlashAttention deserves its own note: it is exact, not an approximation. It tiles the computation and fuses softmax so the n-by-n score matrix is never written to high-bandwidth memory, making attention memory-linear and turning it from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound.

Speculative decoding exploits the same bandwidth bound. A cheap draft model proposes k tokens, the target model scores all k positions in one pass for nearly the cost of one, and a modified rejection-sampling rule accepts the longest valid prefix. The math guarantees the output is distributed exactly as if sampled from the target model alone, so it is lossless. Two to three times speedup, entirely dependent on draft acceptance rate.
sections.heading: Prefill versus decode: two different machines

sections.body:
Temperature divides logits before softmax. Near zero it collapses to greedy, deterministic and best for extraction or code but prone to repetition. Above one it flattens and admits genuinely bad tail tokens.

Top-k keeps a fixed number of candidates regardless of distribution shape, which is wrong in both directions: too permissive when the model is confident, too restrictive when it is genuinely torn. Top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p, so the pool adapts. That is why top-p around 0.9 to 0.95 is the more common default.

Quantization stores tensors as low-bit integers plus scale metadata, per-tensor, per-channel, or per-group. Since decode is bandwidth-bound, four-bit weights can nearly quadruple throughput and let a 70B model fit on one GPU. The difficulty is activation outliers: a few channels have magnitudes orders of magnitude larger than the rest, and a shared scale accommodating them destroys resolution for everything else. LLM.int8 keeps outlier channels in fp16, SmoothQuant migrates scale from activations into weights, GPTQ and AWQ use calibration data to choose roundings that minimize output error. Weight-only four-bit is usually near-lossless on benchmarks, but degradation appears first in long-context retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and rare languages, so evaluate on your own task rather than trusting perplexity.
sections.heading: Sampling and quantization

sections.body:
Scaling laws say loss falls as a smooth power law in compute, parameters, and data. Chinchilla corrected the allocation: for a fixed compute budget, tokens should scale roughly proportionally with parameters, around twenty tokens per parameter, and by that measure GPT-3 era models were badly undertrained. The second-order insight is that compute-optimal for training is not optimal for deployment, so if a model will serve billions of tokens you should deliberately overtrain a smaller one, spending training compute to buy permanently cheaper inference. That is the Llama strategy.

Mixture-of-experts decouples parameters from per-token compute. A router sends each token to the top one or two of many expert MLPs, so total parameters can grow ten to a hundred times while activated FLOPs stay near the dense equivalent. Costs: memory does not shrink since all experts must be resident, routing collapses without an auxiliary load-balancing loss, expert parallelism needs bandwidth-hungry all-to-all communication, and fine-tuning is less stable than dense.

Known weaknesses to be able to explain. Hallucination is rooted in the objective, since next-token prediction rewards plausible text and a confident fabrication is often more likely than a hedge. Lost-in-the-middle means advertised context length is a capacity, not a quality guarantee, driven by recency bias, attention sinks, and scarce long-dependency training data. Arithmetic and character-level tasks fail because tokenization hides character structure and a fixed-depth forward pass cannot run an unbounded carry algorithm, which is why chain-of-thought helps (it converts depth into sequence length) and why calling a calculator is the correct engineering answer. Attention sinks, a few early tokens absorbing attention mass because softmax must allocate a total weight of one, explain why naive sliding-window KV caching blows up perplexity: you evicted the drain, not the content.

Prompt injection is structurally hard because the model consumes one flat token stream with no privilege separation between instructions and data. Unlike SQL you cannot parameterize. Design assuming it will sometimes succeed and put real controls outside the model.
sections.heading: Scaling, MoE, and known weaknesses

lessons.subtitle: Attention, the KV cache, and everything that makes inference fast
lessons.title: Transformers & LLMs

sections.body:
Fine-tuning changes behavior; retrieval changes knowledge. Lead with that and most RAG questions answer themselves.

Fine-tuning bakes information into weights, so updating a fact needs a retraining cycle, you cannot cite a source, you cannot enforce per-user permissions, and deleting a document for a compliance request is essentially impossible. RAG keeps knowledge external, so indexing takes seconds, answers carry verifiable citations, retrieval filters by ACL at query time, and deletion is a row delete. What RAG does not do is teach format, tone, or a skill. Production systems usually need both.
sections.heading: The one-sentence framing

sections.body:
Offline: load and parse documents, chunk them, embed each chunk, write vectors plus metadata plus original text to an index. Online: optionally rewrite the query, retrieve by hybrid search, rerank, assemble a prompt, generate with citations.

The discipline that separates strong candidates: measure each stage separately. Most RAG failures are retrieval failures, and if you only look at the final answer you cannot tell whether the retriever missed the document or the generator ignored it.

Retrieval metrics: recall@k as the headline, since if the right chunk is not in context nothing downstream can save you, plus MRR and nDCG for ranking. Generation metrics conditioned on retrieved context: groundedness (every claim entailed by the context), answer relevance, and citation precision. Include unanswerable questions to measure abstention, because a system that always answers is a system that hallucinates.
sections.heading: The pipeline, and where it breaks

sections.body:
The chunk is simultaneously the unit of embedding, the unit of retrieval, and the unit shown to the generator, and those three want different sizes.

Too large and one vector represents several topics, becoming an average that matches everything weakly and nothing strongly. Too small and the chunk loses its referents: 'the limit is 30 days' is useless without knowing which limit.

What works: split on document structure (headings, sections, paragraphs) rather than blind character counts, keep tables and code blocks intact, add modest overlap so a fact spanning a boundary survives, and prepend the document title and section path so each chunk is self-describing.

Then decouple the sizes with small-to-big retrieval: index small precise chunks for focused embeddings, but expand to the parent section, a sentence window, or the whole short document before generation. Precision in search, completeness in context. Variants: index an LLM-written summary of each section, or index hypothetical questions the section answers, while returning the original text. Store a parent pointer in metadata and deduplicate when several retrieved children share a parent.
sections.heading: Chunking is the highest-leverage knob

sections.body:
Dense retrieval handles paraphrase and intent, matching 'password reset' to 'account recovery'. It is unreliable on exact strings: error code TX-4021, a specific SKU, a person's name, or jargon the embedding model never saw. BM25 is exact on those and blind to synonymy. Run both and fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines by rank position so you avoid calibrating incomparable score scales. This is one of the cheapest large wins available.

Reranking fixes the fundamental limitation of bi-encoder retrieval. In vector search, query and document are embedded independently, which is what makes it precomputable and fast, but the model never sees them together so it cannot judge whether this document answers this question. A cross-encoder concatenates the pair and runs full cross-attention, giving a much better relevance score at the cost of a forward pass per pair. So: retrieve ~100 cheaply for recall, rerank to ~5 for precision. Adding a reranker is usually a bigger quality jump than upgrading the embedding model, and it directly attacks lost-in-the-middle by ensuring what reaches the prompt is genuinely the best material.

Counterintuitively, more context often makes answers worse. Extra chunks add plausible distractors the model may prefer, introduce contradictions with no signal about which to trust, and push the good chunk toward the poorly-attended middle. Treat k as a hyperparameter to tune, typically landing at three to eight reranked chunks rather than twenty raw ones, with a relevance threshold so a query with no good matches triggers abstention instead of padding the prompt with the least-bad results.
sections.heading: Hybrid search and reranking

sections.body:
Embeddings are only comparable within the same model and version, so queries and documents must use the same model and swapping models means a full reindex. Asymmetric models with distinct query and document prefixes need those prefixes applied correctly, a very common silent bug.

Cosine similarity is preferred because magnitude mostly reflects length rather than meaning. Once vectors are L2-normalized, cosine, inner product, and Euclidean induce the same ranking, which is why most stores normalize on write and use dot product.

HNSW builds a layered proximity graph: the bottom layer connects near neighbors, higher layers are sparse with long-range edges like a skip list in metric space. Search enters at the top, greedily walks closer, drops a layer, repeats. Parameters: M (edges per node, driving memory and recall ceiling), efConstruction (build quality), efSearch (the runtime latency-recall dial). It gives excellent recall-latency curves but is memory-hungry and deletes are usually tombstoned.

Product quantization makes billion-scale search fit in RAM. Split each vector into m subvectors, k-means each subspace into 256 centroids, store one byte per subvector. A 768-dim float32 vector goes from ~3KB to ~64 bytes. Distances come from precomputed lookup tables. Recall drops, so rescore top candidates against full-precision vectors. Scalar quantization to int8 is the simpler middle ground: four times compression, almost no recall loss.

Metadata filtering must be integrated with the search, not applied afterward. Post-filtering can return zero results when the filter is selective while relevant documents existed. Pre-filtering is exact but can break ANN graph connectivity on sparse subsets. Filtered ANN evaluates predicates during traversal. This matters most because filters are often security boundaries, not relevance hints.
sections.heading: Vector index internals

sections.body:
Users write short, ambiguous, context-dependent queries. Query rewriting is the highest-value fix in conversational RAG: 'what about the second one?' has no retrievable content, so condense the history into a standalone question before embedding.

Multi-query generates several paraphrases and unions results, raising recall for ambiguous phrasing. Decomposition splits a multi-hop question into sub-questions retrieved separately, since no single chunk answers a comparison across two entities. HyDE has the model write a hypothetical answer and embeds that, which works because questions and answers have different linguistic form and a pseudo-answer lands closer to real answer passages.

Each costs an extra LLM call in the critical path, so cache aggressively and consider a small fast model. Agentic or iterative RAG is worth it for genuine multi-hop, comparisons, and exploratory queries where the right search terms only emerge after seeing initial results, but latency multiplies by rounds and spend becomes unpredictable, so route: send the easy majority down a fast single-shot path and reserve iteration for the hard minority.
sections.heading: Query-side techniques

sections.body:
Freshness. The index is a derived cache, so it needs real sync: detect changes via webhooks or CDC rather than polling, hash chunk content so unchanged chunks skip re-embedding, upsert with deterministic IDs, and hard-delete removed documents. Append-only indexes are a classic bug where the model confidently cites a superseded policy. Run periodic reconciliation comparing source and index inventories, and monitor indexing lag as an SLO, since users experience staleness as wrongness.

Access control. Never rely on the prompt as a security boundary; the model can leak restricted content and injection can override the instruction outright. Enforce in the query path via per-tenant namespaces or mandatory ACL filters inside the ANN search, resolving live group membership rather than a snapshot taken at index time. Remember embeddings are approximately invertible, so the vector store holds sensitive data, and audit-log every retrieval with user, filter, and returned IDs.

Knowledge conflict. Context-versus-parametric conflict is when documents contradict pretraining, and models do not reliably defer to context, especially against a strongly-held prior. Handle with explicit precedence in the prompt plus counterfactual evaluation where you know the right answer contradicts the model's prior. Context-versus-context conflict is usually a hygiene problem: two versions indexed, so add version metadata, prefer recency, and hard-delete on supersession. Requiring citations turns a silent wrong answer into a visible wrong source.

Structured data. Aggregation, joins, and precise numerics are not retrieval problems. Route analytical questions to text-to-SQL, where retrieval still matters but for schema subsets, column descriptions, and verified example queries. Execute through a read-only role with row limits, surface the query for transparency, and have the model narrate returned rows rather than inventing numbers. Evaluate with execution accuracy against gold result sets, not SQL string similarity.

Long context does not remove the need for RAG. It reduces chunking pressure and makes whole-document prompting viable for small corpora, but cost and latency scale with prompt length, quality degrades over long contexts so a reranked top-five often beats a 500k-token prompt, real corpora exceed any window, and permissions, freshness, and auditability need a retrieval layer regardless. The synthesis is RAG with larger, coarser, better-ranked units.
sections.heading: Production concerns

lessons.subtitle: The system most AI engineering interviews actually care about
lessons.title: RAG & Vector Search

sections.body:
Pretraining produces a next-token predictor with broad knowledge and no instruction-following. Given 'write a poem about the sea', a base model might plausibly continue with more writing prompts, because that is genuinely what follows such text on the internet. It has the capability; it has no reason to believe a poem should come next.

Supervised fine-tuning on prompt-response demonstrations closes that objective mismatch, and that stage alone gets you most of the way to a usable assistant. Preference optimization then aligns it with what humans prefer among plausible responses. Safety and refusal behavior is usually shaped in the same preference stage.

Frame it as: SFT teaches what a good answer looks like from examples; preference training teaches how to rank between answers, which is a signal demonstrations cannot express.

Data requirements are lower than people expect. LIMA showed a thousand curated examples producing strong instruction-following, supporting the view that pretraining installs the capability and fine-tuning elicits format and style. A few hundred consistent examples move a narrow task. Consistency matters far more than volume: two examples formatting the same situation differently teach the model to be inconsistent.
sections.heading: The post-training stack

sections.body:
LoRA freezes pretrained weights and learns a low-rank update, using W + BA with rank typically 8 to 64. The premise is that task adaptation lives in a low-dimensional subspace.

Why it dominates: you train well under one percent of parameters, so Adam's optimizer state collapses and a multi-GPU fine-tune fits on one consumer card. Checkpoints are megabytes, so you keep dozens of task adapters against one shared base and hot-swap them, which is a serving win as much as a storage one. Base weights are untouched, so you cannot catastrophically damage the original and can always detach. Merging BA back into W gives zero inference overhead.

Practical settings: target all linear layers including the MLP, not just query and value as the original paper did. Rank 8 to 16 for format and style, 32 to 64+ for genuinely new skills. Since the update is scaled by alpha over rank, sweeping rank without adjusting alpha changes the effective learning rate simultaneously, so set alpha to rank or twice rank. LoRA wants a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, roughly 1e-4 to 3e-4, because adapters start at zero.

QLoRA adds 4-bit NF4 storage for the frozen base, dequantizing per block during compute, plus double quantization and paged optimizers. Since frozen weights only participate in forward and gradient passes, never updates, they do not need full precision. This made 65B fine-tuning feasible on a single 48GB GPU. Cost is speed, so prefer plain LoRA in bf16 if you have the VRAM.

Prompt and prefix tuning learn continuous vectors instead of touching weights at all. The contrast with LoRA is where the intervention lives: LoRA modifies the weight transformation and merges away for free inference, while soft prompts live in activation space, permanently consuming context and adding attention cost with nothing to merge. LoRA also trains more stably. Choose soft prompts when you genuinely cannot modify weights.

Full fine-tuning versus LoRA in outcome: LoRA matches it on typical instruction tuning and moderate adaptation, and its restricted capacity forgets less of the base, which is often a feature. Full fine-tuning pulls ahead when absorbing substantial new knowledge, adapting to a distant domain, or training on very large datasets, where a rank-16 update simply cannot express the needed change.
sections.heading: Parameter-efficient methods

sections.body:
RLHF has three parts. Collect pairwise preferences, because people are far more reliable at saying A is better than B than at absolute scoring. Train a reward model on those comparisons. Optimize the policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty against the SFT reference, and that KL term is essential, not decorative, because it keeps the policy where the reward model remains a valid approximation.

Failure modes are the interesting part. Reward hacking is Goodhart's law in action: the reward model is a learned proxy, accurate near its training distribution, and PPO's entire job is to find high-reward regions, so it reliably discovers where the proxy is wrong. The tell is diverging curves, reward climbing while human evaluation flattens, with artifacts like extreme verbosity, formulaic structure, or excessive caveats. Defenses: the KL penalty as the structural control, early stopping on human evaluation rather than reward, iterative preference collection so the reward model tracks the moving policy, reward model ensembles with pessimistic aggregation, and explicit length normalization since length bias is the most common hack.

Inherited annotator bias is the other big one. People genuinely prefer agreeable, validating, confident answers, so the gradient points toward agreement independent of truth. That is where sycophancy comes from: a model that abandons a correct answer when pushed back on. It is an alignment-induced failure, not a knowledge gap, and it is insidious because it degrades reliability exactly when a user most needs a correct answer.

DPO showed the reward model and RL loop are unnecessary. The optimal policy under a KL-constrained reward objective has a closed-form relationship to the reward, so you invert it, substitute into the Bradley-Terry likelihood, and the reward function cancels. What remains is a simple loss raising the log-probability of the chosen response relative to the rejected one against a frozen reference. Two models in memory instead of four, no reward model, no sampling loop, none of PPO's fragility. Tradeoffs: it is offline so there is no on-policy exploration and data goes stale as the policy improves, it can decrease likelihood of both responses while widening the gap, and well-executed online RL still edges it out at the frontier because a reward model generalizes to novel responses while a static dataset does not.
sections.heading: RLHF and why DPO replaced it in practice

sections.body:
RLAIF replaces human preference labels with AI ones, and Constitutional AI is the version guided by an explicit written set of principles: the model critiques its own output against the constitution, revises, and those comparisons become training signal. The motivation is that human preference data is the alignment bottleneck, being slow, costly, inconsistent, and for harmful content genuinely harmful to annotators. It also has a transparency advantage, since values are written in a document you can read and revise rather than inferred from thousands of crowdworker judgments. Risks: the labeling model's blind spots get amplified, principles can conflict or be gamed, and you still need human validation that AI preferences track human ones.

RLVR, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, replaces the learned reward model with a programmatic check: run the code against tests, compare the numeric answer to ground truth, machine-check the proof. Its significance is that it removes reward hacking as a structural concern. A unit test is not a proxy, it is the objective, so you can optimize aggressively without reward drift, and that is what unlocked the recent reasoning models where long chains of thought are reinforced purely by outcome correctness and self-verification emerges without being demonstrated. Limits: it only applies where cheap verification exists, it rewards outcomes so a model can be reinforced for reaching the right answer by unsound reasoning, and a weak verifier is hackable in its own way.
sections.heading: Newer signals: RLAIF and verifiable rewards

sections.body:
Catastrophic forgetting. Sequential training overwrites weights encoding earlier capability because nothing anchors them. In LLM practice, a model fine-tuned on a narrow domain loses general reasoning or instruction-following. Three families of fix: rehearsal (mix ten to thirty percent general instruction data into the fine-tuning set, the most reliable), regularization (elastic weight consolidation, or just a low learning rate and few epochs), and parameter isolation (LoRA keeps base weights frozen, avoiding the problem structurally).

Alignment tax. Optimizing for helpfulness and preferred style can degrade other capabilities, reduce output diversity, and cause over-refusal on benign requests. Detect it by holding a broad fixed capability suite and running it before and after every alignment stage. Add two evaluations people skip: generation diversity, since preference training measurably collapses it invisibly to accuracy benchmarks, and an over-refusal set of benign-but-sensitive-sounding prompts.

Safety erosion. This is the finding that surprised people: safety alignment is shallow. A handful of adversarial examples can strip refusals, and even entirely benign task-specific fine-tuning degrades them measurably, because gradient descent preserves only what your objective mentions. So treat safety as a regression surface, run a refusal and jailbreak suite on every checkpoint, mix safety examples into training data, prefer parameter-efficient methods that move fewer weights, and layer independent runtime defenses rather than relying on model-internal alignment.

Synthetic data. Standard practice now, but unfiltered generation degrades models through error amplification, diversity collapse toward high-probability modes, and inherited bias. What makes it work is verification: execute code against tests, check math with a solver, validate against a schema, and where mechanical checks are impossible, filter aggressively with a reward model or judge. Engineer diversity deliberately by varying seed prompts, personas, and difficulty, and measure it as a first-class metric. Keep a human-authored anchor in the mixture and a fully human evaluation set.
sections.heading: The costs nobody mentions in the paper

sections.body:
Diagnose the gap first, because each tool fixes a different one.

Missing or changing knowledge, needing citations, permissions, or deletion, means retrieval. Wrong format, tone, or a weak narrow skill despite a well-engineered prompt means fine-tuning. Cost or latency too high with a large model means fine-tune or distill a smaller one, often the highest-ROI fine-tune there is. Capability absent from every available frontier model means a research project, not a feature, and the requirement should be pushed back on.

Then escalate in cost and reversibility order: prompt first because it iterates in minutes and reverts instantly, retrieval next because it keeps knowledge externally editable, fine-tuning after because it commits you to an eval harness, a data pipeline, and a retraining plan on every base model update, and training from scratch essentially never.

Hyperparameters, in order of importance: learning rate (1e-5 to 5e-5 full, 1e-4 to 3e-4 LoRA), epochs (one to three, early-stopped, since more memorizes a small dataset), effective batch size (32 to 128 sequences via gradient accumulation), short warmup then cosine decay, then sequence packing and max length for throughput. Two things that catch people: loss masking so cross-entropy is computed only on completion tokens, not the prompt, and applying the chat template exactly as it will be at inference, since a training-versus-serving template mismatch is the most confusing fine-tuning bug there is.

And validation loss is a weak proxy for quality, so gate releases on task evaluations and human review of samples, using loss only to detect overfitting.
sections.heading: The decision framework interviewers want

lessons.subtitle: SFT, RLHF, DPO, LoRA, and how to choose
lessons.title: Fine-Tuning & Alignment

sections.body:
This is the highest-leverage investment in an LLM project and the one most often skipped. Without a stable target you cannot distinguish improvement from noise, and every prompt tweak becomes unfalsifiable.

Building it also forces you to define what good means, which surfaces stakeholder disagreement while it is still cheap to resolve. Start small: twenty to fifty hand-written cases covering core use cases, obvious edge cases, and what the system should refuse or escalate. That is enough to catch most regressions, and it is dramatically better than the actual alternative, which is nothing.

Then wire it into CI so a prompt change that breaks something is caught before deployment rather than by a user, and feed every real production failure back in as a permanent regression case so the set converges on production reality.
sections.heading: Build the eval set before you optimize

sections.body:
Perplexity is exp of mean cross-entropy per token: how surprised the model is by text. Right for tracking pretraining and comparing checkpoints of the same model. Wrong as a release gate, since it is tokenizer- and corpus-dependent and measures likelihood of text rather than usefulness. A post-trained model often has worse perplexity while being far more useful.

BLEU and ROUGE compare surface n-grams against references. Open-ended generation has many valid phrasings, so a correct answer worded differently scores low while a fluent wrong answer reusing reference words scores high, and neither sees factuality. Fine as cheap regression detectors on highly constrained output, useless otherwise.

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which punishes imbalance so you cannot score well by sacrificing one. But equal weighting is an arbitrary default: F-beta weights recall beta times as much, so F2 for screening where a miss is costly, F0.5 where false alarms are expensive. Choosing beta forces an explicit conversation about the real cost ratio. For multi-class, be deliberate about macro versus micro averaging, since the choice can reverse your conclusion on imbalanced data.

Benchmark contamination undermines public scores: test items appear in pretraining data, so the score partly measures memorization, and unevenly across models so comparisons break in unknown directions. Detect via n-gram overlap searches, pre- versus post-cutoff performance comparisons, and collapse on lightly paraphrased items. The defense is private held-out sets on your own distribution.
sections.heading: Which metrics to trust

sections.body:
It is the only way to evaluate open-ended quality at scale, and every one of its biases has a specific mitigation.

Position bias: the judge favors whichever response comes first, so run both orderings and average, treating disagreement as a tie. Verbosity bias: longer, elaborately formatted answers get preferred even when they add nothing, so control for length or instruct that concision is a virtue. Self-preference: models rate their own family higher, so use a different family than the model under test. Style over substance: confident tone and nice formatting get rewarded over correctness, which is dangerous because that is exactly the failure you are trying to detect. Poor absolute calibration: a one-to-ten score clusters around seven and drifts, which is why pairwise comparison is far more reliable than absolute scoring.

The meta-point: the judge is itself a model needing validation. Measure its agreement with human labels on a sample before trusting it, and if agreement is poor, fix the rubric rather than the model under test.

Inter-annotator agreement bounds all of this. If qualified humans agree only seventy percent of the time, no metric from those labels can distinguish models closer than that noise floor. Measure with Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa rather than raw agreement, since raw agreement looks impressive on skewed distributions by chance alone. Low agreement is information about your task definition, not your annotators: usually the rubric is underspecified or two dimensions have been conflated into one score. Fix upstream with worked examples, explicit decision procedures, calibration sessions, and splitting conflated criteria.
sections.heading: LLM-as-judge, done carefully

sections.body:
For RAG, evaluate stages separately or you cannot attribute failures. Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG against labeled relevant chunks. Generation, conditioned on retrieved context: groundedness, answer relevance, citation precision, and abstention on unanswerable questions.

Groundedness is deliberately distinct from correctness. A true statement not present in the context is still a grounding failure, because the model fell back on parametric knowledge you cannot audit. A false claim faithfully copied from a retrieved document is a data problem, not a generation problem. Keeping them separate is what lets you fix the right component. Implement via claim decomposition plus NLI or judge checks, and require inline citations so each claim can be checked against its own cited chunk.

For agents, measure outcome and process. Outcome: task success against a verifiable end state in a sandbox, not the agent's own claim of success, because agents confidently report completion they did not achieve. Process: tool selection accuracy, argument validity, steps versus optimal, and recovery rate after a failed call, which you should test by deliberately injecting tool failures since brittleness on error is the most common production weakness. Add cost and latency per task, because an agent that succeeds after forty calls is a commercial failure, and an explicit safety count of irreversible or out-of-scope actions attempted. Run multiple trials and report pass rate with variance, since agent runs are noisy.
sections.heading: RAG and agent evaluation

sections.body:
Offline is fast, cheap, reproducible, and safe, so it is the iteration loop and the CI gate, but it only measures what your dataset represents. Online measures real outcomes but is slow, needs traffic for power, and exposes users to risk. When they disagree, that is diagnostic: usually metric misalignment, position bias in logged data, train-serve skew, or a latency regression eating the gain.

A sound A/B test is designed before it launches. Pre-register one primary metric tied to the business outcome plus the minimum detectable effect, run a power analysis for sample size and therefore duration, and do not peek and stop when p drops below 0.05, since that inflates false positives badly; use a sequential method if you need continuous monitoring. Randomize at the user, not the request, so experience is consistent and observations are not correlated. Define guardrails up front on latency, error rate, cost, and safety so a relevance win that costs trust is blocked. Then hygiene: check sample-ratio mismatch as an early signal that assignment or logging is broken, run long enough for weekly seasonality and novelty decay, and correct for multiple comparisons.

Production monitoring should cover more than latency and errors, because LLM systems fail quietly. Sampled judge scores on live traffic for a quality trend. For RAG: retrieval hit rate, empty-result rate, groundedness, citation validity. Behavioral rates: refusals, abstentions, escalations, since a refusal spike is invisible in error logs. Cost and tokens per request with per-tenant attribution, which catches prompt bloat and runaway loops. Input drift and new-topic detection. And feedback signals, both explicit thumbs and implicit retries, copies, and abandonment. Alert on sustained trends, not single samples, and keep a human review queue since automated judges drift too.
sections.heading: Online evaluation and A/B tests

sections.body:
Goodhart's law is the mechanism behind reward hacking, clickbait from engagement optimization, and benchmark overfitting: a metric correlates with the goal only where it was validated, and optimization pressure deliberately searches for where they diverge. Countermeasures: multiple diverse metrics so gaming one shows elsewhere, guardrails that must not regress, a private held-out set the optimizer never sees, periodic revalidation of the cheap proxy against expensive ground truth, and the cultural discipline of treating a fast-improving metric with flat user outcomes as a red flag rather than a win.

Fairness is not one quantity. Demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration are mathematically incompatible when base rates differ, except for a perfect classifier. So the work is choosing which harm dominates, and that belongs to domain experts and affected communities, with your job being to quantify the tradeoff rather than pick silently. Dropping protected attributes does not create fairness, since proxies carry the signal, and it destroys your ability to measure disparity, so keep the attribute for evaluation even when excluding it from features. Always evaluate disaggregated across groups and intersections.

Faithfulness of stated reasoning is a causal property, not a stylistic one. Test it by intervention: truncate the chain and see if the answer changes, insert a mid-chain error and see if the conclusion follows it, or add a biasing cue and check whether answers shift while the stated reasoning never mentions it. This matters because a lot of oversight strategy assumes we can read a model's reasoning, and if chains are unfaithful, monitoring them provides false assurance.

When ground truth arrives late or never, layer your signals: immediate proxies (labeled as satisfaction, not correctness), delayed-label backfill with the discipline that recent cohorts are censored, deliberately purchased human audit stratified toward high-risk cases, off-policy estimation with logged propensities, and label-free drift monitoring. Watch the feedback loop, since the model's own decisions determine which outcomes you ever observe, making your data missing not at random.
sections.heading: Structural problems you should be able to name

lessons.subtitle: The skill that separates people who ship from people who demo
lessons.title: Evaluation & Metrics

sections.body:
Training-serving skew is when a feature is computed one way in training and subtly differently at inference, typically because two code paths exist: a SQL or Spark job offline and application code online, diverging on null handling, timezone, unit, or rounding. Nothing errors; the model just receives out-of-distribution inputs and quietly degrades. It is one of the most common reasons a model that looked great offline underperforms.

Prevention is architectural: one shared implementation used by both paths, which is what a feature store provides along with point-in-time correct historical lookups. Failing that, log served feature vectors and continuously compare distributions against training, which catches skew regardless of cause.

Reproducibility needs everything that determined the output, linked to the output: code SHA, an immutable dataset snapshot or content hash (pointing at 'the users table' means your training set changes daily), full config including seeds, pinned environment including CUDA versions, and the artifact with its evaluation results. The linkage matters most: given a model in production you should retrieve exactly what produced it in one step. Bitwise determinism on GPUs is often impractical, so claim provenance plus statistical reproducibility and say which.

Distinguish the three tools people conflate. Experiment tracking records runs, parameters, and metrics for comparison. The artifact store is blob storage for weights and checkpoints. The model registry is the production interface: named models, numbered versions, lifecycle stages, approvals, and lineage, so serving asks for 'current production version' rather than hardcoding a path. The anti-pattern is deploying by copying a file out of someone's run directory, which works once and then makes 'what is running' unanswerable.
sections.heading: Skew and reproducibility

sections.body:
Batch inference precomputes predictions on a schedule and writes them to a store the application reads. Far simpler operationally, no latency SLO, no autoscaling, trivial retries, non-user-facing failures, and much cheaper because you can use large batches and preemptible capacity. Fits churn, risk, and lead scoring where inputs change slowly. Breaks when the prediction depends on request-time context or freshness in seconds. The most useful pattern is hybrid: precompute the expensive part (embeddings, candidate sets) in batch, keep only cheap ranking online.

Shadow mode sends a copy of real traffic to the new model and discards the output. Zero risk, validates error rates, real-world latency, and prediction distribution against the incumbent, but cannot measure user response. Canary exposes a small traffic percentage for real, giving genuine outcome signal at the cost of exposing users, so it needs guardrail monitoring with automated rollback. Sequence them: shadow to shake out mechanical failures, canary at one to five percent with tight alerting, then progressive rollout with the old version kept warm.

Rollback speed is decided before the incident. Keep the previous version registered and warm, make traffic switching a config change rather than a rebuild, and actually drill it. The part teams get wrong is state: reverting the model does not undo what it did. Predictions written to serving stores, actions triggered, records modified, caches holding bad outputs, and training data contaminated by the model's own outputs all need reconciliation, and you should know in advance which apply. Watch for coupled changes too, since reverting the model but not a feature pipeline change creates an untested combination, which argues for versioning them as one deployable unit.

Retraining triggers: performance-based when labels arrive fast enough, drift-based as the label-free early warning, and schedule or volume-based as a floor. Whatever fires, retraining is not promotion: evaluate the candidate against the incumbent on a fixed held-out set plus a recent time slice, gate on per-slice performance, then shadow or canary. And remember retraining fixes staleness, not bugs, so if the cause is a broken feature pipeline or label regression, retraining faithfully relearns the problem.
sections.heading: Deployment patterns

sections.body:
Continuous batching is the central throughput technique. Static batching runs a batch to completion, so one 1000-token generation makes the GPU compute padding for finished slots while new requests queue. Iteration-level scheduling evicts finished sequences and admits waiting ones every decoding step, keeping the batch full. Since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and the weight load per step is fixed regardless of batch size, packing more sequences in is nearly free throughput, often several times better than static. It requires PagedAttention to manage varying KV allocations in fixed blocks, eliminating fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing.

Prompt caching stores the computed KV state for a repeated prompt prefix. Since a large fraction of most prompts is identical across requests (system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples, a shared document), this cuts both cost and time-to-first-token substantially. It requires prompt layout discipline: cacheable content at the very start, byte-identical, with anything variable after it. Injecting the current timestamp at the top of a system prompt silently destroys your hit rate, and that is a common cause of mysterious cost increases.

GPU capacity planning is hard because capacity is a function of traffic shape, not request rate. Memory is weights plus activations plus a KV cache that scales with concurrent sequences times context length, so ten long-context users can exceed a thousand short ones and the same RPS either fits or OOMs. Throughput is composition-dependent, since a burst of long prompts consumes compute and stalls token generation for everyone streaming. And scaling is slow and coarse: instances take minutes to boot and load weights, capacity may be supply-constrained, and idle GPUs bill at full price. So plan in tokens per second and concurrent sequences, load-test with realistic joint length distributions including the tail, bound the worst case with max context and per-tenant concurrency caps, and keep a warm pool with a queue and admission control so overload degrades into queueing rather than crashes.

To serve many fine-tuned variants, do not give each a dedicated deployment, since each pins full weights and is independently underutilized. LoRA adapters over one shared base with multi-adapter batched serving (S-LoRA, vLLM multi-LoRA) lets different customers' requests share one weight load and one batch, keeping hot adapters resident and paging cold ones. First ask whether per-tenant models are needed at all, since one model plus retrieved customer context is far cheaper to operate.
sections.heading: LLM serving performance

sections.body:
Provider failures need real handling, not immediate retries which amplify outages. Classify errors and retry only transient ones (429, 5xx, timeouts), never invalid-request errors. Exponential backoff with jitter so clients do not synchronize into a thundering herd. Honor Retry-After. Explicit request timeouts, since a hung connection holds a worker and cascades. A circuit breaker so a sustained outage fails fast rather than queueing undrainable work. Then fallbacks: a secondary provider or smaller model, a cached answer, or an honest degraded experience, since a clear unavailable message beats a thirty-second spinner. Budget total retries per user request so latency stays bounded, make handlers idempotent so a retry after a timeout that actually succeeded does not double-charge, and handle mid-stream failures separately since partial output already reached the user.

Cost levers by typical impact: route by difficulty so a small model handles the easy majority; shrink prompts, since input tokens are paid on every call and trimming context often improves quality by reducing distraction; cache at both prompt and semantic levels; cap output length, since output usually costs several times input and verbose answers are often worse; batch and quantize when self-hosting; and remove the model from paths where a query, regex, or small classifier suffices. Measure cost per resolved task rather than per token, so retries and human rework count, and attribute per feature and tenant since you cannot optimize what you cannot localize.

When cost jumps with no code change, decompose: cost per request equals calls times tokens times price, so find which factor moved. Input growth means context creep or accumulating history. Output growth means a prompt change or a silent provider-side model update. Call-count growth means retries or agent loops. And check prompt cache hit rate, since something variable added near the top of the prompt invalidates the prefix on every request and can triple cost with no nearby code change.
sections.heading: Reliability and cost

sections.body:
Agents fail in the middle, so per-request logging is nearly useless. Model it as distributed tracing: one trace per user request, a span per LLM call, retrieval, and tool invocation, linked by trace ID. Each span captures the exact rendered prompt (most agent bugs are obvious the moment you read what the model actually received), the raw response, model and version, token counts, cost, latency, retries, errors, and the decision that produced the next action.

Derive metrics on top: steps per task, tool failure rates, loop detection, cost per task, sampled groundedness. Then handle the practical constraints: prompts contain user data so you need field-level redaction, retention limits, and access controls designed in rather than retrofitted when legal asks; volume is high so sample successful traces while retaining all errors; and build replay, so a captured production trace can be re-run against a new prompt or model version, which turns incidents into permanent regression tests.

ML-specific CI stages beyond normal tests: data validation on schema, types, ranges, null rates, and cardinality, since most production ML incidents are data incidents; deterministic unit tests on feature transformations where silent bugs live; a fast end-to-end smoke run on a tiny sample to catch wiring errors in a minute rather than after a four-hour job; model quality gates against a versioned held-out set with both an absolute bar and a no-regression check, including per-slice results so an aggregate win cannot mask a subgroup break; a skew check that both code paths produce identical features; and artifact integrity. For LLM apps add prompt-level regression tests and a safety suite, since prompts are code and currently the least tested part of most systems.

The silent data failures worth memorizing: schema and semantic changes where a column is repurposed so values stay plausible but meaning changes; default and sentinel shifts from null to zero; partial loads that complete successfully so every aggregate is wrong; duplicates inflating volume features; unit and timezone changes; and label pipeline corruption, the worst case, because retraining then makes the model worse while metrics computed against the same bad labels say it improved.
sections.heading: Observability and CI

sections.body:
Does this need an LLM at all? Use one for open-ended understanding and generation where enumerating rules is impractical. Do not use one for parsing structured formats, applying explicit rules, arithmetic, exact lookup, or high-volume narrow classification where a fine-tuned small encoder is orders of magnitude cheaper, faster, more consistent, and easier to test. The costs of an unnecessary LLM are nondeterminism that breaks testing, per-request cost and latency, an unbounded failure surface including hallucination and injection, and dependence on a provider's roadmap. The strongest architecture is usually narrow: use the model to convert language into structured parameters, then hand execution to deterministic code.

Self-host or call an API? APIs win on time-to-market, frontier quality, zero ops, and elastic scaling with no idle cost. Self-hosting wins at sustained high utilization, when data cannot leave your environment, when you need custom fine-tunes or unusual serving control, or when you need predictable cost and no vendor dependency. Be honest about the costs: engineering time, GPU supply, idle billing, quality gaps, and owning your own reliability and upgrades. Most mature systems end up hybrid.

Model deprecation is inevitable, so treat it as planned maintenance. Pin explicit versions rather than floating aliases, keep an eval suite on your own distribution since vendor benchmarks will not tell you what you need, expect to re-tune prompts because a prompt optimized for the old model is an artifact overfitted to it, and look beyond quality at format changes that break parsers, shifted refusal boundaries, tool-calling reliability, and token count changes affecting cost. A provider abstraction layer helps but does not give real portability; the eval suite is what actually lets you switch.

Responsible deployment requires more than accuracy: disaggregated performance across groups and intersections since aggregates hide unusable segments, human oversight with real context, time, and authority to override for consequential decisions, contestability so affected people can get an explanation and appeal, transparency about capabilities and limits since most harm comes from mismatched expectations, and post-launch monitoring with a named owner. Two shortcuts that fail: dropping demographic attributes does not remove bias but does remove your ability to detect it, and handing this to legal at the end produces documentation rather than a safer system.
sections.heading: Judgment questions

lessons.subtitle: Everything between a good model and a reliable product
lessons.title: MLOps & Serving

sections.body:
Jumping to architecture is the most common failure, because the right design depends on constraints you have not established. Ask: what user problem does this solve and what decision does it drive, since that determines the metric. How is success measured in business terms. Expected traffic now and in a year. Latency budget and cost constraints. What data exists, how it is labeled, how sensitive it is, whether it can leave your environment.

Then the question that reshapes designs more than any other: what happens when the system is wrong? A recommendation with a cheap reversible error tolerates a far more aggressive design than an automated decision about someone's account or health.

State your assumptions out loud so the interviewer can redirect you early, and sketch the simplest architecture that satisfies the requirements before adding sophistication. Justifying complexity against a stated requirement is the actual skill being assessed.
sections.heading: How to run the first five minutes

sections.body:
This recurs everywhere, and recognizing it is worth a lot. You cannot afford an expensive model over a huge candidate set within a latency budget, so you stage: a cheap recall-oriented pass narrows millions to hundreds, then an expensive precision-oriented pass scores what survives.

Recommenders: ANN retrieval over embeddings unioned with heuristic sources (trending, recently viewed, same category) for recall, then a rich ranker with cross features and user history for precision, then often a third re-ranking stage for diversity, freshness, dedup, promotions, and fairness constraints. The asymmetry to name: a recall miss at stage one is unrecoverable, since ranking can only reorder what it is given, which is why retrieval blends multiple sources.

RAG: vector plus BM25 retrieval for recall, cross-encoder reranking for precision. Entity resolution: blocking or LSH for candidate pairs since pairwise comparison is quadratic, then a pairwise classifier, then transitivity resolution via connected components, with the caveat that a loose threshold causes runaway merges where thousands of records collapse through chains of weak links. Search, ad serving, and duplicate detection are all the same shape.

Cold start breaks the collaborative half of this, so fall back to content signals: for new items, text and image features embedded into the same space so they are retrievable immediately; for new users, context (locale, device, referrer, time), onboarding preferences, and popularity priors, updated aggressively during the first session. And reserve exploration slots, because a purely exploitative ranker never shows new items, so they never get impressions, so they never accumulate data, which is a self-reinforcing trap that starves your catalog.
sections.heading: The retrieve-then-rank pattern

sections.body:
A recommender trains on data produced by its own past recommendations, so the log is not a sample of user preference, it is a sample of what the system chose to show. Consequences: popularity concentration, filter bubbles, items never shown never accumulating evidence, and offline evaluation that flatters the incumbent because logged data is biased toward its choices. Retraining more frequently tightens the loop rather than fixing it.

Countermeasures: deliberate exploration (epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, or a bandit formulation) so the log contains counterfactual information, framed as buying data rather than losing revenue; logging propensities at serving time, a small engineering decision with large payoff since without them you cannot do inverse-propensity weighting or doubly-robust off-policy evaluation; explicit diversity and novelty terms in ranking rather than hoping relevance produces variety; a small permanently randomized holdout as an unbiased measurement channel; and monitoring catalog coverage and exposure concentration alongside CTR, because a system can look healthy on short-term engagement while collapsing onto a shrinking item set.
sections.heading: Feedback loops, the failure mode people miss

sections.body:
Do not assume the model dominates. In feed ranking, feature fetching is frequently the largest and most variable slice, since scoring hundreds of candidates means fan-out reads from multiple stores, so with hundreds of reads per request your p99 is set by the slowest read nearly every time. Batched multi-get, colocation, caching, and tail-latency control matter more than shaving model FLOPs.

Candidate retrieval fans out to several sources, so its cost is the slowest source plus fusion, which argues for per-source timeouts and partial-result tolerance rather than blocking on the laggard. Model scoring for a right-sized ranker over a batch is often modest, so the lever there is candidate count. Re-ranking is cheap but sequential.

For LLM features, define the SLO precisely, since time-to-first-token and completion time need completely different optimizations, and hold it at p95 or p99 because the mean hides the experiences that generate complaints. Then: stream tokens, which is often the largest perceived-latency win; cache prompts and answers; parallelize independent stages; cut input tokens since prefill scales with prompt length; cap output since decode usually dominates; right-size the model, because better retrieval with a smaller model frequently beats a large model with weak context on both latency and quality; and use speculative decoding for a lossless 2-3x if you control serving.

Enforce with per-stage timeouts and a defined degraded path, so a slow reranker is skipped rather than breaching the SLO, and make that degradation a designed, monitored product behavior rather than an accident.
sections.heading: Latency budgets

sections.body:
Push back on multi-agent as a default. Every handoff loses context, error rates compound multiplicatively so five ninety-percent steps give sixty percent, cost and latency multiply, and debugging is harder because failures emerge from interaction. A single agent with well-designed tools is more reliable and more debuggable for most tasks.

Multi-agent genuinely wins for parallelism over independent subtasks, for context isolation where a subagent can read a hundred files and return a summary keeping the orchestrator's context clean, and for genuinely different roles needing different models, tools, or permissions. When you build one: prefer a coordinator with parallel workers over free-form agent-to-agent chat, use narrow structured interfaces rather than passing prose since prose handoffs lose or hallucinate information, keep shared state external and authoritative, cap depth and iterations and spend, and design for partial failure, because the dangerous outcome is a worker silently failing while the coordinator confidently synthesizes an incomplete answer.

For any agent taking real actions, the safety architecture is non-negotiable and the principle is that the model is not a security boundary. Tools scoped to least privilege and to the requesting user's own permissions, so a successful injection cannot escalate. Human confirmation for anything irreversible or outward-facing, showing the concrete action rather than a model-written summary of it. Sandboxed execution with no ambient credentials. Egress allowlisting, since exfiltration needs an outbound channel and rendering a model-supplied URL is sufficient. Idempotency keys and rate limits so retries do not double-charge.
