Hard caps on steps and spend. Dry-run modes for high-stakes flows. And full audit logging of every action with its trigger, because reconstructing and reversing an incident is impossible without it. Ask first whether untrusted content and sensitive capability need to be in the same session at all, since separating them eliminates a class of attack rather than mitigating it.
sections.heading: Agents and multi-agent systems

sections.body:
Structured and unstructured together: route rather than force one mechanism. Analytical questions go to text-to-SQL with schema retrieval, column descriptions, and verified example queries, executed read-only with row limits, query surfaced for transparency, model narrating returned rows rather than inventing numbers. Prose goes to RAG. Support combining both, since 'why did my bill increase' needs the policy and the actual charges. Evaluate the SQL path with execution accuracy, not string similarity.

Multi-tenancy: cross-tenant leakage is a security incident, so isolation lives in the data path and never in a prompt. Separate namespaces for the strongest guarantee and cleanest deletion, or a shared index with mandatory filters enforced in a data access layer rather than trusting call sites, with adversarial tests. Then resource isolation, since one tenant's agent loop should not exhaust capacity, and one sending very long contexts consumes disproportionate KV memory. Per-tenant cost attribution from day one, and deletion that propagates to indexes, caches, logs, and traces.

Scarce labels: ship a heuristic or zero-shot baseline first, because a system in production generates the feedback that produces labels. Then active learning to spend annotation budget on uncertain examples, weak supervision via labeling functions, transfer learning, and LLM labeling with sampled human verification. Protect the evaluation set absolutely: it must be human-labeled even when training labels are noisy, or you lose the ability to tell whether anything is improving.

Rule-based to ML migration: respect the rules, since they encode undocumented edge cases and give you both a baseline and a label source. Shadow the model, then focus on disagreements with expert adjudication, which measures readiness credibly and produces high-value labels. Take over incrementally by segment or confidence band, with rules retained as fallback and permanently for hard legal or policy constraints that should not become probabilistic.

Multiple languages: quality will be uneven because pretraining data is, so measure per language rather than reporting an average. Tokenization matters concretely, since non-Latin scripts consume two to four times more tokens, raising cost and eating context. Translate-to-English is a fallback, not a default, since it compounds errors and mangles entities. Design in tiers with explicit graceful degradation, and tell users which languages work best rather than silently serving bad output.
sections.heading: Recurring design questions

sections.body:
Asked constantly in one form or another: you have limited time and no ML infrastructure, what do you do?

Do not build the platform first. That means designing abstractions for requirements you do not understand and arriving with infrastructure and nothing shipped, which also costs the credibility needed to fund phase two.

Pick one use case that is genuinely valuable, narrow enough to finish, and tolerant of errors, preferring internal or assistive over automated customer-facing, since early blast radius is what kills programs. Minimize what you own: hosted APIs rather than self-hosted serving, retrieval rather than fine-tuning, off-the-shelf components. Invest properly in exactly two things from day one, an evaluation harness and tracing, because they make every subsequent iteration measurable and both are painful to retrofit.

Shipping is how you learn what infrastructure you actually need: where your data is broken, what your latency budget truly is, which failure modes matter. That should drive what you build second.

And handle the organizational side: instrument feedback capture at launch, set the expectation that version one is a starting point improved with real data, and pick something with a measurable outcome so you can demonstrate value and earn the next mandate. Defer fine-tuning, since without data and evaluation you cannot even tell whether it would help.

One more scenario worth rehearsing: you are asked to build something you believe will not work. Neither refuse nor comply silently. Name the specific failure mode with evidence, propose a cheap experiment that resolves the disagreement empirically, and distinguish the risk type, since a quality or ROI concern is a legitimate business tradeoff the product owner can accept, while a safety, privacy, or legal risk needs explicit escalation and sign-off. If the decision stands, build it properly and instrument it well, and write down the assumption up front so the result becomes shared learning rather than an argument about who was right.
sections.heading: The three months question

lessons.subtitle: How to run the interview, and the patterns that keep recurring
lessons.title: AI System Design

cards.explanation: A composition of affine maps is itself an affine map, so a 50-layer linear network has exactly the representational power of one linear layer. Nonlinearities are what let depth build hierarchical, non-linear decision boundaries.
cards.modelAnswer: Because composing affine maps just gives another affine map. Multiply W2 by W1 and you have a single equivalent weight matrix, so a fifty-layer linear network is exactly as expressive as one linear layer, no matter how wide. The nonlinearity is what makes depth buy you anything, letting each layer carve the space so the network can represent hierarchical, non-linear functions.
options: To keep gradients from exceeding 1.0
Without them, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear transform
To make the loss function convex
To normalize activations to zero mean
cards.question: Why do neural networks need nonlinear activation functions?

cards.explanation: Sigmoid and tanh saturate: their derivatives approach zero for large |x|, so multiplying many such terms through backprop makes gradients vanish. ReLU passes gradient unchanged for x>0, enabling much deeper training. Its cost is dead units for persistently negative inputs, which Leaky ReLU, ELU, and GELU mitigate.
cards.modelAnswer: Sigmoid and tanh saturate at both tails, where the derivative goes to nearly zero, so in a deep stack backprop multiplies many small numbers and the gradient vanishes before it reaches the early layers. ReLU has derivative exactly one on the positive side, so gradient flows undiminished and you can train genuinely deep networks. The tradeoff is dead units: if a neuron's pre-activation is always negative it gets zero gradient forever, which is why Leaky ReLU, ELU, and GELU exist, and GELU is what transformers actually use because its smoothness helps optimization.
options: It bounds activations, preventing overflow
Its gradient is 1 for positive inputs, so it avoids the saturation that shrinks gradients in deep stacks
It guarantees no dead neurons
It makes the network probabilistic
cards.question: What problem does ReLU solve compared to sigmoid or tanh in hidden layers?

cards.explanation: Backprop is reverse-mode autodiff. A forward pass caches intermediate activations; the backward pass propagates dL/d(output) backward, applying the local Jacobian at each node. Cost is roughly the same order as the forward pass, which is why it beats finite differences (one forward pass per parameter).
cards.modelAnswer: Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to the network's computation graph. The forward pass computes and caches activations, then the backward pass starts from the loss derivative and walks backward, multiplying by each node's local Jacobian via the chain rule. The key efficiency property is that it gets gradients for all parameters in one backward pass costing about the same as a forward pass, whereas finite differences would need one forward pass per parameter. The cost is memory, since you must retain activations, which is exactly the tradeoff gradient checkpointing manages.
options: A method for randomly perturbing weights and keeping improvements
Reverse-mode automatic differentiation: the chain rule applied backward through the computation graph to get all parameter gradients in one pass
An algorithm for propagating data forward through layers
A technique for updating weights without computing gradients
cards.question: What is backpropagation?

cards.explanation: During training each unit is zeroed with probability p, so no feature can be relied on alone, approximating an ensemble over subnetworks. At inference dropout is disabled and activations are rescaled (in practice via inverted dropout during training) so expected magnitudes match. Forgetting to switch to eval mode is a classic bug.
cards.modelAnswer: During training each unit is zeroed independently with probability p, which prevents any single feature from becoming load-bearing and roughly approximates averaging over an exponential family of subnetworks. At inference you turn it off and use the full network, rescaling so the expected activation magnitude matches what the next layer saw during training. Frameworks implement inverted dropout, dividing by one minus p at train time, so inference needs no adjustment. The classic bug is forgetting model.eval, which leaves dropout and batchnorm in training mode and produces noisy, wrong predictions.
options: Drops units randomly during training; at inference all units are active with activations scaled to match expectations
Drops units randomly at both training and inference
Removes the least important weights permanently
Drops training examples that produce high loss
cards.question: What does dropout do at training and at inference time?

cards.explanation: The learning rate is the single most important hyperparameter. Too large and updates overshoot curvature, causing loss spikes or divergence; too small and training is slow and can settle in sharp, poorly generalizing minima. Standard practice: warmup then cosine or step decay, tuned via an LR sweep or range test.
cards.modelAnswer: It's the step size multiplying each gradient, and it's the hyperparameter I tune first because it dominates everything else. Too high and updates overshoot the local curvature, so you see loss spikes, oscillation, or outright divergence to NaN. Too low and you waste compute, and you can get stuck in sharp regions that generalize worse. In practice I run a short range test to find the largest stable rate, then use linear warmup, which matters a lot for transformers and Adam because early second-moment estimates are unreliable, followed by cosine decay.
options: It sets batch size; too high overflows memory
It scales each gradient step: too high diverges or oscillates, too low converges slowly or stalls in poor regions
It controls how many layers update per step
It determines the regularization strength
cards.question: What is the role of the learning rate, and what happens if it's too high or too low?

cards.explanation: BatchNorm standardizes each channel using the mini-batch mean and variance, then rescales with learnable gamma and beta. It smooths the loss landscape, permits higher learning rates, and adds mild regularizing noise. It depends on batch statistics, so it degrades at small batch sizes and requires running averages at inference.
cards.modelAnswer: BatchNorm standardizes each feature or channel using the mini-batch mean and variance, then applies a learned scale and shift so the layer can undo the normalization if that's optimal. The practical wins are faster convergence, tolerance of higher learning rates, and a little regularizing noise from batch sampling. The catch is the dependence on batch statistics: it degrades with small batches, complicates distributed training since statistics are per-device, and needs running averages at inference, which is a train-versus-eval discrepancy. That's why sequence models use LayerNorm instead, which normalizes across features within a single example and has no batch dependence at all.
options: Normalizes the input dataset once before training
Normalizes each feature across the batch dimension using batch statistics, then applies a learned scale and shift
Normalizes weights to unit norm every step
Normalizes gradients to prevent explosion
cards.question: What does batch normalization do?

cards.explanation: Iterations per epoch equals dataset size divided by batch size. Batch size affects gradient noise (smaller = noisier but often better generalization) and hardware utilization. Modern LLM pretraining is often measured in tokens rather than epochs because data is seen roughly once.
cards.modelAnswer: A batch is the group of examples used for one gradient update, an iteration or step is that single update, and an epoch is one complete pass over the training set, so iterations per epoch equals dataset size over batch size. Batch size trades gradient noise against hardware efficiency: smaller batches give noisier gradients that often regularize, larger batches use the accelerator better but typically need a scaled learning rate and warmup. In LLM pretraining people report tokens seen rather than epochs, because the corpus is so large that data is visited roughly once.
options: An epoch is one gradient update; an iteration is one full pass over the data
An epoch is one full pass over the training set; a batch is the subset used per update; an iteration is one such update
They all refer to the same thing at different scales of logging
A batch is a full pass; an epoch is a single example
cards.question: What is the difference between an epoch, a batch, and an iteration?

cards.explanation: Paired with softmax, cross-entropy yields a gradient of (predicted - target), which stays large when predictions are badly wrong. MSE on a saturated sigmoid/softmax multiplies by the activation derivative, which is near zero exactly when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls. Cross-entropy is also the maximum-likelihood loss for a categorical distribution.
cards.modelAnswer: Two reasons. Statistically, cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical distribution, so it's the principled loss for class probabilities, whereas MSE implies Gaussian noise on a variable that isn't. Optimizationally, softmax plus cross-entropy gives a beautifully clean gradient of predicted minus target, which stays large precisely when the model is confidently wrong. MSE through a saturated softmax multiplies in the activation derivative, which is near zero in exactly that regime, so a badly wrong model learns very slowly. That's the vanishing-gradient-at-saturation problem cross-entropy sidesteps.
options: MSE cannot handle more than two classes
Cross-entropy's gradient doesn't vanish when the model is confidently wrong, and it's the correct likelihood for categorical outputs
MSE requires one-hot labels while cross-entropy does not
Cross-entropy is faster to compute
cards.question: Why is cross-entropy preferred over MSE for classification?

cards.explanation: Momentum accumulates an exponential average of gradients to damp oscillation. Adam adds an exponential average of squared gradients and divides by its square root, giving each parameter its own effective step size, plus bias correction for the initial steps. It converges fast with little tuning; SGD+momentum with a good schedule often generalizes slightly better in vision. AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive scaling and is the standard for transformers.
cards.modelAnswer: Momentum keeps an exponentially averaged gradient, which damps oscillation across ravines and accelerates along consistent directions. Adam adds a second moment, an exponential average of squared gradients, and divides the update by its square root, so every parameter gets its own effective step size, which is a huge help when gradient scales differ wildly across layers or for sparse features. It also bias-corrects both moments since they start at zero. The cost is two extra states per parameter, so three times the optimizer memory, and the fact that plain Adam's L2 penalty interacts badly with the adaptive denominator, which is why AdamW decouples weight decay and is the default for transformers. Well-tuned SGD with momentum still edges Adam out on some vision benchmarks.
options: Adam uses a larger fixed learning rate
Adam keeps per-parameter adaptive step sizes from running first and second gradient moments, with bias correction
Adam computes exact second derivatives
Adam removes the need for a learning rate entirely
cards.question: How does Adam differ from plain SGD with momentum?

cards.explanation: With y = x + F(x), the Jacobian contains an identity term, so backprop has a direct highway to earlier layers, avoiding the multiplicative shrinkage that kills gradients in deep plain stacks. It also makes the identity function trivially representable, so extra depth can't hurt and optimization starts from a sensible point.
cards.modelAnswer: Because y equals x plus F of x makes the layer's Jacobian identity plus the Jacobian of F, so backprop always has an unattenuated path to earlier layers instead of multiplying many small factors and vanishing. Just as importantly, it changes what the layer must learn: the identity mapping is free, so each block only needs to learn a correction, which means adding depth can't make the achievable function class worse and optimization starts from a reasonable point. Empirically it's what took networks from tens to hundreds of layers, and every transformer block is a residual stream with attention and MLP writing into it.
options: They reduce the parameter count
They create identity paths so gradients flow to early layers without repeated attenuation, and layers need only learn a residual
They normalize activations across the batch
They prevent overfitting by ensembling
cards.question: Why do residual connections make very deep networks trainable?

cards.explanation: BatchNorm's statistics couple examples in a batch, which is problematic for variable-length sequences, padding, small batches, and autoregressive inference where you process one token at a time. LayerNorm normalizes over the feature dimension of each token independently, so behavior is identical at train and test time with no running statistics. RMSNorm simplifies it further by dropping mean centering.
cards.modelAnswer: BatchNorm's statistics are computed across the batch, which is a bad fit for sequences: lengths vary so padding pollutes the statistics, batches are often small in memory-heavy models, statistics differ per device in distributed training, and at autoregressive inference you're decoding one token at a time so there's no meaningful batch. LayerNorm normalizes across the feature dimension inside each token independently, so it's batch-size agnostic and behaves identically at train and test with no running averages to maintain. Modern LLMs go further with pre-norm placement for stable deep training and RMSNorm, which drops mean subtraction and just divides by the root mean square, saving compute with no quality loss.
options: LayerNorm is cheaper to compute on GPUs
LayerNorm normalizes within each token's feature vector, so it's independent of batch size and sequence padding, and works identically at inference
BatchNorm cannot handle more than 512 features
LayerNorm makes attention scores sum to one
cards.question: Why is LayerNorm used in transformers instead of BatchNorm?

cards.explanation: Backprop multiplies Jacobians across layers or timesteps; if their norms exceed 1 the product grows exponentially, producing huge updates and NaNs. Fixes: clip gradients by global norm (typically 1.0), use residual connections and normalization, scale initialization properly, lower the learning rate, and in mixed precision use loss scaling and watch for overflow.
cards.modelAnswer: Gradients pass backward through a product of layer Jacobians, and if their norms sit above one the product grows exponentially with depth or sequence length, so you get enormous updates that blow the weights out and produce NaN loss. Recurrent networks are the classic case because the same weight matrix is applied at every timestep. My standard mitigations are clipping by global gradient norm, usually at one, which is essentially free insurance and standard in all LLM training; proper initialization like Kaiming or a residual-scaled scheme so activations neither grow nor shrink through depth; residual connections plus LayerNorm to keep the signal well-conditioned; and lowering the learning rate with warmup. In mixed precision I'd also check the loss scaler, since overflow there looks like exploding gradients but is really a numerics problem.
options: Too much regularization; reduce weight decay
Repeated multiplication by Jacobians with norm > 1, especially in deep or recurrent nets; handle with gradient clipping, careful init, and normalization
Learning rate too small; increase it
Using ReLU instead of sigmoid; switch activations
cards.question: What causes exploding gradients and how do you handle them?

cards.explanation: Convolutions assume nearby pixels are related (locality), that a useful feature detector is useful anywhere in the image (translation equivariance via weight sharing), and build hierarchy through stacked receptive fields. This slashes parameters and sample complexity versus a fully connected layer. Vision transformers drop these priors and compensate with much more data or distillation.
cards.modelAnswer: Three things: locality, since a kernel only looks at a neighborhood, reflecting that nearby pixels are correlated; translation equivariance through weight sharing, so an edge detector learned in one corner applies everywhere; and hierarchical composition, since stacking layers grows the receptive field so early layers capture edges and later ones capture objects. An MLP treats pixels as an unordered vector and would have to learn all of that from data, with vastly more parameters and samples. That's exactly the tradeoff vision transformers make: they discard the convolutional prior for a more general attention mechanism, which is why they underperform CNNs on small datasets but overtake them at large scale where the data can supply the structure.
options: Permutation invariance over input features
Locality, translation equivariance, and parameter sharing across spatial positions
Recurrence over time
Sparsity of the output layer
cards.question: What inductive bias does a CNN encode that an MLP does not?

cards.explanation: An RNN's hidden state must be computed step by step, so training can't parallelize across the sequence, and all past information is squeezed into a fixed-size vector with gradients that decay over many steps. Self-attention gives every position direct access to every other in O(1) path length and parallelizes fully across the sequence, at the cost of O(n^2) compute.
cards.modelAnswer: Two structural limits. First, an RNN's state at step t depends on step t minus one, so training is inherently sequential and can't exploit the parallelism modern accelerators are built for, which caps how much data and compute you can throw at it. Second, all history must fit in a fixed-size hidden state, and gradients decay multiplicatively across timesteps, so genuinely long-range dependencies are hard even with LSTM gating. Self-attention makes the path between any two positions length one and parallelizes fully over the sequence during training. The price is quadratic compute and memory in sequence length, which is why linear-attention and state-space models like Mamba are an active attempt to reclaim the RNN's linear scaling without losing trainability.
options: RNNs cannot represent long sequences at all
RNNs process sequentially, preventing parallelism over time, and compress history into a fixed state, which limits long-range dependencies
Transformers use fewer parameters for the same quality
RNNs require labeled data while transformers do not
cards.question: Why did RNNs give way to transformers for sequence modeling?

cards.explanation: If weights are too small, activations shrink layer by layer and gradients vanish; too large and they explode. Xavier scales variance by 1/fan_in (or 2/(fan_in+fan_out)) for symmetric activations like tanh; He uses 2/fan_in to compensate for ReLU zeroing half the inputs. Also note weights must be random, not constant, or all units in a layer compute identical gradients and never differentiate.
cards.modelAnswer: Initialization sets the scale of signal propagation. Too small and activations shrink multiplicatively through depth so gradients vanish; too large and they blow up. Xavier picks variance around one over fan-in so the variance of activations is preserved for symmetric activations like tanh, and He uses two over fan-in for ReLU because ReLU zeroes roughly half its inputs and you need the factor of two to compensate. Separately, weights must be random rather than a constant, otherwise every unit in a layer receives an identical gradient and they never break symmetry. In very deep transformers people also scale residual-branch initialization down by depth so the residual stream doesn't accumulate variance across dozens of blocks.
options: It determines the final minimum reached, since training is convex
It sets the scale so activation and gradient variance stay roughly constant across layers, preventing vanishing or exploding signal
It ensures all weights start identical for stable training
It removes the need for normalization layers
cards.question: Why does weight initialization matter, and what does Xavier/He initialization achieve?

cards.explanation: Pretrained features encode general structure, so you need far fewer labels. With very little data, freeze the backbone and train only a head (linear probing) to avoid overfitting and catastrophic forgetting. With more data or a large domain shift, unfreeze and fine-tune with a low learning rate, often with gradual unfreezing or layer-wise LR decay so early general features change less than late task-specific ones.
cards.modelAnswer: Transfer learning reuses representations learned on a large source task so the target task needs far fewer labels. The freeze-versus-fine-tune call comes down to target data volume and domain distance. With a few hundred examples I freeze the backbone and train just a head, essentially linear probing, because full fine-tuning would overfit and destroy the pretrained features. With more data or a real domain gap, medical images versus natural photos, I unfreeze and fine-tune at a much lower learning rate than pretraining used, often with layer-wise learning rate decay or gradual unfreezing so the general early features move less than the task-specific later ones. I always start with the frozen baseline because it's cheap and tells me how much headroom fine-tuning is actually buying.
options: Copying a dataset between tasks; freeze when the datasets differ
Reusing pretrained representations; freeze the backbone when target data is small or similar to pretraining, fine-tune when you have enough data or a domain gap
Training two models simultaneously and averaging weights
Transferring gradients between GPUs during distributed training
cards.question: What is transfer learning, and when do you freeze versus fine-tune the backbone?

cards.explanation: Half precision halves memory and unlocks tensor cores, but fp16 has a narrow dynamic range and small gradients flush to zero. Multiplying the loss by a large factor shifts gradients into representable range; the optimizer unscales before updating fp32 master weights. bf16 has fp32's exponent range, so it usually needs no loss scaling, which is why it dominates LLM training.
cards.modelAnswer: You do the heavy matmuls in half precision to halve memory traffic and hit tensor cores, while keeping a master copy of weights and the optimizer state in fp32 so small updates don't get lost to rounding. The problem with fp16 specifically is its narrow exponent range: typical gradient magnitudes fall below the smallest representable normal value and flush to zero, so learning silently stops. Loss scaling multiplies the loss by a large constant before backprop, shifting the whole gradient distribution into representable range, then the optimizer divides it back out before applying the update, with dynamic scalers backing off when they detect an overflow. bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range at the cost of mantissa bits, so it generally needs no loss scaling, and that robustness is why bf16 is the default for large model training on modern hardware.
options: It alternates between float32 and int8 layers; scaling prevents quantization error
Compute runs in fp16/bf16 with a master fp32 copy of weights; fp16 gradients underflow to zero, so the loss is scaled up before backprop and unscaled before the update
It trains half the layers at a time to save memory
It uses fp64 for stability in the optimizer only
cards.question: How does mixed-precision training work and why does it need loss scaling?

cards.explanation: Sequential training overwrites weights encoding earlier tasks because nothing anchors them. Mitigations: rehearsal (mix in original data), regularization such as EWC penalizing movement in parameters important to old tasks, parameter isolation via adapters or LoRA so base weights stay frozen, and lower learning rates with fewer epochs. In LLM fine-tuning, mixing in general instruction data is the standard practical defense.
cards.modelAnswer: Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on a new distribution degrades capabilities the model previously had, because gradient descent has no reason to preserve weights that encoded old behavior. In LLM practice you see it as a model fine-tuned on a narrow domain losing general reasoning or instruction-following. Three families of fix. Rehearsal is the most reliable: mix a slice of the original or general instruction data into the fine-tuning set, often ten to thirty percent. Regularization anchors you to the old solution, either an explicit penalty like elastic weight consolidation weighted by Fisher information, or just a low learning rate and few epochs, which is the poor man's version. Parameter isolation avoids the problem structurally: LoRA or adapters keep base weights frozen and put new capability in a small trainable module you can also detach, which is why it's my default when I need to preserve the base model.
options: The optimizer forgetting its momentum state after a checkpoint reload; fix by saving optimizer state
A model losing earlier capabilities when trained on new data; mitigated by replaying old data, regularizing toward old weights, or isolating new parameters
Loss of precision in fp16 accumulation; fix with loss scaling
The learning rate scheduler resetting mid-training
cards.question: What is catastrophic forgetting and how is it mitigated?

cards.explanation: Diverging curves are textbook overfitting: fix with early stopping on validation, stronger weight decay or dropout, data augmentation, more data, or a smaller model. But first sanity-check the split for duplicates and distribution mismatch, and confirm the validation transform matches inference. If both losses are high instead, that's underfitting and calls for the opposite response.
cards.modelAnswer: Diverging curves after a few epochs is textbook overfitting, so my response is early stopping with a checkpoint on best validation, then more regularization: weight decay, dropout, and especially data augmentation since that attacks the root cause rather than the symptom. If I can get more data or use a pretrained backbone, that beats all of it. Before I accept that diagnosis though, I'd validate the setup, because two bugs mimic it: a validation split that's distributionally different or too small to be stable, and a train-versus-eval transform mismatch. I'd also check the gap size in context, since a small persistent gap with still-improving validation loss is fine and not something to fix.
options: Increase model capacity so it fits the validation set too
Recognize overfitting: early-stop, add regularization or augmentation, get more data, or reduce capacity, after first ruling out a leaky or mismatched validation split
Switch the loss function to MSE
Lower the batch size until validation loss falls
cards.question: Your training loss decreases but validation loss rises after epoch 3. What do you do?

cards.explanation: Data parallel: every device holds full weights, processes a different batch shard, and gradients are all-reduced; simple but memory-bound by model size. Tensor (model) parallel: a single matmul is split across devices, requiring high-bandwidth communication every layer, so it stays within a node. Pipeline parallel: consecutive layer groups live on different devices with micro-batches to reduce idle bubbles. Large runs combine all three (3D parallelism) plus ZeRO/FSDP sharding of optimizer state.
cards.modelAnswer: Data parallelism replicates the whole model on every device, gives each a different slice of the batch, and all-reduces gradients. It's simple and scales well, but every device must hold the full weights plus optimizer state, so it hits a memory wall. Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across devices, so one matmul becomes partial products plus a collective. That communicates every single layer, so it needs NVLink-class bandwidth and normally stays inside a node. Pipeline parallelism puts different layer groups on different devices and streams micro-batches through, which communicates only activations at boundaries but introduces bubble overhead at the start and end of each batch. Frontier runs combine all three as 3D parallelism, and layer on ZeRO or FSDP to shard optimizer state, gradients, and parameters, which is really data parallelism with the memory redundancy removed.
options: They are vendor-specific names for the same sharding strategy
Data parallelism replicates the model over data shards; tensor parallelism splits individual layer matrices across devices; pipeline parallelism assigns different layers to different devices
Data parallelism splits layers; pipeline parallelism splits batches
Only data parallelism works across multiple nodes
cards.question: How do data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism differ?

cards.explanation: Normally every activation is kept for the backward pass, and activation memory grows with depth, batch size, and sequence length. Checkpointing keeps only a subset and recomputes the rest on demand, typically cutting activation memory from O(n) to about O(sqrt(n)) for roughly 30% more compute. It's the standard lever when you're memory-bound and want a larger batch or longer context, and it's mathematically exact.
cards.modelAnswer: It trades compute for memory, and crucially it's exact, not an approximation. Normally backprop stores every intermediate activation, and activation memory scales with depth times batch size times sequence length, which is what actually caps context length and batch size in large models. Checkpointing keeps only activations at chosen boundaries and recomputes the intervening forward passes during the backward pass, dropping activation memory to roughly the square root of layer count for about thirty percent extra time. I reach for it whenever I'm memory-bound rather than compute-bound, for example to fit longer context or a batch size large enough to be stable. It composes with FlashAttention, which independently avoids materializing the attention matrix, and with FSDP, and in practice you tune which layers to checkpoint rather than checkpointing everything.
options: Trades accuracy for speed by skipping some gradient computations
Trades extra compute for much lower activation memory by recomputing activations during the backward pass instead of storing them all
Trades disk space for memory by paging activations to SSD
Trades precision for memory by storing activations in int8
cards.question: What does gradient checkpointing trade, and when is it worth using?

cards.explanation: Gradient noise scales roughly as 1/sqrt(batch), so a bigger batch is a more trustworthy direction and permits a larger step; the linear scaling rule multiplies LR by the batch factor (sqrt scaling suits Adam better). But taking large steps from a random initialization diverges, so a linear warmup over a few hundred to few thousand steps is used. Beyond a critical batch size the returns vanish and you're wasting compute.
cards.modelAnswer: Gradient noise falls roughly with the square root of batch size, so a larger batch is a more reliable estimate of the true gradient and you can safely take a bigger step. That's the linear scaling rule from the large-batch ImageNet work, though for Adam square-root scaling tends to fit better because the adaptive denominator already absorbs some scale. Warmup is needed because a large step from a random initialization is exactly where the loss surface is worst-conditioned, and with Adam the second-moment estimate is also unreliable in the first few hundred steps, so an aggressive rate diverges. Ramping linearly for a few hundred to a few thousand steps fixes it. The other thing I'd mention is the critical batch size: past a point, doubling the batch stops buying you a proportional reduction in steps, so you're burning compute for nothing, and that's a measurable property of the task worth checking before scaling out.
options: Because larger batches take longer per step, so the model needs bigger updates to compensate
Larger batches give lower-variance gradients supporting bigger steps (linear or sqrt scaling), but the initially large steps are unstable, so warmup ramps the rate up
Because weight decay must grow with batch size
Because BatchNorm statistics become unstable at large batch sizes
cards.question: Why does a larger batch size often require a scaled learning rate and warmup?

cards.explanation: One-hot labels say only which class is right. A teacher's softened distribution (raised temperature) reveals that a given image looks somewhat like a similar class, encoding learned structure about the problem, often called dark knowledge. This acts as a regularizer and a variance-reduced target, so the small student generalizes better than one-hot training allows. It also lets you distill an ensemble or a much larger model into deployable size.
cards.modelAnswer: Because the teacher's output distribution is a far richer target than a one-hot label. One-hot says only which class is correct, whereas softened teacher logits say this image is mostly a husky but somewhat a malamute and not at all a truck, which encodes learned similarity structure over the label space, what Hinton called dark knowledge. That's a lower-variance, more informative gradient signal per example, and it acts as a regularizer, so a small student trained on it can generalize better than the same architecture trained on hard labels. Practically I'd use a temperature above one to sharpen that signal, mix distillation loss with the true-label loss, and note this is the main route to shipping large-model quality in a latency budget, which in the LLM world shows up as training a small model on a frontier model's outputs or full distributions.
options: The student inherits the teacher's weights directly
Soft teacher probabilities carry relative similarity information across classes, a richer, lower-variance signal than one-hot labels
Distillation increases the effective dataset size by duplication
The student uses a larger learning rate
cards.question: Why can knowledge distillation produce a student that beats training the same architecture from scratch?

cards.explanation: Work from cheapest to most expensive: validate inputs and targets for NaN/inf or corrupt rows; look for numerically unsafe ops (log of zero, division, sqrt at zero, unstable softmax or custom loss); check gradient norms just before the blowup to distinguish explosion from a numerics bug; in fp16, inspect the loss scaler for repeated overflow; and lower the learning rate or add clipping. Framework anomaly-detection modes pinpoint the offending op.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd bisect rather than guess, starting with the cheapest checks. First the data, since a single corrupt row with an inf or a NaN target will poison everything, and I'd confirm whether the failure is reproducible at the same step, which points to data rather than numerics. Second, numerically unsafe operations: log of zero in a custom loss, division without an epsilon, sqrt at zero, or a hand-rolled softmax without the max-subtraction trick. Third, I'd look at the logged gradient-norm history just before the blowup, because a norm spiking over several steps means exploding gradients, calling for clipping and a lower learning rate, whereas an instant jump from normal to NaN means a bad op or bad input. In mixed precision I'd check whether the loss scaler is repeatedly overflowing and whether moving to bf16 fixes it. Tooling-wise, torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly pinpoints the offending backward op, and going forward I'd keep gradient-norm logging and periodic checkpoints so I can resume rather than restart.
options: Restart training with a different random seed and hope it passes
Bisect the cause: check for bad input data, division by zero or log(0), fp16 overflow, exploding gradients, and too-high learning rate, using anomaly detection and gradient-norm logging
Switch optimizers from Adam to SGD
Reduce the number of layers until it stops
cards.question: Your deep model's loss suddenly becomes NaN mid-training. How do you debug it?

cards.explanation: Frankle and Carbin showed that iterative magnitude pruning can find sparse 'winning tickets' that reach full accuracy when rewound to their original init, but fail if reinitialized randomly, so both the structure and the specific initialization matter. It reframes overparameterization as providing many candidate subnetworks for SGD to find, and motivates pruning research, though finding tickets cheaply without first training dense remains largely unsolved.
cards.modelAnswer: Frankle and Carbin's claim is that a randomly initialized dense network already contains a sparse subnetwork, a winning ticket, that can be trained in isolation to match the full network's accuracy in comparable time, provided you rewind its weights to their original initialization. The striking control is that randomly reinitializing the same sparse structure fails, so it's not just the architecture, it's the pairing of structure and initialization. Conceptually it reframes overparameterization: the extra width may be less about representational capacity and more about giving SGD a large pool of candidate subnetworks to discover. Practically its impact is more limited than it sounds, because finding the ticket requires iterative magnitude pruning that trains the dense network first, so it doesn't yet give cheap training, and results are less clean at large scale. It remains the intellectual backdrop for structured pruning and sparsity work in efficient inference.
options: Random seeds determine final accuracy, so you should train many and pick the best
A dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that, trained from the original initialization, matches full performance, suggesting overparameterization mainly aids optimization
Pruning always improves accuracy by removing noise
Only the final layer's weights matter for generalization
cards.question: What does the lottery ticket hypothesis claim, and why does it matter?

cards.explanation: Perplexity is exp of the mean cross-entropy per token: lower means the model assigns higher probability to the observed text. It's excellent for tracking pretraining progress and comparing checkpoints of the same model, but it's not comparable across different tokenizers or evaluation corpora, and it says nothing about instruction-following, factuality, reasoning, or helpfulness. A model can improve on a task while perplexity worsens, which is why post-training is never gated on perplexity alone.
cards.modelAnswer: Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token, so intuitively it's how surprised the model is by the text, or the effective number of equally-likely choices it's picking between at each step. It's the right instrument for tracking pretraining and comparing checkpoints of the same model on the same data. Its limits are what matter in interviews. It's tokenizer-dependent, so two models with different tokenizers aren't comparable, and it's corpus-dependent, so the number is meaningless without saying which data. More fundamentally it measures likelihood of text, not usefulness, so it tells you nothing directly about instruction-following, factual accuracy, reasoning, or safety, and a post-trained model often has worse perplexity than its base while being far more useful. So I'd use it as a training-health signal and never as a release gate.
options: How often the model refuses a request; limited to safety evaluation
The exponential of average negative log-likelihood per token, so how surprised the model is by text; it's tokenizer- and corpus-dependent and correlates weakly with usefulness
The number of distinct tokens a model can generate; limited by vocabulary size
The average length of generated responses; limited by context window
cards.question: What does perplexity measure, and what are its limits as an LLM metric?

cards.explanation: BLEU (precision-oriented, for translation) and ROUGE (recall-oriented, for summarization) compare surface n-grams against one or a few references. Open-ended generation has many valid phrasings, so a correct answer worded differently scores low while a fluent but wrong answer that reuses reference words scores high. They also ignore factuality and coherence. Better options: embedding-based metrics like BERTScore, task-specific checks (exact match, execution accuracy), calibrated LLM-as-judge, and human evaluation.
cards.modelAnswer: They're n-gram overlap metrics designed for a world with a narrow set of correct outputs. BLEU is precision-oriented for translation, ROUGE is recall-oriented for summarization, and both compare surface tokens against one or a few references. The problem with open-ended generation is that there are many equally good phrasings, so a genuinely excellent answer worded differently from the reference scores poorly, while a fluent but factually wrong answer that happens to reuse reference vocabulary scores well. They also can't see factuality, coherence, or instruction compliance at all. They're still fine as cheap regression detectors when output is highly constrained, but for anything open-ended I'd move to task-specific verifiable checks where possible, exact match or execution accuracy, embedding-based metrics like BERTScore as a soft middle ground, and LLM-as-judge validated against human labels for the genuinely subjective dimensions.
options: They are too slow to compute at scale
They measure n-gram overlap with a reference, so they penalize valid paraphrases and reward superficial matching
They only work for classification tasks
They require human annotation for each example
cards.question: Why are BLEU and ROUGE weak metrics for evaluating LLM output?

cards.explanation: Public benchmarks are on the web, so web-scale pretraining likely ingested them, sometimes with answers. A contaminated score reflects recall of the specific items, not generalization, and it inflates comparisons unevenly since different models saw different amounts. Detection methods include n-gram overlap searches against training data, comparing performance on items published before versus after the training cutoff, and checking for suspiciously low variance on paraphrased items. The practical defenses are private held-out sets, freshly written evaluations, and canary strings, which is why teams increasingly rely on internal evals over leaderboards.
cards.modelAnswer: Contamination is when benchmark test items, sometimes with their answers, appear in the model's pretraining corpus, so the reported score partly measures memorization rather than the capability the benchmark was designed to probe. It's essentially unavoidable with web-scale pretraining, since every popular benchmark is on GitHub and in scraped forums, and it's worse than a uniform inflation because different models ingested different amounts, so cross-model comparisons become unreliable in an unknown direction. Detection approaches include n-gram overlap searches against training data where you have access, comparing accuracy on items published before versus after the training cutoff, and testing whether performance collapses on lightly paraphrased versions of the same items, which is a strong tell. The practical response is to stop trusting public leaderboards as your primary signal and build private held-out evaluation sets on your own distribution, refresh them over time, and include canary strings so future contamination is detectable.
options: Mislabeled examples in the benchmark itself
Test items appearing in the model's pretraining data, so the score partly measures memorization rather than capability
Multiple models being evaluated on the same hardware
Using a different prompt format than the benchmark authors intended
cards.question: What is benchmark contamination and why does it undermine reported scores?

cards.explanation: Offline evaluation is fast, cheap, reproducible, and safe, so it's how you iterate, but it only measures what your dataset captures and can't see user behavior or system effects. Online evaluation, through A/B tests, interleaving, or canary releases, measures what actually matters (engagement, task completion, revenue, escalation rate) but is slow, expensive, potentially risky to users, and needs traffic and statistical power. Mature teams use both: offline to filter candidates and prevent regressions, online to confirm real impact before full rollout.
cards.modelAnswer: Offline evaluation runs the model against a fixed labeled dataset before deployment. It's fast, cheap, reproducible, and safe, so it's the loop you iterate in and the gate you put in CI, but it can only measure what your dataset represents, and it can't observe how users actually behave. Online evaluation measures real outcomes in production through A/B tests, interleaving for ranking, or canary rollouts, and it's the only thing that tells you whether the change mattered, but it's slow, needs traffic for statistical power, and exposes real users to a possibly worse experience. The two disagree more often than people expect, which is itself diagnostic: a model that wins offline and does nothing online usually means the offline metric isn't aligned with the KPI, or there's train-serve skew, or a latency regression ate the gain. So I'd use offline to filter candidates and block regressions, and online to make the ship decision.
options: Offline runs on CPU; online runs on GPU
Offline scores a fixed dataset before deployment; online measures real user and business outcomes in production
Offline is automated; online is always manual
Offline evaluates the model; online evaluates the infrastructure
cards.question: What is the difference between offline and online evaluation?

cards.explanation: Building the evaluation set forces you to define what 'good' means concretely, which usually surfaces disagreement between stakeholders early and cheaply. It then gives you a fixed reference so you can attribute changes, detect regressions in CI, and avoid the trap of shipping on vibes. In LLM applications this is the single highest-leverage engineering investment, since prompt and pipeline changes are otherwise unfalsifiable, and it should include real failures from production plus rare high-severity cases.
cards.modelAnswer: Because without it every change is unfalsifiable. LLM application work is a long sequence of prompt tweaks, retrieval changes, and model swaps, and if I can't measure them I'm shipping on vibes and I'll regress things silently. Building the set also has a useful side effect: writing down what a good answer looks like forces stakeholders to make their expectations explicit, and that disagreement is much cheaper to resolve at the start than after launch. Practically I'd start small, twenty to fifty cases is enough to be useful, cover the common paths plus known edge cases and rare high-severity failures, and then continuously add every real production failure to it so the set gets stronger exactly where the system is weak. And I'd wire it into CI so a prompt change that breaks something is caught before deployment rather than by a user.
options: It's required for training to converge
Without a stable target you can't distinguish improvement from noise, and every subsequent decision becomes a guess
It replaces the need for a validation split
It guarantees the model won't overfit
cards.question: Why is a golden evaluation set worth building before you start optimizing?

cards.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which punishes imbalance between them more than an arithmetic mean would, so you can't score well by sacrificing one. But equal weighting is an arbitrary default: F-beta weights recall beta times as much as precision, so F2 suits screening where missing a positive is costly, and F0.5 suits cases where false alarms are expensive. Choosing beta forces you to state the real cost asymmetry, and for multi-class you must also choose macro (equal per class), micro (equal per sample), or weighted averaging.
cards.modelAnswer: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and the harmonic mean is the point: it punishes imbalance, so you can't get a good F1 by maximizing recall and letting precision collapse the way an arithmetic mean would allow. But the equal weighting is just a default, not a principle. F-beta lets you weight recall beta times as heavily as precision, so I'd use F2 for something like disease screening or fraud detection where a miss is far worse than a false alarm that a human will filter, and F0.5 where false positives are expensive, say auto-blocking accounts. I like that choosing beta forces an explicit conversation about the real cost ratio instead of hiding it behind a default. For multi-class I'd also be deliberate about averaging, since macro treats every class equally and surfaces poor performance on rare classes, micro is dominated by frequent classes, and the choice can change your conclusion entirely on imbalanced data.
options: Accuracy and AUC; use F-beta when classes are balanced
Precision and recall via their harmonic mean; use F-beta when one of them matters more than the other
True positives and true negatives; use F-beta for multi-class problems
Training and validation performance; use F-beta to detect overfitting
cards.question: What does an F1 score balance, and when should you use F-beta instead?

cards.explanation: Documented biases: position bias, where the first (or last) response in a pairwise comparison is favored regardless of quality; verbosity bias toward longer, more detailed-looking answers; self-preference, where a model rates its own family's outputs higher; sensitivity to formatting and confident tone over correctness; and unreliable absolute scoring, since a 1-10 scale clusters and drifts. Mitigations: randomize and swap positions then average, use pairwise comparison rather than absolute scores, provide a detailed rubric with explicit criteria, require reasoning before the verdict, use a different model family than the one under test, and validate judge agreement against human labels before trusting it.
cards.modelAnswer: The biases are well documented and each has a specific mitigation. Position bias: in a pairwise comparison the judge favors whichever response comes first, sometimes substantially, so I always run both orderings and average, and treat disagreement between orderings as a tie. Verbosity bias: longer, more elaborately formatted answers get preferred even when they add nothing, so I control for length or explicitly instruct the judge that concision is a virtue. Self-preference: models rate outputs from their own family higher, so I don't judge a model with itself and prefer a different family or an ensemble. Style over substance: confident authoritative tone and nice formatting get rewarded over correctness, which is dangerous because it's exactly the failure I'm trying to detect. And poor absolute calibration, since a one-to-ten score clusters around seven and drifts between runs, which is why pairwise comparison is far more reliable than absolute scoring. The meta-point I'd make is that the judge is itself a model that needs validation: before I trust it I measure its agreement with human labels on a sample, and if agreement is poor the judge is measuring something else and I fix the rubric rather than the model under test.
options: Judges are too strict, so scores are uniformly deflated
Position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference, style-over-substance, and poor calibration on absolute scales
Judges cannot process more than one response at a time
Judges only work for English text
cards.question: What are the main biases of LLM-as-judge evaluation?

cards.explanation: Groundedness is a conditional property: given this context, is every assertion in the response entailed by it? That's deliberately separate from correctness, since a true-but-unsupported claim is still a grounding failure (the model used parametric knowledge), and a false claim faithfully copied from a wrong document is a retrieval or data problem, not a grounding one. Separating them tells you which component to fix. Implementation: decompose the answer into atomic claims and check each against the context with an NLI model or an LLM judge, then report the fraction supported. Requiring inline citations makes this far easier to automate and audit.
cards.modelAnswer: Groundedness asks a conditional question: given exactly this retrieved context, is every claim in the answer entailed by it? I'd stress that it's deliberately distinct from factual correctness. A statement that's true in the world but not present in the context is still a grounding failure, because it means the model fell back on parametric knowledge and I can't audit or control it. Conversely a false claim faithfully reproduced from a retrieved document is a data or retrieval problem, not a generation problem. Keeping those separate is what lets me attribute a failure to the right component. Implementation-wise, the standard approach is claim decomposition: split the answer into atomic factual assertions and check each against the context with a natural-language-inference model or an LLM judge, then report the supported fraction. Requiring the generator to emit inline citations makes this dramatically easier, since I can check each claim against its own cited chunk rather than the whole context, and it also gives users a way to verify. And I'd pair groundedness with answer relevance, because a perfectly grounded answer to a different question is still useless.
options: Check whether the answer is factually true against the open web
Check whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, independent of whether it's true in general
Measure cosine similarity between the answer and the query
Count how many retrieved chunks the answer mentions
cards.question: How do you measure groundedness (faithfulness) in a RAG system?

cards.explanation: Checking repeatedly and stopping when significance appears inflates false positives badly (the peeking problem), so either fix the horizon from a power analysis or use a sequential testing method designed for continuous monitoring. Define one primary metric up front plus guardrails (latency, error rate, cost, safety) so you catch harm even if the primary metric wins. Randomize at the unit where interference happens, usually the user rather than the request, so a single user gets a consistent experience. Also watch for novelty effects, verify sample-ratio mismatch as a sanity check on the assignment mechanism, and correct for multiple comparisons if you evaluate many metrics.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd design it before launching it. Pick one primary metric tied to the actual business outcome and pre-register it, along with the minimum detectable effect I'd care about, then run a power analysis to get the sample size and therefore the duration. That last part matters because the alternative, watching a dashboard and stopping when p drops below 0.05, is the peeking problem and inflates false positives dramatically; if I do need continuous monitoring I'd use a sequential or always-valid testing method built for it. Randomization unit should be the user, not the request, so one person doesn't get an inconsistent experience and so I don't underestimate variance through correlated observations. I'd define guardrail metrics up front, latency, error rate, cost per request, and safety or escalation rates, because a change can win on relevance and lose on cost or trust, and I want that blocking. Then some hygiene: check for sample-ratio mismatch as an early signal the assignment or logging is broken, run long enough to cover weekly seasonality and let novelty effects decay, and correct for multiple comparisons if I'm reading many metrics. And I'd decide the ship criteria before seeing data, so the decision isn't retrofitted to the result.
options: Ship to 50% of users and check daily until the difference looks significant
Pre-register the primary metric and MDE, run a power analysis for sample size, randomize at the right unit, and analyze once at the planned end with guardrail metrics
Compare the first 1,000 users on each arm
Run both models on the same users and compare their reactions
cards.question: How do you set up a statistically sound A/B test for a model change?

cards.explanation: Abstention introduces a coverage-accuracy tradeoff, so a single number can't capture it: a model answering 60% of questions at 95% accuracy may be far more valuable than one answering everything at 75%. Report selective accuracy against coverage, ideally as a risk-coverage curve, and check the selectivity is meaningful by including unanswerable questions and confirming abstention rates are much higher there. Also decide the operating point from real costs, since in medical or legal settings a wrong confident answer can be far more expensive than an escalation, while in low-stakes search excessive abstention makes the product useless.
cards.modelAnswer: Abstention creates a coverage-versus-accuracy tradeoff, so collapsing it to one number hides the thing you care about. A system that answers sixty percent of questions at ninety-five percent accuracy and escalates the rest may be far more valuable than one that answers everything at seventy-five percent, and both could show similar aggregate scores depending how you count. So I'd report selective accuracy, meaning accuracy on the items it chose to answer, alongside coverage, and ideally plot the full risk-coverage curve so stakeholders can pick an operating point knowingly. Then I'd test that the abstention is actually informative rather than random: include genuinely unanswerable questions and questions outside the knowledge base in the eval set, and verify the abstention rate is much higher there than on answerable ones, because a model that abstains uniformly is just less useful, not more careful. Finally I'd set the threshold from real costs rather than a default, since in a clinical or legal context a confident wrong answer can be catastrophic while an escalation is cheap, and in a low-stakes search product over-abstention makes the feature pointless.
options: Treat abstentions as errors, since the user got no answer
Score answered and abstained cases separately: accuracy on attempted items plus coverage, and check that abstentions concentrate on genuinely hard or unanswerable cases
Exclude abstentions from evaluation entirely
Count abstentions as correct, since the model avoided a mistake
cards.question: What is the right way to evaluate a model that must sometimes abstain?

cards.explanation: Final-answer-only evaluation is fragile for agents: it can't distinguish a lucky success from a sound process, gives no signal about where a failure occurred, and hides expensive or dangerous intermediate behavior. So measure outcome (task completion against a verifiable end state, ideally checked in a sandboxed environment rather than by string match) plus process: correct tool selection, valid arguments, number of steps versus optimal, whether it recovered from a failed call, and whether it took any irreversible or unsafe action. Also track cost and latency per task, since agents can succeed unaffordably, and evaluate on trajectories with injected failures to test robustness.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd measure outcome and process, because either alone is misleading for agents. Outcome first: define task success against a verifiable end state in a sandboxed environment, so did the file actually get written, did the ticket actually get created, rather than matching the agent's own claim of success, since agents confidently report completion they didn't achieve. Then process, for two reasons: it localizes failures, telling me whether the agent picked the wrong tool, passed malformed arguments, misread a result, or looped, and it catches behavior that succeeded badly. So I'd track tool-selection accuracy, argument validity, step count versus an optimal trajectory, and recovery rate after a failed call, which I'd test deliberately by injecting tool failures and timeouts, since real environments are flaky and brittle-on-error is the most common production weakness. I'd add cost and latency per task as first-class metrics, because an agent that succeeds after forty calls and four dollars is a failure commercially. And I'd have an explicit safety dimension counting irreversible or out-of-scope actions attempted, since one destructive action outweighs a lot of successes. Given how noisy agent runs are, I'd also run multiple trials per task and report pass rate with variance rather than a single run.
options: Only the final answer, since intermediate steps don't matter to the user
Both outcome and process: task success rate plus tool-call correctness, step efficiency, recovery from errors, and cost/latency per task
The number of tool calls made per task
The perplexity of the agent's reasoning trace
cards.question: How do you evaluate an agent that takes multi-step actions with tools?

cards.explanation: If humans only agree 65% of the time, no metric derived from those labels can meaningfully distinguish models closer than that margin, so agreement is effectively a ceiling on measurement precision. Low agreement is diagnostic, not just noise: it typically means the rubric is ambiguous, the task is genuinely subjective, annotators were trained inconsistently, or the examples are edge cases. The fix is upstream, sharpening definitions with worked examples, adding a decision procedure for hard cases, running calibration sessions, and splitting a conflated dimension into separate ones. Measure it with Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa rather than raw agreement so chance agreement is accounted for, and retain genuinely ambiguous items only if you handle them as ties rather than forcing a label.
cards.modelAnswer: Inter-annotator agreement sets the ceiling on measurement precision. If two qualified humans only agree on a label seventy percent of the time, no metric built from those labels can reliably distinguish two models whose true difference is smaller than that noise floor, so I'd know up front that a two-point improvement is unmeasurable in that setup. I'd measure it with Cohen's kappa for two raters or Fleiss' kappa for more, rather than raw percent agreement, since raw agreement looks impressive on skewed label distributions purely by chance. When it's low, I treat it as information about my task definition, not about the annotators. Usually it means the rubric is underspecified, two distinct dimensions have been conflated into one score, or the task is genuinely subjective. So the fix is upstream: sharpen the definitions with worked examples of borderline cases, write an explicit decision procedure for the hard ones, run calibration sessions where raters discuss disagreements, and split conflated criteria into separate questions like factual accuracy and helpfulness rated independently. For items that remain genuinely ambiguous after that, I'd keep them but record them as ties rather than forcing a coin-flip label, because forcing labels on ambiguous data injects pure noise into every downstream comparison.
options: It measures annotator speed; low agreement means hiring more annotators
It bounds how well any model can be measured, so low agreement usually means the task or rubric is underspecified and must be fixed first
It only matters for classification, not generation tasks
Low agreement means the model is performing well on ambiguous cases
cards.question: Why does inter-annotator agreement matter, and what do you do when it's low?

cards.explanation: Pre-deployment evaluation can't cover the live input distribution, so you need continuous quality signals. Useful ones: sampled LLM-judge scores on real traffic, groundedness and citation validity for RAG, refusal and abstention rates (spikes indicate over-refusal or an upstream break), retrieval hit rates and empty-result rates, cost and token counts per request to catch prompt bloat, input distribution drift and new-topic detection, output length and format-compliance rates, plus explicit user feedback and implicit signals like retries, copy events, and escalation to human support. Alert on trends rather than single events, and keep a sampled human review queue since automated proxies drift too.
cards.modelAnswer: Latency and error rates tell me the service is up, not that it's good, and LLM systems fail quietly. So I'd add several layers. Quality proxies on sampled live traffic, running an LLM judge over a small percentage continuously so I have a quality trend rather than a snapshot from launch week. For RAG specifically, retrieval hit rate, empty-result rate, groundedness scores, and citation validity, since a broken indexing job shows up there long before users complain. Behavioral rates: refusals, abstentions, and escalations to human support, because a spike in refusals usually means either an upstream prompt change or an over-restrictive tweak, and both are invisible in error logs. Cost and tokens per request, which catches prompt bloat and runaway agent loops, ideally with per-tenant attribution. Input drift and new-topic detection, since users will ask things the system was never evaluated on, and that's where quality goes first. And feedback signals, both explicit thumbs and implicit ones like retries, rephrasings, copy events, and abandonment, which are noisier but far more abundant. I'd alert on sustained trends rather than single samples to avoid pager fatigue, keep a human review queue over sampled and flagged conversations because automated judges drift too, and feed every real failure back into the offline eval set so the same bug can't recur silently.
options: Only token throughput and GPU utilization
Output quality proxies, groundedness and citation rates, refusal and escalation rates, cost per request, input drift, and user feedback signals
Model weights checksum and container health
Nothing else; quality is validated pre-deployment
cards.question: What should an LLM application's production monitoring cover beyond latency and errors?

cards.explanation: Every metric is a proxy for something you actually care about, and the proxy correlates with the goal only within the region where it was validated. Strong optimization pressure pushes the system out of that region, into the gap between proxy and goal, which is why reward hacking in RLHF, clickbait in engagement optimization, and benchmark overfitting are all the same phenomenon. Countermeasures: use multiple diverse metrics so gaming one is visible in another, add guardrails that must not regress, periodically revalidate the proxy against expensive ground truth like human review, keep a private held-out set the optimizer never sees, and treat a rapidly improving metric with unchanged user outcomes as a red flag rather than a win.
cards.modelAnswer: Goodhart's law says that when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, and in ML that isn't a philosophical aside, it's the mechanism behind several of our biggest failure modes. Reward hacking in RLHF, clickbait from engagement optimization, and benchmark overfitting are the same thing: a metric is a proxy that correlates with the true goal only in the region where it was validated, and optimization pressure deliberately searches for the region where they diverge, because that's where the proxy is cheapest to satisfy. The stronger the optimizer, the more reliably it finds that gap, so this gets worse as our methods get better. Working around it is a set of practices rather than a solution. Use multiple diverse metrics, since gaming one usually shows up as a decline in another, and pair every optimization target with guardrails that must not regress. Keep a private held-out evaluation the optimizer never touches, and refresh it, because anything you iterate against becomes a training signal eventually. Periodically revalidate the cheap proxy against expensive ground truth, human review or real business outcomes, and treat divergence as the signal to re-derive the proxy. And culturally, treat a metric improving fast while user outcomes stay flat as a red flag to investigate rather than a win to announce, which is the discipline most often missing.
options: Because metrics always have measurement error that compounds over time
Because optimizing a proxy hard enough breaks its relationship to the true goal, so you need multiple metrics, guardrails, and periodic revalidation against ground truth
Because benchmarks become contaminated once published
Because human evaluation is more expensive than automated evaluation
cards.question: Why is Goodhart's law central to ML evaluation, and how do you work around it?

cards.explanation: The impossibility results (Kleinberg et al., Chouldechova) show that when base rates differ between groups, you cannot simultaneously achieve calibration within groups, equal false positive rates, and equal false negative rates except when the classifier is perfect or base rates are equal. So fairness is not one metric to maximize but a choice about which harm matters most, and that choice belongs to domain and policy stakeholders, not to the modeler alone. Also note that dropping protected attributes does not produce fairness, since proxies like zip code carry the information, and it removes your ability to even measure disparities. Practically: measure disaggregated performance across groups and intersections, report multiple definitions, check for disparate impact on the actual decision, and document the tradeoff explicitly.
cards.modelAnswer: Fairness isn't a single quantity you maximize, it's a family of mutually incompatible criteria, and the first job is choosing which one applies. Demographic parity asks that positive rates match across groups; equalized odds asks that error rates, false positives and false negatives, match; calibration asks that a predicted probability means the same thing in each group. The impossibility results from Kleinberg and colleagues and from Chouldechova show that when base rates genuinely differ between groups, you cannot have calibration and equal false positive and false negative rates simultaneously, except in the degenerate cases of a perfect classifier or identical base rates. That's a mathematical fact, not an engineering shortfall, so the real work is deciding which harm dominates in this context, and that's a decision for domain experts, affected communities, and legal stakeholders, with my job being to make the tradeoff explicit and quantified rather than to pick silently. Two practical points I'd add. Dropping protected attributes does not create fairness, since proxies like zip code, name, or purchase history carry the signal, and it destroys your ability to measure disparity at all, so I'd keep the attribute for evaluation even where I exclude it from features. And I'd evaluate disaggregated performance across groups and intersections rather than aggregates, because a strong overall number routinely conceals a group where the model is unusable, and I'd measure the disparity in the actual downstream decision and its consequences, not just in model output.
options: Measure accuracy per group; a fair model has equal accuracy everywhere
Choose among definitions like demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration, which are mathematically incompatible except in degenerate cases, so the choice must be justified by context
Remove protected attributes from the features, which guarantees fairness
Fairness is a legal question, not a measurable property
cards.question: How do you evaluate fairness, and why can't you satisfy all fairness definitions at once?

cards.explanation: Effective red-teaming starts from a threat model: who would attack this, for what gain, and what's the worst realistic outcome given the system's actual capabilities and data access. From there, cover categories deliberately (harmful content, prompt injection including indirect via retrieved documents and tool output, data exfiltration and PII leakage, permission escalation, denial of wallet, and application-specific misuse), use both humans, who find creative and culturally-specific attacks, and automated generation, which gives scale and regression coverage. Then treat findings like security bugs: reproduce, triage by severity, fix, and add a regression test, so the same attack can't return. Crucially it must be continuous, since every prompt change, tool addition, or model upgrade can reopen a hole, and public jailbreak lists are a floor, not a substitute for attacks tailored to your system.
cards.modelAnswer: It starts with a threat model rather than a prompt list, because what matters depends entirely on what the system can do. An agent with database write access and email sending has a completely different worst case than a documentation chatbot, so I'd ask who would attack this, for what gain, and what the maximum realistic damage is given the actual permissions and data reachable. From there I'd cover categories deliberately: harmful content generation, prompt injection with emphasis on the indirect path through retrieved documents and tool outputs since that's the one people under-test, data exfiltration and PII leakage including through the model repeating context it shouldn't, permission escalation via tools, resource exhaustion or denial of wallet, and misuse specific to the domain. Method-wise I'd combine humans and automation: humans find creative, culturally-specific, and multi-turn attacks that automated generators miss, while automated attack generation gives scale and, more importantly, a regression suite.
