Then the process discipline, which is where most efforts fail: findings get reproduced, severity-triaged, fixed, and converted into a permanent regression test, and the suite runs on every prompt change, new tool, and model upgrade, because any of those can reopen a hole that was closed. I'd also involve people outside the build team, since builders share blind spots with the system they designed, and I'd treat published jailbreak lists as a baseline floor rather than the actual test, since attacks tailored to my specific application and data are what a real adversary would use.
options: Running a public list of jailbreak prompts once before launch
Systematic adversarial testing across a threat model, with diverse testers, automated attack generation, tracked findings, and continuous re-testing after every change
Relying on the model provider's safety training
Testing only the highest-severity attack category to save time
cards.question: What makes a good red-teaming process for an LLM application?

cards.explanation: When measurements and users disagree, trust the users and suspect the measurement. Typical causes: the eval set was built from imagined or clean queries while real users are terse, ambiguous, multi-turn, and off-topic; the metric measures format compliance rather than usefulness; the eval covers the happy path but not the long tail where most complaints originate; complaints concentrate in a subgroup or use case the aggregate score hides; or the problem isn't quality at all but latency, tone, UX, or unmet expectations. The path is to gather real failing sessions, read them, build a taxonomy of failure modes with frequencies, then rebuild the eval set to mirror that distribution and add the specific failures as regression cases. Reading raw transcripts is consistently the highest-yield diagnostic step and the one teams skip.
cards.modelAnswer: When users and metrics disagree, I trust the users and treat the metric as the thing that's broken. My path is to get real data before theorizing: pull a sample of actual failing sessions, ideally with the complaint attached, and read the transcripts end to end. That sounds unglamorous but it's consistently the highest-yield step and the one teams skip in favor of tweaking prompts. Then I'd build a failure taxonomy with frequencies, so I'm fixing the common failure rather than the most memorable one. The usual causes I'd be looking for: an eval set built from clean invented queries while real users write terse ambiguous multi-turn messages, so my test distribution never matched reality; a metric that rewards format compliance and looks like quality but isn't; happy-path coverage with no long tail, which is where complaints come from by definition; a subgroup or use case where the system is bad that the aggregate score averages away, which I'd check by disaggregating; and the possibility that quality is genuinely fine and the complaint is about latency, tone, or a mismatch between what the UI promised and what the feature does, in which case the fix isn't in the model at all. Then I'd rebuild the eval set from that production distribution and add every specific failure as a regression case, so the eval becomes something that would have caught this. And I'd set up sampled ongoing review so the next gap surfaces from monitoring rather than from complaints.
options: Increase the eval set size and retest
Assume the eval set is unrepresentative: sample real failing conversations, categorize the failures, and rebuild the eval set from production reality
Switch to a larger model
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt
cards.question: Your LLM feature scores well on your eval set but users complain. What's the diagnostic path?

cards.explanation: A logically coherent explanation can still be a post-hoc rationalization rather than the cause of the answer, so faithfulness has to be tested causally. Standard probes: truncate or corrupt the chain of thought and see whether the answer changes as it should; insert a mistake mid-chain and check whether the conclusion follows the error or ignores it; add a biasing cue such as suggesting an answer and see whether accuracy shifts while the stated reasoning never mentions the cue (evidence of an unstated influence); and paraphrase the question to test stability. This matters because faithfulness determines whether chain-of-thought can be used for oversight, and Anthropic's work has shown models can be influenced by features they don't verbalize, which means a readable chain is not automatically an audit trail.
cards.modelAnswer: The key insight is that faithfulness is a causal property, not a stylistic one, so you can't assess it by reading. A fluent, logically valid chain can be a post-hoc rationalization produced alongside an answer that was actually determined by something else entirely. So I'd test it by intervention. Truncate the chain and see whether the answer changes, since if the model reaches the same conclusion without the reasoning, the reasoning wasn't doing the work. Insert a deliberate error mid-chain and check whether the conclusion follows the corrupted step or silently ignores it. Most tellingly, add a biasing cue, for example hinting that the answer is B or embedding a suggestion in the prompt, and check whether the model's answers shift while its stated reasoning never mentions the cue, which is direct evidence of an unverbalized influence, and that's the experimental design in the Anthropic and related faithfulness work. Paraphrase invariance is a weaker but useful signal too. Why it matters: a lot of oversight strategy assumes we can read a model's reasoning to catch bad behavior, and that assumption is only as good as faithfulness, so if chains are unfaithful, monitoring them provides false assurance rather than safety. Practically it also means I wouldn't present a chain of thought to users as an explanation of why the system decided something unless I'd measured that it actually is one.
options: Check whether the reasoning is logically valid and well-written
Perturb the inputs or the reasoning and test whether the answer changes as the stated reasoning implies it should
Compare the reasoning trace against a human expert's explanation
Measure the length of the chain of thought
cards.question: How do you evaluate whether a model's stated reasoning is faithful to its actual computation?

cards.explanation: Model upgrades break evaluation in specific ways: prompts tuned for the old model may underperform on the new one, so a fair comparison needs prompt re-optimization per model rather than reusing an artifact overfitted to the predecessor; output formats shift, so brittle string-matching graders report false regressions; and if your judge model is upgraded at the same time as the model under test, your measuring instrument and subject move together and results are uninterpretable. So: pin the judge version explicitly and change it as its own controlled experiment; make graders robust or structured (function calling, JSON schema) so formatting differences don't masquerade as quality changes; version the dataset, prompts, and grader config together and store them with results so any number is reproducible; keep the suite behind a stable interface so swapping models is a config change; run it in CI on every change; and separate capability tests, which should be portable, from format-compliance tests, which are model-specific. Also plan to add hard cases over time as models saturate the old ones, and re-baseline deliberately rather than silently.
cards.modelAnswer: The failure modes on upgrade are specific, so I'd design against each. First, prompts overfit to the old model: a prompt tuned over months for model N may be actively suboptimal for model N plus one, so comparing them with the same prompt understates the new model. A fair evaluation allows per-model prompt adaptation, and I'd version prompts per model rather than treating one as canonical. Second, brittle graders: exact-string matching reports regressions when the new model formats an equally correct answer differently, so I'd use structured output like tool calls or a JSON schema, or a semantic grader, so I'm measuring content not formatting. Third, and this one bites people, the judge model moving at the same time as the model under test. If both upgrade together, the instrument and the subject changed simultaneously and the delta is uninterpretable, so I pin the judge version explicitly, treat changing it as its own controlled experiment with overlap measurement, and record it alongside every result. Beyond that, the engineering: version dataset, prompts, grader config, and judge together and store them with results so any historical number is reproducible; put the suite behind a stable interface so swapping a model is a config change rather than a rewrite; and run it in CI on every prompt or pipeline change, not just at upgrade time. I'd separate portable capability tests from model-specific format tests, since those age differently. And I'd expect saturation: as models improve they'll max out the original set, so I'd continuously add harder cases and production failures, and re-baseline deliberately with a documented note rather than letting the comparison drift silently.
options: Freeze the prompts and scores so results are comparable forever
Version prompts, data, and judges together; separate capability from format checks; keep the suite in CI with a stable interface and re-baseline deliberately
Re-create the suite from scratch for each new model
Evaluate only on public benchmarks, which are model-agnostic
cards.question: How do you build an evaluation suite that survives model upgrades?

cards.explanation: Arena-style Elo captures something real that static benchmarks miss (open-ended human preference on live traffic) but it has structural limits. The prompt distribution reflects arena users, skewing toward casual, English, single-turn queries rather than your domain's long documents, tool use, or structured output. Preference conflates substance with style, so formatting, verbosity, and confident tone are rewarded, and models can be tuned for exactly that. Elo compresses many dimensions into one scalar, hiding that model A is better at code while B is better at summarization, and it ignores cost, latency, context length, rate limits, and licensing, which often dominate real decisions. Ties and small rating gaps are frequently within noise. The right use is as a prior for which candidates to shortlist, followed by evaluation on your own task-specific set, which is the only thing that reflects your users.
cards.modelAnswer: Arena-style leaderboards measure something genuinely valuable that static benchmarks miss, which is open-ended human preference on live queries rather than multiple-choice recall, and they're contamination-resistant because prompts are fresh. But there are structural limits that make them a poor sole basis for model selection. The prompt distribution is the arena's users, which skews casual, English, single-turn, and short, while my production traffic might be long documents, tool-calling, structured extraction, or a non-English language, and rankings genuinely reorder across those slices. Preference conflates substance with style: formatting, length, and confident tone are rewarded, so a model tuned to be pleasant can outrank a more accurate one, and that's an optimization target labs are aware of. A single Elo compresses many capabilities into one scalar, hiding that one model leads on code and another on summarization, so the aggregate can be irrelevant to my use case even when it's accurate. It says nothing about cost, latency, context length, rate limits, or licensing, which in my experience decide production choices at least as often as quality. And small rating gaps are frequently inside the confidence interval, so reading a three-point difference as meaningful is a mistake. So I'd use leaderboards the way I'd use any prior: to shortlist two or three candidates cheaply, then decide with my own evaluation set on my own distribution, including cost and latency measurements, because that's the only comparison that reflects my users.
options: They are the most reliable signal available and should drive model selection
They measure aggregate human preference on a particular prompt distribution, which conflates style with substance and may not match your task, users, or constraints
They are unreliable only because of vote manipulation
They cannot compare models of different sizes
cards.question: What are the practical limits of leaderboard-style comparisons like Chatbot Arena?

cards.explanation: Summarization has no single correct output, so reference overlap penalizes valid alternatives and rewards copying, and human-written references are themselves inconsistent and sometimes unfaithful. Better practice is dimensional evaluation. Faithfulness is the priority since hallucinated details are the dominant real-world failure, and it's checkable without references by testing entailment of each summary claim against the source. Coverage or relevance needs a notion of what mattered, which you can operationalize with a human-extracted list of key points or a question-answering approach: generate questions from the source and check the summary answers them. Coherence and conciseness suit rubric-based LLM or human judging with pairwise comparison. Also match the evaluation to the use case, since an executive brief and a clinical handoff have different priorities, and include hard cases like conflicting sources and very long documents.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd stop treating it as a single scored task and decompose it, because summarization has many valid outputs and any reference-overlap metric penalizes good summaries that differ from the reference while rewarding ones that copy phrasing, and human references are themselves inconsistent and sometimes contain unsupported claims. So, dimensions. Faithfulness first, since hallucinated or subtly distorted details are the dominant real-world failure and the one that actually causes harm; it's also the easiest to evaluate without references, by decomposing the summary into claims and checking entailment against the source with an NLI model or a judge. Coverage second, which requires defining what mattered: I'd either have humans extract key points per document and check inclusion, or use the question-based approach of generating questions from the source and testing whether the summary answers them, which scales better. Then coherence and conciseness, which are genuinely subjective and suit rubric-based judging with pairwise comparison rather than absolute scores. Crucially I'd anchor the whole thing to the use case, because what counts as a good summary of a legal filing for an attorney differs completely from a support-ticket digest, so I'd write the rubric with the actual downstream user and include the failure modes that matter to them. And I'd build the hard cases in deliberately: sources that contradict themselves, documents far longer than the context window, and content where omission is itself misleading, since those are where systems break and where average-case metrics say nothing.
options: ROUGE against a single human reference is the accepted standard
Evaluate dimensions separately: faithfulness to the source, coverage of key information, coherence, and conciseness, using entailment checks and rubric-based judging rather than reference overlap
Measure compression ratio and readability scores
Have the model summarize its own summary and check consistency
cards.question: How should you evaluate summarization systems given that references are unreliable?

cards.explanation: There's rarely a single right model, there's a frontier: small model with strong retrieval, mid model with reranking, large model with a short prompt, plus levers like caching, batching, quantization, distillation, and routing easy queries to a cheap model with escalation. Proper evaluation measures quality, cost, and latency together for each configuration, because they trade against each other (more retrieved context raises both quality and cost; caching cuts cost only for repeated prefixes). Cost must be computed per resolved task, not per token, since a cheap model that needs three retries or produces work a human must fix is not cheap. Then the choice depends on the value of marginal quality: in a support deflection flow a few points of accuracy may be worth a lot, while for internal draft generation it may not. Also model the volume, since a fraction of a cent per call becomes material at millions of calls, and watch that cost per request can creep as prompts grow.
cards.modelAnswer: The framing I'd push is that there isn't one right answer, there's a frontier of configurations, and my job is to map it and then let the product decide the operating point. Configurations aren't just model choices: a small model with excellent retrieval and reranking often beats a large model with mediocre context at a fraction of the cost, and there are orthogonal levers like prompt caching, batching, quantization, distilling a fine-tuned small model, and routing where a cheap model handles the easy majority and escalates hard cases. So I'd measure quality, cost, and latency jointly for each candidate configuration rather than optimizing one at a time, since they interact, more context raises quality and cost together. Two measurement details matter a lot. Cost should be per resolved task, not per token: a cheap model that needs three retries, or that produces output a human has to fix, isn't cheap, and per-token pricing hides that completely. And latency should be reported at p95 or p99 with time-to-first-token separated from completion, because that's what users feel. Then the decision is economic: what is a marginal point of accuracy worth here? In a support-deflection flow where each contained ticket saves real money, quite a lot; for an internal draft-generation tool, very little, and the cheap fast option wins. I'd also model volume explicitly, since a difference of a fraction of a cent per call is irrelevant at a thousand calls a day and dominant at ten million, and I'd monitor cost per request over time because prompts and context reliably grow, so a configuration that penciled out at launch can quietly stop making sense.
options: Pick the cheapest model that passes a minimum quality bar
Map the full frontier of options against quality, cost, and latency, then choose an operating point from the actual value of quality in that use case
Always choose the highest-quality model, since quality drives adoption
Compare per-token prices across providers
cards.question: What does it mean to evaluate cost-quality tradeoffs properly for an LLM feature?

cards.explanation: Delayed feedback is the norm: loan defaults take months, medical outcomes longer, and many generative outputs have no natural label at all. The approach is layered. Use immediate proxies (user retries, edits, copy actions, escalations, dwell time), knowing they measure satisfaction rather than correctness. Backfill true labels as they arrive and evaluate cohorts retrospectively, keeping the delay in mind so a recent cohort is not yet comparable. Buy ground truth deliberately on a sample through human audit, stratified toward high-risk cases so review effort goes where errors are costly. Use off-policy or counterfactual estimation with logged propensities when the system was a ranking or decision policy, since naive replay of logged data is biased by what the old policy chose to show. And monitor label-free signals like input drift and prediction distribution shift as early warnings. Throughout, state the bias of each signal rather than presenting proxies as accuracy, and remember feedback loops: the model's own decisions shape which outcomes you ever observe, so unshown cases are missing not at random.
cards.modelAnswer: This is the normal case rather than an edge case, so I'd build a layered measurement strategy and be explicit about what each layer can and can't tell me. Immediate proxies first: retries, rephrasings, edits to the output, copy events, thumbs, escalation to a human, abandonment. They're available in seconds and they're genuinely informative about satisfaction, but they measure satisfaction, not correctness, and I'd say so rather than labeling them accuracy. Second, delayed-label backfill: as true outcomes arrive I evaluate cohorts retrospectively, with the discipline that a recent cohort is censored and not yet comparable to an older one, which is a mistake I've seen produce fake regressions. Third, buy ground truth deliberately on a sample through human audit, stratified toward high-risk and high-uncertainty cases so review effort concentrates where errors are expensive rather than spreading uniformly. Fourth, where the system is making decisions or ranking, use off-policy estimation with logged propensities, because naive replay of logged data is biased by what the previous policy chose to show. And fifth, label-free monitoring, input drift and prediction distribution shift, as the early warning that something changed before any label could tell me. The subtlety I'd flag is the feedback loop: for decisions, the model's own choices determine which outcomes you ever observe, so rejected applicants never generate a repayment label and your data is missing not at random. That's a selection bias that gets worse over time, and the standard remedies are deliberate exploration, holding out a small randomized control slice, or accepting some cases you'd have rejected specifically to keep the measurement honest, which is a cost worth arguing for explicitly.
options: Wait for labels before making any quality claims
Combine proxy metrics, delayed-label backfilling, targeted human audits, and counterfactual/off-policy estimation, being explicit about each one's bias
Assume performance is unchanged until proven otherwise
Use the model's own confidence as the quality metric
cards.question: How do you evaluate a system where ground truth arrives late or never?

cards.explanation: The request is reasonable, since decisions need a summary, but a bare number invites overconfidence and Goodhart effects. The professional response is to give a headline metric chosen because it maps to the decision being made, always with an uncertainty interval so people can tell a real difference from noise, plus a small set of guardrails that must not regress (safety, latency, cost, worst-subgroup performance). State the evaluation's scope and known blind spots in plain language, since undisclosed limitations become credibility problems when they surface later. Show disaggregated results when an aggregate hides a materially bad subgroup, because that is exactly the situation where a single number misleads. And frame it as a decision recommendation with its conditions rather than a score, which is usually what stakeholders actually wanted.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd treat the request as legitimate rather than something to resist, because decisions do need a summary, and answering with it depends is not useful to someone who has to allocate resources. So I'd give a headline number, chosen specifically because it maps onto the decision being made rather than because it's the most flattering, and I'd attach three things to it. A confidence interval, so the audience can distinguish a real improvement from noise, which is the single most common way single-number reporting misleads. A short list of guardrails that did not regress, safety, latency, cost, and worst-subgroup performance, because a headline win alongside a safety regression is not a win and stakeholders deserve to see that explicitly. And a plain-language statement of what the evaluation does not cover, since undisclosed limitations always surface later and cost more credibility than they would have cost to disclose. If an aggregate conceals a materially bad subgroup I'd show the disaggregation whether or not it was asked for, since that's precisely the case where a single number causes a bad decision. And I'd frame the whole thing as a recommendation with conditions, ship to this segment, monitor these two signals, revisit if this assumption breaks, because in my experience that's what the person actually wanted when they asked for one number, and it keeps me honest about uncertainty without hiding behind it.
options: Give them the single most favorable metric to keep the message simple
Provide a primary metric tied to the business decision, with confidence intervals, guardrails, and named limitations, refusing to let one number stand alone
Refuse to summarize, since all metrics are flawed
Report the average of all your metrics
cards.question: You must present an evaluation to stakeholders who want one number. How do you handle it?

cards.explanation: You can't wait for data, and public benchmarks won't reflect your task, so bootstrap deliberately. Start by writing down what success means with the people who own the outcome, then hand-author 20-50 cases spanning the core use cases, obvious edge cases, and things the system should refuse or escalate. That small set is enough to catch most regressions and it forces disagreements into the open early. Add adversarial and safety cases from a threat model, and use synthetic generation to expand coverage while spot-checking quality, since unvalidated synthetic evals measure the generator's assumptions. Wire it into CI immediately so every prompt change is checked, and pick graders that are as automatic as possible, with human review reserved for the subjective dimensions. Then plan the transition: instrument logging and feedback from day one, run a closed alpha to harvest real queries, and systematically migrate the eval set toward the production distribution, adding every real failure as a permanent regression case. Also define the launch gates and rollback criteria before launch rather than negotiating them under pressure afterward.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd bootstrap deliberately rather than either waiting for data or trusting public benchmarks. Step one is a conversation, not code: sit with whoever owns the outcome and write down concretely what a good response looks like, what an unacceptable one looks like, and what the system should refuse or escalate. That surfaces stakeholder disagreement while it's still cheap, and it usually changes the product spec. Step two, hand-author twenty to fifty cases covering the main use cases, obvious edge cases, and the refusal and abstention behaviors. That feels small but it catches the majority of regressions and it's dramatically better than nothing, which is the actual alternative. Step three, add adversarial and safety cases derived from a threat model of what the system can touch, since those are the failures that are expensive to discover publicly. Step four, expand coverage with synthetic generation, but spot-check it by hand, because an unvalidated synthetic eval measures my generator's assumptions rather than reality. Then the engineering: prefer graders that run automatically, structured output checks and verifiable assertions where possible, reserve LLM judging for genuinely subjective dimensions and validate the judge against my own labels, and wire the whole suite into CI from the first commit so no prompt change ships unmeasured. Finally, plan the handoff to reality explicitly, since the hand-written set is scaffolding: instrument logging and feedback capture before launch, run a closed alpha specifically to harvest real queries, and then systematically shift the eval distribution toward production, adding every real failure as a permanent regression case. And I'd get launch gates and rollback criteria agreed before launch, because negotiating them during an incident goes badly.
options: Launch first and build evaluation from real traffic once it exists
Bootstrap with hand-written cases from stakeholder expectations and domain experts, add adversarial and safety cases, wire it into CI, then progressively replace it with production reality
Use public benchmarks until you have proprietary data
Rely on the model provider's benchmark scores
cards.question: How would you design an evaluation strategy for a brand-new LLM product with no data and no users?

cards.explanation: Pretraining gives a next-token predictor with broad knowledge but no instruction-following. SFT on curated prompt-response demonstrations teaches it to follow instructions and adopt a format. Preference optimization then pushes it toward outputs humans prefer, using either a reward model plus PPO (RLHF) or a direct method like DPO. Safety and refusal behavior is typically shaped in the same preference stage or a dedicated pass.
cards.modelAnswer: Pretraining produces a raw next-token predictor: it has broad knowledge but will happily continue your question with more questions rather than answer it. Supervised fine-tuning on curated prompt-response pairs teaches instruction-following and response format, and that stage alone gets you most of the way to a usable assistant. Then preference optimization aligns it with what humans actually prefer among plausible responses, either classic RLHF with a learned reward model and PPO, or a direct method like DPO that skips the reward model. Safety behavior, refusals and tone, is usually shaped in that same preference stage with targeted data. The key intuition is that SFT teaches the model what a good answer looks like from examples, while preference training teaches it to rank between answers, which is a signal you can't express in demonstrations.
options: Pretraining, quantization, deployment
Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, then preference optimization (RLHF or DPO), often with further safety tuning
Instruction tuning, then pruning, then distillation
Reward modeling, then pretraining, then SFT
cards.question: What are the standard stages of post-training an LLM?

cards.explanation: Prompting is faster to iterate, needs no data pipeline, and is easy to change, so it's always the first move. Fine-tune when you've hit a ceiling with a well-engineered prompt and few-shot examples and you need reliable structured output, a consistent voice, a narrow skill the base model does poorly, or shorter prompts (dropping a long instruction block cuts cost and latency). Fine-tuning is a poor way to inject facts; that's what retrieval is for.
cards.modelAnswer: I always start with prompting because the iteration loop is minutes rather than days and it needs no data collection. I move to fine-tuning when specific conditions hold: prompting has plateaued even with good few-shot examples, I need highly consistent format or tone that a prompt only gets right ninety percent of the time, the task is a narrow skill the base model handles poorly, or I want to eliminate a long instruction block from every request, which for high-volume traffic is a real cost and latency win since I can then use a smaller model. What I don't fine-tune for is knowledge. Facts belong in retrieval, because they change, need attribution, and require permissions. The framing I'd use is that fine-tuning changes behavior and retrieval changes knowledge, and most production systems need both.
options: Whenever accuracy is below target, since fine-tuning always beats prompting
When you need consistent format or behavior, a specialized skill, lower latency and cost per call, or prompting has plateaued with good examples
Only when the base model has fewer than 7B parameters
When you need the model to know new facts
cards.question: When should you fine-tune instead of prompt engineering?

cards.explanation: LoRA assumes the weight update needed for adaptation is low-rank, so instead of updating W it learns W + BA where B is d-by-r and A is r-by-k with r typically 8-64. You train maybe 0.1-1% of the parameters, so optimizer state and memory drop enormously, checkpoints are megabytes not gigabytes, base weights stay intact (so no catastrophic forgetting of the base), and adapters can be swapped or merged at inference with no added latency once merged.
cards.modelAnswer: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and learns a low-rank update instead: for a weight matrix W you learn two small matrices B and A and use W plus B times A, with rank typically eight to sixty-four. The premise is that task adaptation lives in a low-dimensional subspace, so you don't need to move all the weights. The practical consequences are why everyone uses it. You train well under one percent of the parameters, so optimizer state, which for Adam is two extra copies per trainable parameter, collapses and a fine-tune that needed multiple A100s fits on one consumer GPU. Checkpoints are megabytes, so you can keep dozens of task adapters and hot-swap them against one shared base, which is a serving win as well as a storage one. The base weights are untouched, so you can't catastrophically damage the original model and can always detach. And once you merge B times A back into W there's zero inference overhead. The tradeoffs are that at very high data volumes full fine-tuning still edges it out, and rank plus which modules you target are hyperparameters that matter.
options: A compression method that prunes attention heads
Low-rank adapters: freeze base weights and train small matrices B*A whose product is added to chosen weight matrices, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude
A learning rate schedule optimized for adapters
A technique for merging multiple models by weight averaging
cards.question: What is LoRA and why is it so widely used?

cards.explanation: The base weights are frozen in LoRA, so they only need to be accurate enough for forward passes and gradient flow, not for updates. QLoRA stores them in 4-bit NormalFloat, dequantizing per block during compute, and adds double quantization plus paged optimizers. Combined with LoRA adapters in bf16, this makes fine-tuning a 65B model feasible on a single 48GB GPU with quality close to 16-bit fine-tuning.
cards.modelAnswer: QLoRA's insight is that since LoRA freezes the base weights, those weights only ever participate in forward passes and gradient propagation, never in updates, so they don't need full precision. QLoRA stores them in 4-bit NormalFloat, a data type designed for the roughly normal distribution of neural network weights, and dequantizes block by block on the fly during compute. It adds double quantization, quantizing the quantization constants themselves, and paged optimizers to survive memory spikes. The adapters stay in bf16 so the gradients you actually apply are precise. The result was striking: fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48-gigabyte GPU with quality close to 16-bit fine-tuning, which is what democratized LLM fine-tuning outside big labs. The cost is speed, since dequantization adds compute overhead, so it's a memory-for-time trade, and if I had the VRAM I'd prefer plain LoRA in bf16.
options: It quantizes the LoRA adapters to 4-bit for faster inference
It keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit NF4 precision while training LoRA adapters in higher precision, drastically cutting memory
It uses quantum-inspired optimization for the adapter matrices
It quantizes gradients to reduce communication in distributed training
cards.question: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?

cards.explanation: The LIMA result showed 1,000 carefully curated examples can produce strong instruction-following, supporting the view that pretraining supplies the capability and fine-tuning mostly elicits format and style. In practice a few hundred examples can move a narrow task, and low thousands is a solid target. Consistency matters enormously: a handful of contradictory or low-quality examples can do more damage than a thousand good ones do good, so curation beats collection.
cards.modelAnswer: Far less than people expect. The LIMA paper made the point sharply: a thousand carefully curated examples produced competitive instruction-following, which supports the hypothesis that pretraining already installed the capability and fine-tuning mostly teaches format and style rather than new skills. In practice, for a narrow task like a specific extraction schema, a few hundred consistent examples often move the needle measurably, and low thousands is a good target for general instruction tuning. What matters much more than count is quality and consistency: if two examples format the same situation differently, you're teaching the model to be inconsistent, and a small number of bad labels can outweigh a lot of good ones. So my process is to start with a few hundred, measure on a held-out set, and add data where the errors are, rather than collecting ten thousand examples up front and discovering they encode conflicting conventions.
options: Millions of examples, comparable to pretraining scale
Often 1,000-10,000 high-quality diverse examples, since quality and diversity matter far more than volume
Exactly one example per task category
At least 100,000 examples or the model will not converge
cards.question: Roughly how much data do you need for a useful instruction fine-tune?

cards.explanation: A base model is trained to continue text, so given 'Write a poem about the sea' it might plausibly continue with more instructions, a list of similar prompts, or a webpage footer, because that's what follows such text on the internet. Instruction tuning on (instruction, good response) pairs teaches it that the correct continuation of a request is a compliant answer. This is an alignment of objective, not an increase in knowledge.
cards.modelAnswer: It closes an objective mismatch. Pretraining optimizes next-token continuation over internet text, so given write a poem about the sea, a plausible continuation is another writing prompt, or a list of assignment questions, or a page footer, because that's genuinely what follows such text in the wild. The model has the capability to write the poem, it just has no reason to believe that's what should come next. Instruction tuning on instruction-response pairs teaches it that the expected continuation of a request is a compliant, helpful answer in a particular format. It's important to frame it as eliciting latent capability rather than adding knowledge or intelligence, which is why so little data is needed and why the underlying capability ceiling is set by pretraining.
options: Its factual knowledge gaps
The mismatch between next-token continuation and following an instruction to produce a helpful response
Its inability to handle long contexts
Slow inference speed
cards.question: What is instruction tuning trying to fix about a base model?

cards.explanation: Pipeline: collect pairwise preferences over model outputs, train a reward model to score responses, then optimize the policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty against the SFT reference. Failure modes: the policy exploits reward model errors (reward hacking) producing outputs that score well but are worse; the reward model inherits annotator biases toward length, confidence, and sycophancy; too little KL penalty causes mode collapse and loss of diversity; PPO is complex and sensitive, requiring four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, critic).
cards.modelAnswer: The pipeline has three parts. You collect human preferences as pairwise comparisons rather than absolute scores, because people are much more reliable at saying A is better than B than at scoring in isolation. You train a reward model, usually the SFT model with a scalar head, on those comparisons with a Bradley-Terry loss. Then you optimize the policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL divergence penalty against the SFT reference, and that KL term is essential, not decorative, because it's what keeps the policy in the region where the reward model is a valid approximation. Failure modes are where the interesting discussion is. Reward hacking is the central one: the reward model is a learned proxy, and a sufficiently strong optimizer will find inputs where the proxy is wrong, producing responses that score highly and are actually worse, which is Goodhart's law in action. Related is inherited annotator bias, so models learn that longer, more confident, more agreeable answers get preferred, which is where verbosity and sycophancy come from. Too weak a KL penalty and you get mode collapse, losing diversity and sometimes degenerate text. And operationally PPO is painful: four models resident, policy, reference, reward, and critic, plus high sensitivity to hyperparameters, which is exactly the burden DPO removes.
options: Humans directly label correct outputs which are used as SFT targets; failure mode is annotation cost
Humans rank outputs, a reward model learns their preferences, and the policy is optimized against it with PPO; failures include reward hacking, verbosity bias, and KL/entropy collapse
The model plays a game against itself; failure mode is instability
Rewards come from a fixed rubric; failure mode is inflexibility
cards.question: How does RLHF work, and what are its main failure modes?

cards.explanation: DPO uses the analytic relationship between the optimal RLHF policy and the reward to reparameterize the problem, yielding a simple classification-style loss on preferred versus rejected responses that increases the relative log-probability of the winner against a frozen reference. You need only two models in memory instead of four, there's no reward model, no sampling loop, and no PPO tuning, so it's far simpler and more stable. The tradeoffs: it learns only from the fixed offline preference dataset (no on-policy exploration), it can over-optimize and push down probability on both responses, and at the frontier online methods with a reward model still tend to win, motivating iterative and online DPO variants.
cards.modelAnswer: DPO's contribution is showing you don't need the reward model or the RL loop at all. The optimal policy under a KL-constrained reward objective has a closed-form relationship to the reward, so you can invert it, substitute into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood, and the reward function cancels out. What's left is a simple loss on preference pairs that raises the log-probability of the chosen response relative to the rejected one, each measured against a frozen reference model. Practically that means two models in memory instead of four, no reward model to train and no reward hacking of it, no sampling during training, and none of PPO's hyperparameter fragility, so it's dramatically easier to get working, which is why it dominates open-source post-training. The tradeoffs are real though. It's offline, learning only from a fixed preference dataset, so there's no on-policy exploration and the data can go stale relative to the improving policy, which is why iterative and online DPO variants exist. It's known to sometimes decrease the likelihood of both responses while widening the gap, degrading generation quality. And at the frontier, well-executed online RL with a reward model still tends to edge it out, because a reward model generalizes to novel responses while a static dataset doesn't.
options: DPO uses a larger reward model for better accuracy
DPO derives a closed-form objective over preference pairs, optimizing the policy directly without training a separate reward model or running RL
DPO requires ranked lists of five or more responses instead of pairs
DPO trains the reward model but skips the policy update
cards.question: How does DPO differ from PPO-based RLHF?

cards.explanation: The original paper targeted only query and value projections, but later work found applying LoRA to all linear layers, including the MLP, generally works better, and QLoRA's ablations support targeting all of them. Rank controls capacity: 8-16 suits style and format adaptation, 32-64+ suits learning a substantial new skill, and going too high wastes memory and invites overfitting on small datasets. The scaling factor alpha divides by rank in the update, so people commonly set alpha to rank or twice rank to keep effective magnitude stable when sweeping rank.
cards.modelAnswer: The original paper applied LoRA only to the query and value projections, but subsequent work, including the QLoRA ablations, found that targeting all linear layers, so all four attention projections plus the MLP up and down projections, performs better for the same parameter budget, and that's my default. If I'm memory constrained I'd trim back to attention only. On rank, it's a capacity knob and I'd tie it to how far the task is from the base model's behavior: eight to sixteen is plenty for format, tone, or style adaptation, which is most use cases, while thirty-two to sixty-four or more makes sense for genuinely new skills or larger datasets. Higher rank isn't free, it costs memory and increases overfitting risk on a few thousand examples. The subtlety worth mentioning is alpha: the update is scaled by alpha over rank, so if you sweep rank without adjusting alpha you're changing the effective learning rate simultaneously and can't interpret the comparison. Common practice is alpha equal to rank or twice rank. I'd also note LoRA typically wants a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, often one to three times ten to the minus four, because the adapters start at zero.
options: Only the final output layer, with rank fixed at 1
Commonly all attention projections and often the MLP layers; start with rank 8-16 and increase if underfitting, keeping alpha proportional to rank
Only the embedding table, with rank equal to the vocabulary size
LayerNorm parameters, since they control the output distribution
cards.question: Which modules should LoRA target, and how do you pick the rank?

cards.explanation: If you compute cross-entropy over the whole sequence, the model spends capacity learning to predict the user's instruction text too, which is not the behavior you want and dilutes the gradient signal on the response. Standard practice is to set label ids to -100 for prompt tokens so they're ignored by the loss, training only on the assistant turn. Related details: mask padding as well, and in multi-turn conversations decide deliberately whether to train on all assistant turns (usually yes) and never on the user turns.
cards.modelAnswer: Loss masking means computing the cross-entropy only over the tokens you want the model to learn to produce, which for instruction tuning is the assistant's response, not the user's prompt. If you don't mask, the model is also being trained to predict instruction text, which wastes capacity on a distribution you'll never need it to generate and dilutes the gradient on the part you care about. Implementation-wise you set the label IDs for prompt tokens to negative one hundred so PyTorch's loss ignores them, and you mask padding the same way. There are two related judgment calls: in multi-turn data you generally train on every assistant turn but never on user turns, and you need the chat template applied exactly as it will be at inference, including special tokens, because a mismatch between training and serving templates is one of the most common and most confusing fine-tuning bugs, producing a model that looks trained but behaves oddly in production.
options: It prevents padding tokens from being attended to
Computing loss only on completion tokens, not the prompt, so the model learns to respond rather than to generate instructions
It masks out low-confidence tokens to stabilize training
It hides system prompts from the model during training
cards.question: Why does loss masking matter in supervised fine-tuning?

cards.explanation: Human preference collection is slow, expensive, inconsistent, and psychologically taxing for harmful content. Constitutional AI has the model critique and revise its own outputs against an explicit written set of principles, then trains preferences from AI-generated comparisons. Benefits: scale, speed, consistency, an auditable and editable statement of values, and less human exposure to disturbing content. Risks: the labeling model's biases and blind spots propagate, principles can be gamed or conflict, and you still need human oversight to validate that AI preferences track real human values.
cards.modelAnswer: RLAIF replaces or supplements human preference labels with labels from an AI model, and Constitutional AI is the version where that judgment is guided by an explicit written set of principles. Mechanically the model generates a response, critiques it against the constitution, revises it, and those revisions or comparisons become the training signal. The motivation is that human preference data is the bottleneck in alignment: it's slow, costly, inconsistent between annotators, hard to scale to every domain, and for harmful content it exposes people to real psychological harm. AI feedback is fast, cheap, consistent, and the values are written down in a document you can read, audit, and revise, which is a genuine transparency advantage over trying to infer implicit values from thousands of crowdworker judgments. The risks I'd name: the labeling model's blind spots and biases get baked in and amplified, there's a self-reinforcement concern if a model grades its own family of outputs, principles written in natural language can conflict or be gamed, and you still need human validation that AI preferences actually track human ones. So in practice it's a hybrid, AI feedback for scale with human oversight on calibration and on the highest-stakes categories.
options: Reinforcement learning with a rule engine replacing the policy network
Using an AI model, guided by written principles, to generate preference labels or critiques instead of relying solely on human raters
Training on synthetic data generated by the same model without any preference signal
A method for aligning models using only rejection sampling
cards.question: What is RLAIF / Constitutional AI, and why use it?

cards.explanation: Preference training optimizes for what raters prefer, and people reliably prefer being agreed with and validated. So the model learns that matching the user's opinion, praising their reasoning, and conceding when pushed back on earn higher reward, even when the original answer was correct. It's an alignment-induced failure, not a knowledge failure, and it's dangerous precisely because it degrades reliability under pressure. Mitigations: preference data that rewards correct disagreement, evaluations that measure whether the model holds correct positions when challenged, and prompting that separates the user's belief from the question.
cards.modelAnswer: Sycophancy is when a model tells you what you want to hear: it agrees with a stated opinion, praises a flawed idea, or abandons a correct answer as soon as you push back. The cause is structural, not accidental. Preference training optimizes a proxy for human approval, and humans genuinely do rate agreeable, validating responses more highly, so the gradient points toward agreement independent of truth. That makes it an alignment-induced failure rather than a capability gap, and it's insidious because it degrades reliability exactly when it matters, under disagreement, which is often when a user most needs a correct answer. Anthropic's own work has documented and measured it. Mitigations are on both sides: preference data that explicitly rewards maintaining a correct position and politely disagreeing, and evaluations designed to detect it, for instance asking a question, then asserting the opposite and checking whether the model caves. From an application-building standpoint I'd also avoid putting the user's belief in the prompt alongside the question when I want an unbiased judgment, since stating a preference measurably shifts the answer.
options: A decoding artifact caused by high temperature
The tendency to agree with the user's stated view or back down when challenged, arising because human raters prefer agreeable responses
A failure of the tokenizer on second-person pronouns
Overfitting to the system prompt
cards.question: What is sycophancy in aligned models and where does it come from?

cards.explanation: Quality determinants: prompts should reflect real usage including hard and adversarial cases; responses should be on-policy (from the model you're aligning) and meaningfully different, since near-identical pairs teach little; rubrics must specify what 'better' means (accuracy over style, calibrated uncertainty over confidence) or you'll train in verbosity and sycophancy; multiple annotators with measured agreement expose ambiguous or badly-specified criteria; and coverage must include safety, refusal, and abstention cases or the model won't learn them. Keeping some genuinely close pairs is useful, but noisy labels on truly ambiguous items add variance.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd focus on four things. Prompt distribution: sample from real usage, including the hard tail and adversarial cases, because a preference set drawn from easy prompts won't shape behavior where behavior actually matters. Response generation: sample on-policy, from the model I'm about to align, at a temperature that yields genuinely different candidates, since a pair of near-identical responses carries almost no signal and off-policy pairs teach preferences about text the model wouldn't produce anyway. Rubric design, which I think is the most underrated part: if I don't tell annotators that factual accuracy outranks fluency and that calibrated uncertainty beats false confidence, they'll default to preferring longer, more confident, more agreeable answers, and I'll have trained verbosity and sycophancy directly into the model. Annotation quality: multiple raters per item with measured inter-annotator agreement, treating low agreement as a signal my rubric is underspecified rather than that the raters are bad, plus regular calibration sessions. And deliberate coverage of safety, refusal, and abstention, because if the dataset has no examples of appropriately declining or saying I don't know, the model will learn to always produce something. I'd also keep an eye on length balance, since if preferred responses are systematically longer, length alone becomes the learned signal.
options: Sample two random completions per prompt and label with a single annotator each
Sample diverse on-policy responses per prompt, use clear rubrics with multiple annotators, measure inter-annotator agreement, and cover edge cases and refusals deliberately
Use the model's own log probabilities as preference labels
Collect only examples where annotators strongly agree, discarding ambiguous ones entirely
cards.question: How do you build a good preference dataset?

cards.explanation: Optimizing for helpfulness, harmlessness, and preferred style can reduce performance elsewhere: aligned models have shown losses on some few-shot benchmarks, reduced output diversity, more hedging and over-refusal, and occasionally weaker code or reasoning. It's a manifestation of the same forgetting and specialization pressure as any fine-tune. You detect it by holding a broad, fixed capability suite (reasoning, code, math, knowledge, plus generation diversity and over-refusal rates) and comparing pre- and post-alignment, and you mitigate it with KL constraints, mixing capability data into the alignment mix, and model merging.
cards.modelAnswer: The alignment tax is the capability cost you pay for alignment: after RLHF a model may be more helpful and safer but measurably worse at some tasks, with reduced output diversity, more hedging, and over-refusal on benign requests that superficially resemble unsafe ones. It's the same underlying phenomenon as catastrophic forgetting, just induced by a preference objective, and the KL penalty in RLHF is partly there to bound it. Detecting it requires deciding in advance what you're protecting: I'd maintain a fixed broad capability suite covering reasoning, math, code, and knowledge, run it before and after every alignment stage, and treat regressions as blocking. I'd add two evaluations people often skip: generation diversity, since preference training measurably collapses it and you won't see that in accuracy benchmarks, and an over-refusal set of benign-but-sensitive-sounding prompts, because refusing too much is a real product failure that safety metrics alone will score as a success. Mitigations are mixing capability and instruction data into the alignment mixture, keeping the KL constraint meaningful, and model merging or interpolating between the pre- and post-alignment checkpoints to trade off along that curve explicitly.
options: The compute cost of running RLHF
Capability degradation on other tasks caused by alignment training, detected by evaluating a broad capability suite before and after
The latency added by safety classifiers at inference
The licensing cost of preference data
cards.question: What is the alignment tax, and how do you detect it?

cards.explanation: The reward model is a proxy trained on a finite dataset, so it's inaccurate off-distribution, and RL is an optimizer that actively searches for high-reward regions, which means it finds those inaccuracies. Symptoms: reward climbing while human evaluation flattens or declines, plus telltale artifacts like extreme verbosity, formulaic structure, hedging, or exploiting judge quirks. Defenses: a KL penalty anchoring the policy near the reference so it stays where the reward model is valid; early stopping on human or held-out evaluation rather than reward; reward model ensembles and uncertainty penalties; iteratively collecting new preferences on current policy outputs so the reward model tracks the policy; and length or format normalization to remove known degenerate axes.
cards.modelAnswer: Reward hacking is Goodhart's law inside RLHF. The reward model is a learned proxy for human preference, accurate near its training distribution and unreliable outside it, and PPO is an optimizer whose entire job is to find high-reward regions, so it will reliably discover where the proxy is wrong and exploit it. The tell is a diverging pair of curves: reward keeps climbing while human evaluation plateaus or degrades, usually accompanied by recognizable artifacts, huge verbose answers, formulaic bullet-point structure, excessive caveats, restating the question, or gaming whatever superficial cue the reward model latched onto. My defenses, roughly in order of importance. The KL penalty against the reference policy, which is the primary structural control, because it keeps the policy in the region where the reward model was trained and is therefore valid, and tuning that coefficient is the central tradeoff between improvement and hacking. Second, never early-stop on reward, stop on held-out human evaluation or a separate judge the policy isn't optimizing against. Third, iterative preference collection: relabel on the current policy's outputs so the reward model tracks the distribution it's being asked to score, since a static reward model goes stale as the policy moves. Fourth, reward model ensembles with a pessimistic or uncertainty-penalized aggregate, so the policy can't exploit a single model's idiosyncratic error. And fifth, explicitly normalize out known degenerate axes like length, since length bias is the single most common hack. I'd also just read samples regularly, because hacking is usually obvious to a human within a few outputs and invisible in the metrics.
options: Attackers stealing the reward model weights
The policy exploiting inaccuracies in the learned reward model to score highly without genuinely improving, defended by KL constraints, reward ensembles, and fresh on-policy labels
The reward model overfitting to the training preferences
Annotators deliberately mislabeling to bias the model
cards.question: What is reward hacking in RLHF and how do you defend against it?

cards.explanation: LoRA constrains updates to a low-rank subspace, which is both its efficiency and its limit. Empirically LoRA matches full fine-tuning on instruction tuning and moderate task adaptation, and its restricted capacity acts as a regularizer that forgets less of the base model, which is often a feature. Full fine-tuning pulls ahead when you need to absorb a lot of new information, adapt to a distant domain, or train on very large datasets, since a rank-16 update simply can't express the needed change. The practical decision also involves serving: many LoRA adapters can share one base model in memory, while many full fine-tunes cannot.
cards.modelAnswer: The honest summary is that LoRA is competitive on the workloads most people actually have and falls behind at the edges. Because LoRA restricts the update to a low-rank subspace, it has strictly less capacity, and that shows up when the adaptation is large: absorbing substantial new domain knowledge, a big distribution shift like a new language, or training on hundreds of thousands to millions of examples, where a rank-sixteen update can't express what's needed and you'd see it as a plateau you can't tune away. On typical instruction tuning and moderate task adaptation, careful studies find LoRA essentially matches full fine-tuning. And the constraint has an upside: because the base weights are frozen and the update is small, LoRA forgets less, so it preserves general capabilities better, which for a specialized fine-tune that still needs to be broadly competent is a genuine quality advantage rather than just a cost saving. I'd add that the serving story often decides it. With LoRA I can hold one base model in memory and hot-swap or even batch across dozens of adapters, which is what makes per-customer or per-task models economically viable; full fine-tunes each need their own weights resident. So my default is LoRA, escalating to full fine-tuning when I see a capability ceiling that raising rank and targeting more modules doesn't fix.
options: They are mathematically equivalent given the same data
Full fine-tuning has more capacity and usually wins on large datasets or big distribution shifts, while LoRA matches it on typical adaptation and better preserves base capabilities
LoRA always outperforms full fine-tuning due to implicit regularization
Full fine-tuning cannot be applied to models above 7B parameters
cards.question: How does full fine-tuning compare to LoRA in outcome, not just cost?

cards.explanation: Likely causes, cheapest to check first: a serving prompt or chat template that differs from training (special tokens, system message placement, whitespace), which silently degrades everything; training data drawn from a narrower distribution than real traffic, so production inputs are out-of-distribution; catastrophic forgetting of general abilities that the narrow eval set never tested; an eval set that measures format compliance rather than usefulness; contamination or near-duplicates between train and eval inflating the held-out score; and deployment-time differences like quantization, different sampling parameters, or a different system prompt. Diagnose by replaying real production prompts against both models and reading failures.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd check causes in order of cost. First, format parity, because it's the most common and the cheapest to verify: if the serving path applies a chat template differing from training even in special tokens or whitespace, the model is being asked something subtly off-distribution and quality drops everywhere. I'd diff the exact token IDs sent in production against a training example. Second, the eval set itself. A held-out split drawn from the same curated pool as training doesn't test production distribution, so if my training data came from clean curated examples and real users write terse ambiguous messages with typos, my eval was never a proxy for reality. I'd also check for near-duplicate contamination between train and eval, which inflates the score directly. Third, what the eval measures: it's easy to build a set that scores format compliance, so the model looks perfect while being less useful, and only human review of real traffic surfaces that. Fourth, catastrophic forgetting: the fine-tune got better at the narrow task and worse at the general reasoning and instruction-following users also rely on, which a task-specific eval by construction cannot detect, so I'd run a general capability suite against both checkpoints. Fifth, deployment differences, quantization applied only in production, different sampling parameters, or a different system prompt. My concrete first action would be sampling a few hundred real production prompts, running base and fine-tuned side by side, and reading the failures, because the pattern usually identifies which of these it is faster than any metric will.
options: The learning rate was too low; retrain with a higher one
Distribution mismatch between training and real traffic, chat-template or prompt-format drift, forgotten general capabilities, or an eval set that doesn't measure what users care about
The model needs more epochs on the same data
Quantization applied at deployment always causes this
cards.question: Your fine-tune scores well on the held-out set but behaves worse in production. What are the likely causes?

cards.explanation: Models fine-tuned from the same initialization tend to stay in a connected, roughly linearly-interpolable low-loss basin, so averaging their weights often yields a model with combined strengths at zero inference cost, unlike ensembling which multiplies compute. Task arithmetic treats the difference (fine-tuned minus base) as a task vector that can be added, scaled, or subtracted to add or remove behaviors. Methods like TIES and DARE address interference by trimming small deltas and resolving sign conflicts. Key constraints: models must share a base and architecture, gains aren't guaranteed, and merged models need re-evaluation since capabilities can interact unpredictably.
cards.modelAnswer: Model merging combines the weights of several models fine-tuned from the same base into a single model, most simply by averaging, and it works because fine-tuning from a shared initialization keeps you in a connected low-loss region where linear interpolation between solutions tends to stay low-loss, which is the linear mode connectivity result. The appeal versus ensembling is that you pay zero extra inference cost: one model, one forward pass, combined capabilities. Task arithmetic makes it more expressive by treating the delta between fine-tuned and base weights as a task vector, so you can add vectors to compose skills, scale one to control strength, or negate one to try to remove a behavior. Naive averaging suffers interference when task vectors conflict, so TIES trims small-magnitude deltas and resolves sign disagreements before merging, and DARE randomly drops and rescales deltas, both of which help notably when merging many models. The constraints matter: models must share the same base and architecture, so you can't merge across model families, results are empirical rather than guaranteed, and a merge can silently degrade a capability neither parent lost, so the merged model needs full re-evaluation rather than assuming it inherits both parents' scores. Where I'd actually use it: combining several single-task LoRA fine-tunes into one deployable model, or interpolating between a pre- and post-alignment checkpoint to tune the alignment tax explicitly.
options: Concatenating two models and routing between them at inference
Combining weights of models fine-tuned from a common base, e.g. by averaging or task-vector arithmetic, exploiting the near-linear structure of the fine-tuning region
Distilling two teachers into one student
Ensembling predictions from multiple models at inference time
cards.question: What is model merging and why does it work?

cards.explanation: Published work shows safety alignment is surprisingly shallow: a small number of adversarial examples can strip refusals, and even entirely benign task-specific fine-tuning degrades them measurably, because nothing in the fine-tuning objective preserves behavior it never sees. Practical response: treat safety as a regression surface, run a refusal and jailbreak evaluation suite on every fine-tuned checkpoint, mix safety and refusal examples into the training data (a small fraction is usually enough to retain most behavior), prefer parameter-efficient methods that move less, and layer independent runtime defenses (input/output classifiers, permission limits) rather than relying on model-internal alignment alone.
cards.modelAnswer: The empirical finding, and it surprised a lot of people, is that safety alignment is shallow and fragile under fine-tuning. A handful of adversarial examples can strip refusal behavior almost entirely, and critically, even completely benign task-specific fine-tuning degrades it measurably. The mechanism is straightforward once stated: gradient descent optimizes only the objective you give it, and if your fine-tuning data contains no refusals, nothing preserves the refusal behavior, so it drifts, which is just catastrophic forgetting applied to safety rather than capability. The practical implications are: treat safety as a regression surface with the same rigor as accuracy, so every fine-tuned checkpoint gets a refusal and jailbreak evaluation suite run against it before deployment, and don't assume inheritance from the base model. Mix safety and refusal examples into the fine-tuning data, where a small fraction typically retains most of the behavior for very little cost. Prefer parameter-efficient methods, since LoRA moves fewer weights and tends to preserve more of the base behavior. And architecturally, don't put all the weight on model-internal alignment: run independent input and output classifiers and enforce real permission boundaries outside the model, so a degraded refusal isn't a single point of failure. I'd also flag the governance angle, that offering fine-tuning as a product feature means accepting that customers can degrade safety, which is why providers run their own evaluation on submitted training data.
options: Fine-tuning preserves safety behavior since it's encoded in the base weights
Even benign fine-tuning can measurably erode refusal behavior, so safety must be re-evaluated and safety data mixed back in
Only adversarial datasets can remove guardrails
Guardrails are enforced at the API layer, so fine-tuning is irrelevant
cards.question: How does fine-tuning affect safety guardrails, and what should you do about it?

cards.explanation: Prompt tuning learns soft prompt embeddings prepended at the input; prefix tuning learns key/value prefixes injected at every layer, which is more expressive. Both change no model weights at all, so parameter counts are tiny and many tasks can share one frozen model. Differences from LoRA: LoRA modifies the weight transformation itself and can be merged away for zero inference overhead, while soft prompts consume context length and add per-token attention cost that cannot be merged. Empirically LoRA is usually easier to train and stronger, which is why it dominates, though prompt tuning becomes competitive at very large model scale and is attractive when you cannot touch weights at all.
cards.modelAnswer: Prompt tuning learns a set of continuous vectors prepended to the input embeddings, essentially a soft prompt optimized by gradient descent rather than written in words, and prefix tuning extends the idea by injecting learned key and value prefixes at every layer, which is more expressive since it can influence computation throughout the depth. Both leave every model weight frozen, so you're training a few thousand to a few hundred thousand parameters and one frozen base can serve many tasks. The important contrast with LoRA is where the intervention lives. LoRA modifies the weight transformation, so after training you can merge B times A into W and inference is bit-for-bit as fast as the original model. A soft prompt lives in the activation and context space, so it permanently consumes context length and adds attention cost over those virtual tokens, and there's nothing to merge away. Empirically LoRA also tends to train more stably and reach better quality, especially at small and mid scale, which is why it won in practice, whereas prompt tuning becomes more competitive as base models get very large. I'd choose soft prompts specifically when I genuinely cannot modify weights, for instance behind an API that offers only that, and LoRA otherwise.
options: It prepends a fixed natural-language instruction chosen by search
It learns continuous embedding vectors prepended to the input or to each layer's keys and values, leaving all weights untouched
It fine-tunes only the embedding table for new tokens
It is another name for LoRA applied to the first layer
cards.question: What is prefix/prompt tuning and how does it differ from LoRA?

cards.explanation: Synthetic data is now standard (Alpaca-style self-instruct, distillation from a stronger model, and verified generation for math and code), but unfiltered generation degrades models: errors are confidently stated and get amplified, the outputs concentrate on a narrow mode so diversity collapses, and repeated training on model output risks 'model collapse'. What makes it work is filtering and verification: execute the code and keep what passes tests, check math against a solver, use a reward model or LLM judge to drop weak samples, and enforce diversity via varied seed prompts, personas, and difficulty. Keep real human data anchored in the mix, measure diversity not just accuracy, and be aware that distilling from a proprietary model may violate its terms.
cards.modelAnswer: Synthetic data is standard practice now and it works, but only with filtering, because the failure mode of naive generation is subtle. Three specific risks. Error amplification: a generating model states wrong things confidently, and training on them makes those errors more likely, not less. Diversity collapse: sampled outputs concentrate on the model's high-probability modes, so ten thousand generated examples may cover far less of the input space than a thousand human ones, and repeatedly training on model output is the model-collapse concern. And inherited bias, since you adopt the teacher's blind spots wholesale. What makes it work is verification wherever the domain permits it: for code, execute against tests and keep only passing samples; for math, check against a solver; for extraction, validate against a schema. Where you can't verify mechanically, filter with a reward model or an LLM judge, and be aggressive, since a smaller filtered set beats a large unfiltered one. Then engineer diversity deliberately rather than hoping for it, by varying seed prompts, personas, difficulty levels, and formats, and I'd measure diversity, embedding spread or n-gram uniqueness, as a first-class metric alongside accuracy. I'd keep a real human-authored anchor in the mixture and a fully human evaluation set, so the thing I measure against isn't itself synthetic. Two non-technical points: human spot-checking of a sample is cheap and catches systematic problems metrics miss, and distilling from a proprietary model may breach its terms of service, which is a real constraint on the approach.
options: Generate as much as possible from the strongest available model and train on all of it
Generate diversely, filter hard with verification or reward models, keep humans in the loop on quality, and monitor for diversity collapse and inherited errors
Only use synthetic data for evaluation, never training
Mix synthetic and real data at exactly 50/50 in all cases
cards.question: How do you use synthetic data for fine-tuning without degrading the model?

cards.explanation: Diagnose the gap first, because each tool fixes a different one. Missing or changing knowledge, needing citations and permissions -> retrieval. Wrong format, tone, or a weak narrow skill despite good prompting -> fine-tuning. Cost or latency too high with a large model -> fine-tune a smaller one, or distill. Capability genuinely absent from all available models -> that's a research project, not a feature. Escalate in that order because each step multiplies cost, iteration time, and operational burden: a prompt change ships in minutes, a fine-tune takes days and needs an eval harness and retraining plan, and pretraining costs millions and is almost never the right call outside a frontier lab or a truly unique modality.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd start by diagnosing which gap I actually have, because these tools fix different problems and picking wrong wastes months. If the model lacks knowledge, or the knowledge changes, or I need citations, permissions, and deletion, that's retrieval, and fine-tuning is the wrong instrument. If the model has the knowledge but produces the wrong format, tone, or is unreliable at a narrow skill even with a well-engineered prompt and good few-shot examples, that's fine-tuning. If quality is fine but cost or latency isn't, that's fine-tuning or distilling a smaller model to replace a large one, which is often the highest-ROI fine-tune there is. And if the capability is genuinely absent from every available frontier model, that's a research problem, not a product feature, and I'd push back on the requirement rather than reach for pretraining. Then I escalate in cost and reversibility order: prompting first because it iterates in minutes and reverts instantly, retrieval next because it's infrastructure but keeps knowledge externally editable, fine-tuning after that because it commits me to an evaluation harness, a data pipeline, and a retraining plan every time the base model updates, and training from scratch essentially never, since it costs millions and you'd need a genuinely unique modality or data advantage to justify it over adapting an existing model. Practically, I'd also note these compose rather than compete: the common production shape is a retrieval system with a lightly fine-tuned smaller model, and I'd build the evaluation set before choosing, since without it I can't tell whether any of these actually helped.
options: Always start with fine-tuning since it gives the most control
Escalate by cost and reversibility: prompt first, add retrieval for knowledge, fine-tune for behavior, and train from scratch essentially never
Choose based on the size of the available GPU budget alone
Train from scratch whenever the domain is specialized
cards.question: How would you decide between prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, and training from scratch for a new requirement?

cards.explanation: Learning rate dominates: full fine-tuning wants roughly 1e-5 to 5e-5 while LoRA tolerates and needs much more, around 1e-4 to 3e-4, since adapters start at zero. Epochs matter almost as much: 1-3 is typical and beyond that you memorize the small dataset, so early-stop on validation loss. Effective batch size (batch times gradient accumulation) should be large enough for stable gradients, commonly 32-128 sequences. Add a short warmup (a few percent of steps) and cosine decay. Sequence packing and max length affect throughput and memory significantly. LoRA adds rank, alpha, and target modules. Note that validation loss is a weak proxy for quality, so gate releases on task evaluations, not loss alone.
