cards.modelAnswer: Learning rate first, by a wide margin, and the right value depends on the method: full fine-tuning wants something small like one to five times ten to the minus five, because you're perturbing pretrained weights and too much destroys them, whereas LoRA wants roughly an order of magnitude more, one to three times ten to the minus four, since the adapters initialize at zero and have to travel. Epochs second: one to three is the normal range, and going past that on a few thousand examples memorizes rather than generalizes, so I early-stop on validation. Effective batch size, meaning batch times gradient accumulation steps, matters for gradient stability and I'd target something like thirty-two to a hundred and twenty-eight sequences, using accumulation to reach it when memory won't allow it directly. Then a short linear warmup of a few percent of total steps followed by cosine decay, which is the standard and rarely worth deviating from. Max sequence length and sequence packing are worth attention because they drive both memory and throughput, and packing short examples together can cut training time substantially, though you need attention masking so packed examples don't attend across boundaries. For LoRA specifically, add rank, alpha, and which modules to target. The caveat I'd stress is that validation loss is a weak proxy for what you care about: a checkpoint with slightly worse loss can be clearly better on the actual task, so I gate releases on task evaluations and human review of samples, and use loss only to detect overfitting.
options: Batch size only; everything else can be left at defaults
Learning rate and epochs above all, plus effective batch size, warmup, schedule, and sequence packing, with LoRA typically at 1e-4 to 3e-4 for 1-3 epochs
Dropout and weight decay, tuned by grid search over 50 runs
Temperature and top-p, since they control output quality
cards.question: What hyperparameters matter most for an LLM fine-tune, and what are sensible starting points?

cards.explanation: In domains where correctness is mechanically checkable, you don't need a learned reward model: run the code against tests, check the proof, compare the final answer to ground truth. That removes the central failure mode of RLHF, since you can't hack a unit test the way you can hack a preference proxy, so you can optimize much harder without reward drift. This is the core of recent reasoning-model training, where long chains of thought are reinforced purely by outcome correctness, producing emergent self-checking and backtracking. Limits: it only applies where verification exists (math, code, formal logic), it can reward correct answers reached by bad reasoning, and it can encourage test-gaming if the checker is weak, so verifier design matters.
cards.modelAnswer: RLVR replaces the learned reward model with a programmatic correctness check: run the generated code against unit tests, evaluate the final numeric answer against ground truth, machine-check the proof. Its significance is that it removes RLHF's central failure mode. A learned reward model is a proxy you can hack by finding its blind spots, which is why the KL penalty has to constrain how hard you optimize. A unit test isn't a proxy, it's the actual objective, so you can optimize aggressively without reward drift, and that's what unlocked the recent generation of reasoning models, where long chains of thought are reinforced purely by outcome correctness and behaviors like self-verification and backtracking emerge without being demonstrated. The limits are important. It only applies where cheap automated verification exists, so math, code, and formal logic yes, but essay quality, tone, helpfulness, and safety no, which is why RLVR complements rather than replaces preference-based methods. It rewards outcomes, so a model can reach the right answer by unsound reasoning and get reinforced for it, which is a faithfulness concern for the chains you then show users. And a weak verifier is hackable in its own way, models will special-case tests or exploit gaps in coverage, so verifier quality becomes the new bottleneck. The interesting open direction is extending verifiability into softer domains via rubrics or generative verifiers.
options: RL where a human verifies each reward before it is applied
RL against automatically checkable correctness signals, like unit tests or a math solver, avoiding a learned reward model entirely
A verification layer that audits reward model outputs for bias
RL where the reward is the model's own log-likelihood
cards.question: What is RLVR (RL with verifiable rewards) and why is it significant?

cards.explanation: Order of work matters: define what failure means with domain experts and build a stratified evaluation set including rare high-severity cases before touching training, since without it you cannot tell improvement from regression. Use retrieval for facts so answers are citable and auditable and knowledge can be corrected without retraining, and reserve fine-tuning for format and behavior. Prefer LoRA so the base model is preserved, changes are small and reversible, and versioning is cheap. Require provenance and versioning for every training example, expert review of both data and model outputs, calibration and abstention so the system escalates rather than guesses, and human-in-the-loop for consequential decisions. Ship behind a shadow or assistive deployment first, monitor per-subgroup performance, and keep rollback and audit trails. Also treat safety and fairness as blocking evaluations, not afterthoughts.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd invert the usual order and build evaluation before training. With domain experts I'd define an error taxonomy, what kinds of mistakes exist and which are catastrophic versus tolerable, then build a stratified evaluation set that deliberately over-samples rare high-severity cases, because an aggregate accuracy number will hide exactly the failures that matter in a regulated setting. Without that harness I can't distinguish improvement from regression and every subsequent decision is a guess. Architecturally I'd push facts into retrieval rather than weights, so every answer is citable back to a source document, an auditor can trace the reasoning, and a wrong or updated policy is fixed by reindexing rather than retraining. Fine-tuning then handles only format and behavior, and I'd use LoRA specifically because it preserves the base model, produces small reversible artifacts, and makes versioning and rollback cheap. On data, every example needs provenance and versioning, with expert review, because in this setting the training set is an auditable artifact. On behavior, I'd train and evaluate for calibrated abstention, so the system escalates to a human when uncertain rather than guessing confidently, and I'd treat over-confidence as a defect on par with a wrong answer. Deployment would be staged: shadow mode comparing against current practice, then assistive with a human making the final call, and only then any degree of automation, with per-subgroup monitoring since aggregate metrics mask disparate performance and that's both a fairness and a compliance issue. Throughout, rollback, audit logging of inputs, retrieved context, and outputs, and a documented model card. And I'd say plainly to stakeholders that the correct target here is a reliable assistant with human oversight, not full automation, and I'd want that expectation set at the start rather than discovered at review.
options: Maximize dataset size and train the largest model that fits the budget

Build the evaluation harness and error taxonomy first, involve domain experts in data and review, prefer parameter-efficient tuning with retrieval for facts, and gate deployment on stratified evaluation plus human oversight
Skip fine-tuning entirely; regulated domains prohibit it
Train on all available data and rely on the model's calibration to flag uncertainty
cards.question: You need to fine-tune a model for a regulated domain where errors are costly. How do you structure the project?

cards.explanation: Bias is systematic error from a model too simple to capture the true signal (underfitting). Variance is how much the fitted model changes if you resample the training data (overfitting). Total expected error decomposes into bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise. Increasing capacity usually lowers bias and raises variance.
cards.modelAnswer: Expected test error decomposes into bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is the error I get because my hypothesis class is too restrictive to represent the truth, like fitting a line to a curve. Variance is how much my fitted function swings if I redraw the training set. Simple models sit high-bias low-variance, flexible models the reverse, so I tune capacity, regularization, and data volume to minimize the sum rather than either term alone. Worth noting that in the overparameterized deep learning regime the classic U-curve can turn into double descent, so I treat the tradeoff as a guide, not a law.
options: Bias is training error, variance is test error, and they always sum to a constant
Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample
Bias comes from unbalanced labels; variance comes from unscaled features
Bias applies to regression and variance applies only to classification
cards.question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff?

cards.explanation: Every decision made by looking at the test set is a form of fitting to it. After many such choices, test performance stops being an unbiased estimate of generalization. Use a validation split (or cross-validation) for all model and hyperparameter selection and touch the test set once, at the end.
cards.modelAnswer: Because selection is a form of fitting. Each time I compare configurations on the test set and keep the winner, I bake test-set noise into my choice, so the final number is optimistic and no longer estimates generalization. The discipline is a three-way split: train to fit parameters, validation to choose hyperparameters and architecture, test touched once at the very end. If data is scarce I use k-fold cross-validation inside the training portion and still hold out a clean test set.
options: It slows training down because the test set is usually large
Test labels are typically unavailable during training
It leaks test information into model selection, so the reported score is optimistically biased
It violates the i.i.d. assumption required by gradient descent
cards.question: Why should you never tune hyperparameters on the test set?

cards.explanation: With 99% negatives, predicting 'negative' always scores 99% accuracy while catching nothing. Accuracy also treats a false positive and a false negative as equally bad, which is rarely true in fraud, medical screening, or moderation. Prefer precision/recall, F-beta, PR-AUC, or an explicit cost matrix.
cards.modelAnswer: Accuracy breaks down under class imbalance and asymmetric costs. If one percent of transactions are fraud, a constant negative prediction gets ninety-nine percent accuracy and zero business value. Accuracy also implicitly says a false positive and a false negative hurt equally, which is almost never true. I'd move to precision and recall at a chosen operating point, PR-AUC for ranking quality on the rare class, and ideally a cost matrix tied to the real decision so the threshold falls out of the economics.
options: Whenever the model is a neural network rather than a linear model
Under heavy class imbalance, or when error costs differ between classes
Only for multi-class problems with more than ten classes
Whenever features are correlated with each other
cards.question: When is accuracy a misleading metric?

cards.explanation: Regularization adds a preference for simpler solutions: an L1/L2 penalty, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, or weight sharing. It shrinks the space of functions the model effectively explores, cutting variance at the cost of some bias.
cards.modelAnswer: Regularization biases the fit toward simpler hypotheses so the model generalizes instead of memorizing. Concretely that's an L2 penalty shrinking weights toward zero, L1 encouraging sparsity, dropout injecting noise so no unit is load-bearing alone, early stopping capping effective capacity, or augmentation expanding the data manifold. It's a deliberate variance-for-bias trade, and the strength is a hyperparameter I tune on validation.
options: Speeds up convergence by rescaling gradients
Constrains effective model capacity to reduce variance, usually trading a little bias for it
Removes outliers from the training data automatically
Guarantees the optimizer reaches a global minimum
cards.question: What does regularization do?

cards.explanation: The L1 penalty has a constant-magnitude gradient, so it can push a coefficient to exactly zero and hold it there, giving built-in feature selection. L2's gradient shrinks proportionally to the weight, so weights approach zero without reaching it, spreading shrinkage across correlated features.
cards.modelAnswer: L1 gives sparsity, L2 gives shrinkage. The L1 subgradient has constant magnitude, so it can drive a coefficient exactly to zero and pin it there, which acts as embedded feature selection and produces interpretable models. L2's gradient is proportional to the weight, so everything shrinks smoothly but stays nonzero, and it handles correlated predictors more gracefully by splitting weight among them. Elastic net combines both when I want sparsity but have correlated feature groups.
options: L1 shrinks weights smoothly; L2 drives many weights exactly to zero
L1 drives many weights exactly to zero (sparsity); L2 shrinks all weights smoothly
They are mathematically equivalent under gradient descent
L1 works only for classification, L2 only for regression
cards.question: What is the practical difference between L1 and L2 regularization?

cards.explanation: Supervised learning maps x to a human-provided y. Unsupervised learning models structure in x alone (clustering, density estimation, dimensionality reduction). Self-supervised learning invents a supervised task from unlabeled data, e.g. predicting a masked token, which is how modern LLMs and vision encoders are pretrained.
cards.modelAnswer: Supervised learning fits a mapping from inputs to human-provided targets. Unsupervised learning has no targets and models the structure of the inputs themselves, like k-means or PCA. Self-supervised learning is the bridge that unlocked modern foundation models: you manufacture the labels from the raw data, for example masking a token and predicting it, or predicting the next token. The optimization is fully supervised but the annotation cost is zero, which is why it scales to internet-sized corpora.
options: Supervised uses labels; unsupervised finds structure without labels; self-supervised builds labels from the data itself
Self-supervised is just unsupervised learning with a neural network
Unsupervised learning requires reinforcement signals
Supervised learning needs no validation set because labels are known
cards.question: What distinguishes supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised learning?

cards.explanation: If one feature ranges 0-1 and another 0-100000, the loss surface becomes a stretched ravine and gradient descent zig-zags. Standardizing or normalizing conditions the problem so one learning rate suits all directions. Tree-based models are scale-invariant and don't need this.
cards.modelAnswer: Because scale differences make the loss surface ill-conditioned. With one feature in the unit interval and another in the hundred-thousands, the curvature along those axes differs by orders of magnitude, so any single learning rate either diverges on the steep direction or crawls on the flat one, and gradient descent zig-zags down a ravine. Standardizing fixes the conditioning. It also matters for anything distance- or penalty-based, like k-NN, SVMs, and L2 regularization, which would otherwise be dominated by the largest-scale feature. Tree ensembles split on order statistics, so they're scale-invariant and don't care.
options: It reduces the number of parameters the model must learn
Wildly different feature scales create ill-conditioned loss surfaces, so a single learning rate works poorly
It makes the loss function convex
Unscaled features break the chain rule
cards.question: Why do gradient-based models often need feature scaling?

cards.explanation: k-fold CV partitions the data into k folds, trains k times, and averages the held-out scores, giving a lower-variance estimate of generalization and a spread across folds. Cost is k trainings, so it shines on small/medium tabular data and is usually impractical for large deep models, where a single large validation split suffices.
cards.modelAnswer: k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, trains k models each holding out a different part, and averages the held-out scores. The value is a lower-variance estimate plus a standard deviation across folds, which tells me whether a difference between two models is real or noise. The cost is k times the training compute, so I use it on small to medium datasets, and for large deep models I fall back to one big validation split. For time series I use forward-chaining splits instead, since random folds would let the model peek at the future, and for imbalanced targets I stratify.
options: Training on multiple GPUs to cross-check results; worth it for large models
Rotating which fold is held out so every point is validated once; worth it when data is limited and a single split would be noisy
Validating against a second model's predictions to detect bugs
Splitting features rather than rows to test feature importance
cards.question: What is cross-validation and when is it worth the cost?

cards.explanation: If y = f(x) + e with e ~ N(0, sigma^2), the log-likelihood contains -(y - f(x))^2 / (2 sigma^2) plus terms independent of f. Maximizing it is exactly minimizing the sum of squared residuals. Similarly, a Bernoulli likelihood yields cross-entropy and a Laplace likelihood yields MAE.
cards.modelAnswer: Write the model as y equals f of x plus Gaussian noise. The log-density of a Gaussian is a negative quadratic in the residual, so the log-likelihood is minus the sum of squared residuals over twice the variance, plus constants that don't depend on the parameters. Maximizing likelihood is therefore identical to minimizing MSE. The same lens explains the other standard losses: assume Bernoulli outputs and you get cross-entropy, assume Laplace noise and you get mean absolute error, which is also why MAE is the robust choice under heavy tails. And adding a Gaussian prior on the weights turns MAP estimation into L2 regularization.
options: Because the Gaussian is the only distribution with finite variance
Because the log of a Gaussian density is a negative quadratic in the residual, so maximizing it minimizes squared error
Because MSE is the only differentiable loss function
They are not equivalent; the connection only holds for linear models
cards.question: Why is maximizing likelihood under a Gaussian noise assumption equivalent to minimizing MSE?

cards.explanation: Leakage means the model sees information it won't have at inference, inflating offline scores. Classic causes: fitting a scaler, imputer, or target encoder on all data before splitting; features computed from the future; row duplicates spanning train and test; and IDs correlated with the label. Fix: fit every transform inside the training fold via a pipeline, and split by time or entity.
cards.modelAnswer: Leakage is when training sees information that won't exist at prediction time, so offline metrics look great and production collapses. The most common vector is preprocessing fit before splitting: you standardize or target-encode on the full dataset, so test statistics bleed into training. Others are features computed using future information, near-duplicate rows straddling the split, and identifiers that proxy the label. My defenses are wrapping every transform in a pipeline fit only on the training fold, splitting by time for temporal problems and by entity when rows cluster per user, and getting suspicious whenever a single feature's importance looks too good to be true.
options: Training data escaping to production logs; caused by poor access control
Information unavailable at prediction time influencing training; commonly via preprocessing fit on the full dataset before splitting
Gradients leaking across mini-batches when shuffling is disabled
Duplicated rows in the training set
cards.question: What is data leakage and what is the most common way it sneaks in?

cards.explanation: Bagging trains many high-variance models in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them, cutting variance (random forests add feature subsampling to decorrelate further). Boosting trains weak learners sequentially, each correcting the current ensemble's errors, which mainly cuts bias and can overfit if run too long without shrinkage.
cards.modelAnswer: Bagging attacks variance, boosting attacks bias. Bagging fits many high-variance learners independently on bootstrap resamples and averages them, and since the errors are partly decorrelated the average is far more stable. Random forests push that further with per-split feature subsampling. Boosting is sequential: each weak learner fits what the current ensemble still gets wrong, typically the gradient of the loss, so the ensemble bias steadily drops. That means boosting can overfit if you keep going, which is why you control it with learning-rate shrinkage, tree depth, subsampling, and early stopping on a validation fold. In practice gradient boosting is my default for tabular data and it's usually stronger than a random forest, but it needs more tuning.
options: Bagging reduces bias by fitting residuals; boosting reduces variance by averaging
Bagging reduces variance by averaging decorrelated models; boosting reduces bias by sequentially fitting residual errors
Both reduce variance; boosting is simply faster
Bagging works only with trees; boosting works only with linear models
cards.question: How do bagging and boosting differ in what they reduce?

cards.explanation: The ROC curve sweeps the decision threshold and plots true positive rate against false positive rate; AUC is the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative. Because FPR has a huge negative denominator, ROC-AUC can look excellent when the positive class is rare. Precision-recall curves condition on predicted positives and expose that weakness.
cards.modelAnswer: ROC sweeps the threshold and plots true positive rate against false positive rate, and the area under it is the probability a random positive outranks a random negative, so it's a threshold-free measure of ranking quality. The catch is that false positive rate divides by the number of negatives, which is enormous under imbalance, so thousands of false alarms barely move the curve and ROC-AUC stays flatteringly high. Precision-recall conditions on what you predicted positive, so it exposes exactly that. For fraud, rare disease, or moderation I report PR-AUC plus precision and recall at the operating threshold the business will actually deploy.
options: ROC plots precision against recall; PR-AUC is better for balanced data
ROC plots TPR against FPR across thresholds; PR-AUC is better under severe class imbalance
ROC measures calibration; PR-AUC measures ranking
They are identical up to a monotone transformation
cards.question: What does the ROC curve show, and when is PR-AUC the better summary?

cards.explanation: Volume grows exponentially with dimension, so any fixed sample becomes vanishingly sparse and the ratio between nearest and farthest neighbor distances tends to 1. Distance-based methods (k-NN, kernel density, clustering) lose discriminative power. Remedies: dimensionality reduction, learned embeddings, feature selection, and strong priors.
cards.modelAnswer: As dimension grows, the volume of the space explodes, so any realistic sample is vanishingly sparse and every point is roughly equidistant from every other. That concentration of distances is what actually hurts: anything relying on a meaningful neighborhood, like k-NN, kernel density estimation, or clustering, degrades because near and far stop being distinguishable. The practical escape is that real data lies on a much lower-dimensional manifold, so I reduce with PCA or better a learned embedding, do feature selection, and lean on inductive biases like convolution or attention that impose structure instead of treating the input as an unstructured cloud.
options: Training time grows exponentially with the number of features
As dimensions grow, data becomes sparse and distances concentrate, so neighborhood-based notions of similarity degrade
High-dimensional models cannot be regularized
Gradients always vanish above a few hundred dimensions
cards.question: What is the curse of dimensionality in practical terms?

cards.explanation: There is no single fix. Options: class-weighted loss, undersampling the majority, oversampling or SMOTE on the minority, focal loss, or treating it as anomaly detection. Critically, resample only the training fold, evaluate on the real distribution, tune the decision threshold for the business cost, and prefer PR-AUC over accuracy.
cards.modelAnswer: I start by asking what decision the model drives, because that sets the metric and the threshold. Then the toolkit: class weights in the loss as the cheapest first move, majority undersampling when data is plentiful, minority oversampling or SMOTE when it isn't, focal loss for extreme skew in deep models, or reframing as anomaly detection if positives are truly scarce. Two rules I never break: resample only inside the training fold so validation reflects the real prior, and tune the threshold explicitly against the cost of a miss versus a false alarm rather than defaulting to 0.5. I report PR-AUC and recall at fixed precision, and if I resampled I recalibrate the probabilities afterward since resampling shifts them.
options: Always oversample the minority class until classes are equal
Combine resampling or class weights with threshold tuning and imbalance-aware metrics, validating on the untouched distribution
Switch to unsupervised learning
Delete the majority class rows that are hardest to classify
cards.question: How do you handle severe class imbalance?

cards.explanation: Calibration means that among samples predicted at 0.7, about 70% are actually positive. Measure with reliability diagrams and expected calibration error. Modern deep nets are typically overconfident; temperature scaling (one parameter fit on validation) is the standard cheap fix, with isotonic regression when you have more data and non-monotone distortion.
cards.modelAnswer: Calibrated means the probabilities are literally trustworthy: of all the cases scored 0.7, roughly seventy percent should be positive. It matters whenever a downstream system consumes the number rather than the argmax, like expected-value thresholding, triage, or ensembling. I measure it with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error, not accuracy, because a model can rank perfectly and still be badly calibrated. Deep networks are systematically overconfident, so temperature scaling, a single parameter fit on held-out data, usually fixes most of it without touching the ranking. Isotonic regression is more flexible when I have enough validation data, and Platt scaling is the classic choice for SVMs.
options: That it achieves high accuracy; fix by training longer
That predicted probabilities match observed frequencies; fix with Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or temperature scaling on a held-out set
That its features are standardized; fix by rescaling inputs
That precision equals recall; fix by moving the threshold
cards.question: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated, and how do you fix miscalibration?

cards.explanation: k-means minimizes within-cluster variance via Lloyd's algorithm, which converges only to a local optimum, so use k-means++ initialization and multiple restarts. The squared-Euclidean objective implicitly assumes isotropic, comparably sized clusters, so it fails on elongated or density-varying structure, where GMMs, DBSCAN, or spectral clustering do better.
cards.modelAnswer: k-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance, and that objective quietly assumes clusters are roughly spherical, similar in size, and separated by variance rather than density. Lloyd's algorithm only reaches a local optimum, so I use k-means++ seeding and multiple restarts. Features must be scaled or the largest-range one dominates. And k is mine to pick, so I look at the elbow, silhouette scores, or a gap statistic while remembering the objective decreases monotonically in k, so it can't select k for me. When clusters are elongated, nested, or density-defined, I switch to a Gaussian mixture for soft elliptical clusters, DBSCAN or HDBSCAN for density-based shapes with noise, or spectral clustering for manifold structure.
options: It assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters and is sensitive to initialization, scaling, and the choice of k
It is deterministic, so results are always reproducible
It requires labeled data for the centroid update step
It finds the global optimum of the within-cluster sum of squares
cards.question: Why does k-means need care, and what are its key assumptions?

cards.explanation: PCA finds an orthonormal basis ordered by explained variance, computed as the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix or via SVD of the centered data. Projecting onto the top k components is the best rank-k linear approximation in squared error. It is unsupervised and linear, so it can discard low-variance but highly predictive directions, and it only decorrelates rather than making components independent.
cards.modelAnswer: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance, which are the leading eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and in practice you get them from an SVD of the centered data matrix for numerical stability. Projecting onto the top k is provably the best rank-k linear reconstruction in squared error. Two caveats I keep front of mind: it's unsupervised, so a direction with tiny variance can still be the one that predicts the label, and it's linear, so for curved manifolds I'd reach for UMAP or an autoencoder. It also requires centering and usually standardizing, since otherwise the highest-variance unit dominates, and it decorrelates components without making them statistically independent, which is what ICA is for.
options: The features most correlated with the label, ranked by mutual information
Orthogonal directions of maximal variance, equivalently the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, minimizing squared reconstruction error
A nonlinear embedding that preserves local neighborhoods
A rotation that makes all features independent and Gaussian
cards.question: What does PCA actually compute, and what does it optimize?

cards.explanation: A discriminative model learns the decision boundary p(y|x) directly (logistic regression, most classifiers). A generative model models how data is produced: p(x, y) or p(x), enabling sampling, density estimation, and handling of missing inputs. Discriminative models usually win on pure classification accuracy given ample labels; generative models are more data-efficient in the low-label regime and underpin modern LLMs and diffusion models.
cards.modelAnswer: A discriminative model goes straight for the conditional p of y given x, so it spends all capacity on the decision boundary. A generative model models the joint or the input density, so it can sample, score likelihoods, and cope with missing features. Naive Bayes versus logistic regression is the textbook pair, and the classic result is that with lots of labels the discriminative model has lower asymptotic error while the generative one converges faster with few labels. The modern relevance is that generative pretraining, next-token prediction or diffusion, is how we absorb unlabeled data at scale, then we adapt that representation to discriminative tasks.
options: Generative models are always neural networks; discriminative models are always linear
Generative models model the joint p(x, y) or p(x); discriminative models model p(y | x) directly
Generative models require more labels than discriminative ones
Discriminative models can sample new data; generative models cannot
cards.question: What is the difference between a generative and a discriminative model?

cards.explanation: Classical capacity bounds are vacuous for modern nets. Empirically, test error follows a double-descent curve: it peaks near the interpolation threshold, then falls again as capacity grows. The explanation is implicit regularization: gradient descent prefers minimum-norm, flatter interpolating solutions, and architectural priors plus overparameterized smoothness keep effective capacity far below the parameter count.
cards.modelAnswer: Parameter count is a poor proxy for effective capacity. In the overparameterized regime the loss landscape contains a huge space of solutions that all interpolate the training data, and SGD doesn't pick one at random, it's implicitly biased toward small-norm, flat, low-complexity solutions. Combine that with architectural priors and you get the double-descent curve: error rises to a peak at the interpolation threshold, where the model is just barely able to fit and is forced into a brittle solution, and then falls again as you add capacity and the optimizer regains room to choose a smooth interpolator. It's also why the label-randomization result matters: the same network can memorize noise, so generalization has to come from the data-plus-optimizer interaction, not from a capacity constraint.
options: Because the extra parameters are automatically pruned during training
Because SGD plus architecture imposes an implicit bias toward low-complexity interpolating solutions, producing double descent
Because test sets are usually easier than training sets
It cannot; this always indicates a leakage bug
cards.question: Why can a model with more parameters than training points still generalize well?

cards.explanation: Covariate shift: input distribution moves but the mapping holds, so importance weighting can correct it. Label shift: class priors move (e.g. disease prevalence), correctable by prior adjustment or recalibration. Concept drift: the relationship itself changes, so no reweighting saves you and you must retrain on fresh labels. Diagnosis differs: monitor input distributions, prediction distributions, and, when labels arrive, actual error.
cards.modelAnswer: Covariate shift means p of x moves while the conditional stays put, so the model is still correct but is being asked about regions it saw rarely, and importance weighting or retraining on reweighted data can help. Label shift means the class priors move, like disease prevalence rising, and since the class-conditionals hold you can correct it analytically by adjusting the prior or recalibrating. Concept drift is the dangerous one: the mapping itself changed, so fraud tactics evolved or user taste moved, and no reweighting of old data recovers it, you need fresh labels and retraining. Operationally I monitor input feature distributions and prediction distributions continuously since those need no labels, then true error once labels land, because that ordering tells me which of the three I'm facing.
options: They are three names for the same phenomenon
Covariate shift changes p(x), label shift changes p(y), concept drift changes p(y | x)
Covariate shift affects training only; the others affect inference only
Concept drift changes p(x) while covariate shift changes p(y | x)
cards.question: How do you distinguish covariate shift, label shift, and concept drift?

cards.explanation: A feature can be highly predictive purely because it shares a common cause with the target, or because it is a downstream consequence of it. Acting on such a feature changes nothing. Additionally, impurity-based importances are biased toward high-cardinality features, and correlated features split credit arbitrarily. Causal claims need an identification strategy: randomization, instrumental variables, or an explicit DAG with adjustment.
cards.modelAnswer: Because prediction and intervention are different questions. A feature can be strongly predictive because it shares a confounder with the target, because it's actually a consequence of the target, or because conditioning on a collider induced the association, and in none of those cases does changing the feature change the outcome. There are mechanical traps too: impurity-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features, and with correlated inputs the credit gets split arbitrarily so permutation importance understates both. If someone wants to act on the finding I insist on a causal framing, ideally an experiment, otherwise a stated DAG with a defensible adjustment set, an instrument, or a difference-in-differences design, and I'd use SHAP only to explain the model's behavior, never as evidence about the world.
options: Because importance scores are always numerically unstable
Because predictive association can arise from confounding, collider bias, or reverse causation, so intervening on the feature may not change the outcome
Because tree models cannot compute importance for continuous features
Because causal effects require neural networks to estimate
cards.question: Why is correlation-based feature importance dangerous for causal conclusions?

cards.explanation: NFL says superiority is impossible uniformly across all conceivable target functions. Real-world problems are a tiny, highly structured subset, so choosing an algorithm whose assumptions match that structure is exactly where the leverage is: convolutions for translation-equivariant images, attention for long-range sequence dependencies, trees for axis-aligned tabular interactions.
cards.modelAnswer: It says averaged uniformly over every conceivable target function, all learners tie, so there's no universally best algorithm and no way to justify a model choice without assumptions. The practitioner's takeaway isn't nihilism, it's that the assumptions are the product. Real problems occupy a tiny structured corner of function space, so leverage comes from matching inductive bias to structure: convolutions when the signal is translation-equivariant, attention when dependencies are long-range and content-based, gradient-boosted trees when the structure is axis-aligned interactions in heterogeneous tabular features. It's also why I benchmark empirically on my data rather than trusting a leaderboard from a different domain.
options: No algorithm can ever beat random guessing on real data
Averaged over all possible problems no learner is better than another, so real progress comes from inductive biases matched to the problems we care about
Ensembles are always better than single models
Deep learning is theoretically optimal for all tasks
cards.question: What does the no-free-lunch theorem actually imply for practitioners?

cards.explanation: Common culprits: the offline metric doesn't move the target KPI; the offline set is biased because it was logged under the old policy, so gains don't transfer (selection/position bias); train/serve feature skew; a latency increase that costs more engagement than the accuracy gains; a guardrail capping impact; or genuinely insufficient statistical power. Diagnose with counterfactual/off-policy evaluation, feature parity checks, and a power analysis before the test.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd work through a short list. First, metric alignment: AUC measures ranking, but the KPI might be revenue or retention, and a ranking gain concentrated in the tail may never surface to users. Second, the offline data was logged under the old policy, so position and selection bias mean my replay flatters the new model, which is what off-policy or counterfactual evaluation exists to correct. Third, train-serve skew, meaning features computed differently online than in the training pipeline, which is the single most common silent killer. Fourth, latency: if the new model added a hundred milliseconds, the engagement loss can cancel the relevance win. Fifth, the test itself, so I'd check the power analysis, the randomization unit, and whether network effects or a guardrail throttled exposure. I'd instrument to distinguish these rather than guess, starting with feature parity because it's cheapest to verify.
options: The A/B test must be underpowered; ship the model anyway
Metric-to-business misalignment, feedback loops, train/serve skew, position bias in logged data, or latency regressions eating the gains
AUC is never correlated with business metrics
Offline data is always stale, so offline evaluation is meaningless
cards.question: Your model's offline AUC improved but the online A/B test showed no lift. What are the likely causes?

cards.explanation: Gradient-boosted trees remain state of the art on most tabular problems: they handle mixed types, missing values, monotone constraints, and need little tuning relative to nets. Linear models give auditable coefficients and calibrated behavior for regulated settings. Deep learning wins where representation learning matters: text, images, audio, and very large datasets.
cards.modelAnswer: I pick by data modality and constraints, not by prestige. On heterogeneous tabular data, gradient-boosted trees are still the strongest baseline and usually the strongest model, because they handle mixed types, missing values, and axis-aligned interactions natively and need far less tuning. A regularized linear or logistic model wins when I need auditable coefficients, monotonicity guarantees, or a regulator-facing explanation, and it's a superb baseline that reveals whether the problem is hard at all. Deep learning earns its complexity when representation learning is the bottleneck, so text, images, audio, or huge datasets where I can amortize the engineering. I also weigh total cost: a tree model that retrains in five minutes and is debuggable often beats a network that's two points better offline but nobody can maintain.
options: Never; deep networks dominate all tabular tasks
When data is limited, features are tabular and heterogeneous, interpretability or auditability is required, or latency and maintenance budgets are tight
Only when the team lacks GPUs
Whenever the target is continuous rather than categorical
cards.question: When is a simple linear or tree model the right choice over a deep network?

cards.explanation: Label-free monitoring: track per-feature distributions (PSI, KL, KS tests) against a training reference; watch the predicted score distribution and mean confidence for shifts; monitor missing-value and out-of-range rates for pipeline breaks; and use proxy or delayed signals plus a small human-labeled audit sample. Combine with shadow deployment of a candidate model for comparison.
cards.modelAnswer: Labels usually arrive late or never, so I build a label-free monitoring layer. At the input level I track per-feature distributions against a training reference with PSI or a KS test, plus null rates, cardinality, and out-of-range counts, since most real incidents are broken pipelines rather than genuine drift. At the output level I watch the predicted score distribution, mean confidence, and prediction entropy, because a sudden shift there is a strong early warning. Then I add cheap ground truth on purpose: a small continuously human-labeled audit sample, and any fast proxy signal like a click or a downstream override rate. I also keep a champion-challenger shadow deployment so I have a live comparison. Alerts go on sustained deviation with a sensible window, because per-batch noise will page you at three in the morning for nothing.
options: You cannot; degradation is only measurable with ground-truth labels
Monitor input drift, prediction distribution shift, confidence/entropy trends, and proxy signals, with alerting on statistical distance measures
Retrain daily regardless of any signal
Compare against a random baseline continuously
cards.question: How would you detect that a deployed model has silently degraded, before labels arrive?

cards.explanation: Skew occurs when the same logical feature is produced by two code paths, typically a SQL or Spark pipeline offline and application code online, so definitions diverge subtly: different null handling, timezone, rounding, or unit. The model then sees inputs unlike anything it trained on and degrades silently, since nothing errors. Prevention: compute features with one shared implementation used by both paths, or use a feature store providing offline and online consistency by construction; log serving-time features and compare distributions against training; and add assertions on ranges and null rates in both paths.
cards.modelAnswer: Training-serving skew is when a feature is computed one way during training and a subtly different way at inference. The classic cause is two code paths for the same logical feature, a SQL or Spark job offline and application code online, and they diverge on details like null handling, timezone, unit, or rounding. It's insidious because nothing throws an error: the model just receives inputs unlike its training distribution and quietly gets worse, and it's one of the most common reasons a model that looked great offline underperforms in production. Prevention is architectural rather than procedural. Ideally one shared implementation of each transformation used by both paths, which is what a feature store buys you along with point-in-time correct historical lookups. Failing that, log the exact feature vectors served in production and continuously compare their distributions against training, since that comparison catches skew regardless of cause, and add explicit range and null-rate assertions in both paths so violations fail loudly instead of silently.
options: A difference in hardware between training and serving; prevent by using identical GPUs
Features computed differently at training and inference time; prevent with shared transformation code or a feature store
Model weights drifting after deployment; prevent with checksums
Latency differences between batch and online inference
cards.question: What is training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?

cards.explanation: Reproducibility needs the whole input set, not just the output. Code version (git SHA), the exact dataset snapshot (a hash or immutable dataset version, since 'the users table' changes daily), the full config including hyperparameters and random seeds, the environment (pinned dependencies and base image, plus CUDA/driver versions for numerics), and the produced artifact with its evaluation results. Crucially these must be linked, so from a deployed model you can retrieve exactly what produced it, which is what lets you debug, audit, and roll back. Full bitwise determinism on GPU is often impractical, so the realistic goal is provenance plus statistical reproducibility.
cards.modelAnswer: You need everything that determined the output, linked to the output. Code by git SHA. Data as an immutable snapshot or content hash, which is the piece people miss, because pointing at the users table means the training set changes daily and results become unreproducible by definition. Configuration including every hyperparameter and the random seeds. The environment, with pinned dependency versions and the base image, plus CUDA and driver versions if numerics matter. And the resulting artifact together with its evaluation results. The linkage is the important part: given a model running in production, I should be able to retrieve exactly the code, data, and config that produced it in one step, because that's what makes debugging a regression, satisfying an audit, or rolling back tractable. I'd also be realistic that bitwise determinism on GPUs is often impractical given nondeterministic kernels and reduction ordering, so the achievable goal is complete provenance plus statistical reproducibility, and I'd document which one I'm claiming.
options: The model weights only
Code, data, configuration and hyperparameters, environment/dependencies, and the resulting model artifact, linked together
The training notebook and the final metrics
The Docker image, which captures everything relevant
cards.question: What should be versioned to make an ML system reproducible?

cards.explanation: Batch scoring writes predictions to a store that the application reads, so serving is a cheap key lookup. It's far simpler operationally (no latency SLO, no autoscaling, retries are trivial, failures are non-user-facing) and much more efficient since you can use large batches and spot instances. It fits recommendations, risk scores, churn, and lead scoring where inputs change slowly. It fails when the prediction depends on request-time context, when the input space is too large to enumerate, or when freshness matters in seconds. A common hybrid is precomputing embeddings or candidates in batch and doing only lightweight ranking online.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd choose batch whenever the prediction doesn't depend on request-time input and can be precomputed on a schedule, because it's substantially simpler and cheaper. You score offline, write results to a key-value store or table, and the application does a lookup, so there's no latency SLO on the model, no autoscaling, retries are free, and a failed job isn't user-facing. You also get to use big batches and cheap preemptible capacity, so the cost per prediction is a fraction of online serving. It fits churn scores, risk scores, lead scoring, and recommendation candidate generation, where the inputs change on a daily rather than per-second basis. It breaks down when the prediction genuinely depends on what just happened in the request, when the input space is too large to enumerate ahead of time, or when the business needs seconds-fresh results. The pattern I'd reach for most often is actually the hybrid: precompute the expensive part, embeddings or a candidate set, in batch, and keep only cheap ranking or feature assembly online, which gets most of the cost benefit while remaining responsive.
options: Whenever the model is large
When predictions can be precomputed on a schedule and don't depend on fresh request-time input, which is simpler, cheaper, and more throughput-efficient
Only for models that cannot be containerized
When the model requires a GPU
cards.question: When is batch inference preferable to real-time serving?

cards.explanation: Shadow (or mirror) mode runs the new model on real production inputs without its predictions affecting anyone, so it's zero-risk and validates latency, error rates, and prediction distributions against the incumbent, but it can't measure user response because nobody sees the output. Canary exposes a small percentage of real traffic to the new model, so you do get real outcome signal, at the cost of exposing some users to a potentially worse experience, which is why it's paired with automated rollback on guardrail breaches. The usual sequence is shadow to validate mechanics, then canary at a small percentage with monitoring, then progressive rollout.
cards.modelAnswer: Shadow mode, sometimes called mirroring, sends a copy of real production traffic to the new model but throws the predictions away, so no user is affected. That makes it zero-risk and it's excellent for validating the things that don't need a user: does it handle the real input distribution without errors, what's its actual latency under production load, and how does its prediction distribution compare to the incumbent on identical inputs. What it can't tell you is whether users respond better, because nobody sees the output. Canary sends a small percentage of live traffic to the new model for real, so you get genuine outcome and behavioral signal, but you're exposing some users to a possibly worse experience, which is why it needs guardrail monitoring with automated rollback on error rate, latency, or business metric breaches. In practice I'd sequence them: shadow first to shake out the mechanical failures cheaply, then canary at one to five percent with tight alerting, then progressive rollout while watching, keeping the old version warm for fast rollback.
options: They are the same thing under different vendor names
Canary sends a small slice of live traffic to the new model and observes real outcomes; shadow sends a copy of traffic to the new model but discards its output
Canary is for models; shadow is for infrastructure only
Shadow deployment replaces the old model instantly with automatic rollback
cards.question: What is a canary or shadow deployment, and how do they differ?

cards.explanation: Prefill cost scales with prompt length, so a long system prompt, tool definitions, or a large shared document is recomputed on every request. Prompt caching stores the key/value state for that prefix so later requests reuse it, typically reducing cost substantially for cached tokens and materially cutting time-to-first-token. To exploit it you must keep the reusable content at the very beginning of the prompt and byte-identical, placing anything variable afterward, since a single differing character invalidates the cache from that point. It's distinct from semantic caching, which returns a previously generated answer for a similar query.
cards.modelAnswer: Prefill cost and time-to-first-token scale with prompt length, and in most real applications a large fraction of every prompt is identical across requests: a long system prompt, tool or function definitions, few-shot examples, or a document the user is asking multiple questions about. Prompt caching stores the computed key-value state for that prefix so subsequent requests skip recomputing it, which cuts both cost on the cached portion and latency to first token, and for long-prefix workloads like document Q&A or agents with big tool schemas it's one of the largest single wins available. The engineering requirement is prompt layout discipline: the cacheable content must sit at the very start and be byte-identical, with anything variable, the user's question, timestamps, retrieved chunks, placed after it, because a single differing character invalidates everything downstream of it. That means things like injecting the current time at the top of a system prompt silently destroy your cache hit rate. I'd distinguish it from semantic caching, which is a different layer that returns a previously generated answer for a semantically similar query and skips the model entirely.
options: It stores complete responses so repeated questions are free
It caches the computed attention state for a repeated prompt prefix, cutting cost and time-to-first-token on subsequent calls sharing that prefix
It caches embeddings to speed up retrieval
It compresses prompts to fit more into the context window
cards.question: Why does prompt caching matter for LLM applications?

cards.explanation: With static batching, a batch is assembled, run to completion, and only then replaced, so if one request generates 1000 tokens and others finish at 20, the GPU spends most of its time computing padding for finished sequences while new requests wait in a queue. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules per decoding step: completed sequences are evicted and queued requests are admitted immediately, keeping the batch full. Since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and a fuller batch amortizes each weight load across more sequences, this can improve throughput by several times, and it's why vLLM and TGI use it, typically alongside PagedAttention to manage the varying KV cache allocations.
cards.modelAnswer: The problem with static batching is that generation lengths vary enormously, so a batch runs until its longest sequence finishes. If one request generates a thousand tokens while the rest finish at twenty, you're computing padding for finished slots for most of the batch's life while newly arrived requests sit in a queue, so both utilization and latency suffer. Continuous batching, also called iteration-level scheduling, makes the batch composition dynamic: at every decoding step, finished sequences are evicted and waiting requests are admitted, so the batch stays full. That matters specifically because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, meaning the cost is dominated by streaming the weights once per step regardless of batch size, so packing more sequences into each step is nearly free throughput, and the gains are often several times over static batching. The complication it creates is memory management, since sequences of different and growing lengths come and go, which is exactly what PagedAttention solves by allocating the KV cache in fixed blocks like OS virtual memory rather than contiguous per-sequence buffers, eliminating fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing. That pairing is the core of vLLM and TGI.
options: It uses larger batches, which are always more efficient
It lets finished sequences leave and new requests join at each decoding step, instead of the whole batch waiting for the longest generation
It batches requests by similarity so the KV cache can be shared
It moves batching from the GPU to the CPU
cards.question: Why does continuous batching improve LLM throughput over static batching?

cards.explanation: APIs win on time-to-market, access to frontier quality, zero ops, and elastic scaling with no idle cost, so they're the right default and the right choice at low or spiky volume. Self-hosting becomes attractive at sustained high volume where you can keep GPUs busy, when data cannot leave your environment for regulatory reasons, when you need custom fine-tunes or unusual control over decoding and batching, or when you need predictable cost and no vendor dependency. The honest costs of self-hosting are engineering time, GPU supply and reserved-capacity commitments, the fact that idle GPUs still bill, quality gaps versus frontier models on hard tasks, and ownership of your own reliability, security, and upgrade path. The realistic answer for most teams is hybrid: APIs for hard low-volume reasoning, a self-hosted small model for high-volume narrow tasks.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd frame it as five questions rather than a preference. Volume and utilization: hosted APIs bill per token with no idle cost, while a GPU bills whether or not it's busy, so self-hosting only pencils out at sustained high utilization, and spiky traffic is where it goes wrong because you provision for peak and pay for the trough. Compliance and data residency: if data legally cannot leave a boundary, or an agreement forbids third-party processing, that can decide it outright regardless of cost. Quality: frontier hosted models still lead on hard reasoning, so I'd ask whether my task needs that or whether a small open model with good retrieval clears the bar, which for narrow tasks it very often does. Control: self-hosting is what lets me run custom fine-tunes, control decoding and batching, guarantee no upstream model deprecation changes behavior under me, and hit tight predictable latency. And engineering cost, which people underestimate, since I now own capacity planning, GPU supply, upgrades, security, and reliability, and that's a team, not a weekend. My default is to start on an API to find out whether the product works at all, then measure actual token volume and quality requirements, and self-host the high-volume narrow workloads once the economics are clear. Most mature systems end up hybrid: a small self-hosted or fine-tuned model handling the bulk of easy traffic, escalating the hard minority to a frontier API.
options: Self-host always, since it's cheaper at any scale
Weigh cost at your actual volume, data residency and compliance needs, latency and control requirements against engineering burden, quality gaps, and utilization risk
Use APIs for prototypes and always self-host in production
Decide purely on model quality benchmarks
cards.question: How do you choose between self-hosting an open model and calling a hosted API?

cards.explanation: Useful ML CI stages: schema and data validation (types, ranges, null rates, expected cardinalities) so bad data fails loudly; a fast end-to-end pipeline run on a tiny sample to catch shape and wiring errors without waiting for full training; deterministic unit tests for feature transformations, which is where silent bugs live; evaluation of the produced model against a versioned held-out set with a minimum-quality gate and a no-regression check, including per-slice results so an aggregate win can't mask a subgroup break; and a check that training and serving code produce identical features for identical inputs. For LLM applications add prompt-level regression tests and a safety/refusal suite. Full retraining per commit is usually too slow, so it runs on a schedule or on data/model changes.
cards.modelAnswer: Normal software CI plus several ML-specific stages. Data validation first, since most production ML incidents are data incidents: schema, types, ranges, null rates, and category cardinalities checked against expectations so a broken upstream job fails the pipeline loudly instead of silently training a worse model. Deterministic unit tests on feature transformation code, because that's where silent correctness bugs live and they're perfectly testable. A fast end-to-end smoke run of the whole pipeline on a tiny sample, which catches shape mismatches and wiring errors in a minute rather than after a four-hour training job. Then model quality gates: evaluate the produced artifact against a versioned held-out set with both a minimum absolute bar and a no-regression check against the current production model, and I'd insist on per-slice results in that gate, because an aggregate improvement that breaks one important segment should block. A skew check that training and serving code paths produce identical features for identical inputs. And artifact integrity, so the model loads, has the expected signature, and passes a few known-input assertions. For LLM applications I'd add prompt-level regression tests and a safety and refusal suite, run on every prompt change, since prompts are code and they're currently the least tested part of most systems. Full retraining is usually too slow for per-commit, so I'd trigger that on data or model changes, or on a schedule.
options: Only linting and type checks, since model behavior can't be tested automatically
Data validation, pipeline smoke tests on a small sample, model quality gates on a fixed eval set, and checks for skew and artifact integrity
Full retraining on the complete dataset for every commit
Manual review of notebook outputs before merge
cards.question: What belongs in CI for a machine learning project beyond normal unit tests?

cards.explanation: Three trigger styles, usually combined. Performance-based is ideal but needs labels, so it only works where feedback is reasonably fast. Drift-based uses label-free signals (input distribution shift, prediction distribution shift) as an early proxy. Volume or schedule-based retrains when enough new data has accumulated or after a fixed period, which is a safety net rather than a diagnosis. Whichever fires, retraining must not auto-promote: the candidate is evaluated against the incumbent on a fixed held-out set plus recent data, gated on per-slice results, then shadow or canary deployed. Note that retraining fixes staleness, not bugs, so if the problem is a broken feature pipeline or a label quality issue, retraining just relearns the problem, which is why diagnosing before retraining matters.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd combine three triggers. Performance-based is the one I actually want: retrain when measured quality on real labeled outcomes drops below a threshold. It's the most direct signal but it requires labels arriving fast enough to act on, so it's viable for click prediction and not for loan defaults. Drift-based as the early-warning proxy where labels are slow: sustained input distribution shift or prediction distribution shift, which is available immediately and tells me something changed even if I can't yet tell whether quality suffered. And schedule or volume-based as a floor, retrain monthly or once N new examples accumulate, which is a safety net rather than a diagnosis. Whatever fires, the important discipline is that retraining doesn't mean promoting: the candidate gets evaluated against the incumbent on a fixed held-out set plus a recent time-based slice, gated on per-slice performance so it can't silently break a segment, then shadow or canary before full rollout, with the old model retained for rollback. The failure mode I'd warn about is treating retraining as a general remedy. It fixes staleness. If the actual problem is a broken feature pipeline, a label quality regression, or a concept change your features can't express, retraining faithfully relearns the problem and you've spent a cycle confirming the bug. So I'd diagnose before retraining rather than making it the reflex.
options: On a fixed weekly schedule regardless of conditions
Trigger on measured degradation, drift, or sufficient new data, with a scheduled fallback, and validate every candidate before promotion
Only when users report problems
Continuously, with each new example applied as an online update
cards.question: How do you decide when to retrain a model?

cards.explanation: Its core value is solving two hard problems. First, offline-online consistency: one definition of a feature serves both the training pipeline and the low-latency online path, eliminating a major source of training-serving skew. Second, point-in-time correctness: when building a training set you must join each label with the feature values as they were at that moment, not current values, or you leak future information; feature stores implement that time-travel join, which is fiddly and easy to get wrong by hand. Secondary benefits are reuse and discovery across teams and backfilling. The cost is real infrastructure and operational complexity, so it's usually only worth it with multiple models, teams, and shared features rather than for a single model.
cards.modelAnswer: Two problems justify it, and both are genuinely hard to solve by hand. First, offline-online consistency: a feature is defined once and served both to the training pipeline in batch and to the online inference path at low latency, which structurally eliminates the most common cause of training-serving skew, namely two implementations drifting apart. Second, and this is the one people underrate, point-in-time correctness. When assembling a training set you have to join each label with the feature values as of that label's timestamp, not their current values, otherwise you leak information from after the prediction moment and your offline metrics are inflated. That as-of join across many feature tables with different update cadences is fiddly, and getting it subtly wrong is a classic silent leakage bug, so having it implemented once and correctly is real value. Beyond that you get reuse and discovery, so teams stop rebuilding the same customer-lifetime-value feature five slightly different ways, plus backfill support. The honest counterweight is that it's substantial infrastructure with real operational cost, so for a single model with a handful of features it's over-engineering, and I'd reach for it when there are several models and teams sharing features, or when point-in-time correctness has already bitten us.
options: A database of pretrained model weights
Consistent feature definitions served both offline for training with point-in-time correctness and online at low latency, plus reuse and discovery across teams
Automatic feature engineering from raw data
A cache of model predictions
cards.question: What does a feature store provide?

cards.explanation: Levers, roughly by typical impact: route by difficulty so a small cheap model handles the easy majority and only hard cases escalate; shrink the prompt, since long system prompts, oversized few-shot blocks, and excessive retrieved context are paid on every request; enable prompt caching for stable prefixes and semantic caching for repeated questions; batch aggressively when self-hosting, since decode throughput scales with batch size; cap output tokens, as output is usually the most expensive part and verbose responses are often worse anyway; quantize or distill a fine-tuned small model for narrow high-volume tasks; and remove the model from paths where deterministic code, a database query, or a classifier suffices. Measure cost per resolved task rather than per token so retries and human rework are counted, and attribute cost per feature and tenant so you know where money actually goes.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd order them by typical impact. First, routing and right-sizing: most traffic in a real application is easy, so classify difficulty and send the bulk to a small cheap model, escalating only the hard minority, which often cuts cost by a large multiple with little quality loss. Second, prompt and context reduction, because you pay for input tokens on every single call, so a bloated system prompt, oversized few-shot block, or twenty retrieved chunks where five would do is a permanent tax, and trimming context often improves quality too by reducing distraction. Third, caching at two levels: prompt caching for stable prefixes, which requires putting the invariant content first and keeping it byte-identical, and semantic caching to serve near-duplicate questions without calling the model at all, which in support workloads can absorb a large share of traffic. Fourth, output length, since output tokens usually cost several times input and verbose answers are often worse, so capping length and instructing concision saves money and improves the product simultaneously. Fifth, if self-hosting, batching and quantization, since decode throughput scales with batch size and quantization directly cuts the bytes moved per token. And sixth, the architectural one: take the model out of paths that don't need it, where a database query, a regex, or a small classifier is cheaper, faster, and more reliable. On measurement, I'd track cost per resolved task rather than per token, so retries and human rework are counted, and attribute spend per feature and per tenant, because you can't optimize what you can't localize, and unattributed LLM spend is how budgets get away from teams.
options: Only choosing a cheaper model
Model right-sizing and routing, prompt and context reduction, prompt/semantic caching, batching, output length limits, and moving work off the model entirely
Reducing the number of users served
Switching cloud providers
cards.question: What are the main cost levers for a high-volume LLM application?

cards.explanation: Immediate retries amplify an outage and, on a 429, actively worsen it. The pattern: classify errors, retrying only transient ones (429, 5xx, timeouts) and never invalid-request errors; use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms; honor Retry-After when provided; set explicit request timeouts, since a hung request holds resources; add a circuit breaker so a sustained outage fails fast instead of queueing indefinitely; and have a fallback path, a secondary provider or model, a cached or cheaper response, or an honest degraded experience. Also budget retries per user request so latency stays bounded, make handlers idempotent, and remember that for streaming responses a failure mid-stream needs its own handling since partial output was already sent.
cards.modelAnswer: Immediate retries are the wrong reflex, because on a rate limit they make things worse and during an outage they turn one failure into a retry storm. The pattern I'd implement starts with error classification: retry only transient failures, 429s, 5xxs, and timeouts, and never retry invalid-request errors since those will fail identically forever. Then exponential backoff with jitter, the jitter specifically so many clients don't synchronize their retries into a thundering herd, and honor Retry-After when the provider sends it since that's authoritative. Explicit request timeouts, because a hung connection holds a worker and cascades into your own capacity problem. A circuit breaker so that during a sustained outage you fail fast rather than queueing work you'll never drain, and recover with a probe rather than reopening the floodgates. Then fallbacks, which is where product thinking enters: a secondary provider or a smaller model, a cached or semantically cached answer, or an honest degraded experience, and I'd argue that a clear it's-unavailable message beats a thirty-second spinner. Some details that matter: budget total retries per user-facing request so latency stays bounded rather than multiplying, make handlers idempotent so a retry after a timeout that actually succeeded doesn't double-charge or double-send, and handle mid-stream failures separately since partial output has already reached the user. And I'd monitor rate-limit headroom proactively rather than discovering the ceiling during a traffic spike.
options: Retry immediately until the request succeeds
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on retryable errors only, with timeouts, circuit breakers, fallback models, and graceful degradation
Queue all requests and process them serially
Increase the rate limit request and wait for approval
cards.question: How should an LLM application handle provider failures and rate limits?

cards.explanation: Experiment tracking captures each training run's parameters, metrics, and code version so you can compare and reproduce attempts, which is a research and iteration concern. The artifact store is the underlying blob storage for weights, checkpoints, plots, and datasets, addressed by run. The model registry sits above both as the production interface: a named model with numbered versions, lifecycle stages like staging and production, approval and lineage metadata, and the ability for a serving system to resolve 'current production version' without hardcoding a path. Conflating them causes real problems, notably deploying by copying a file from someone's run, which loses lineage and makes rollback and audit impossible.
cards.modelAnswer: They sit at different layers and conflating them causes real operational pain. Experiment tracking is the iteration layer: every training run logs its hyperparameters, metrics, code version, and environment, so I can compare fifty attempts, understand what helped, and reproduce a specific one. That's primarily a research-velocity tool. The artifact store is just the storage layer underneath, blob storage holding weights, checkpoints, plots, and dataset snapshots, addressed per run. The model registry is the production interface on top: a named model with numbered versions, lifecycle stages like staging, production, and archived, approval metadata, and lineage back to the run that produced it. The value is that a serving system asks for the current production version of a named model rather than hardcoding a path to somebody's checkpoint, which is what makes promotion, rollback, and audit tractable. The anti-pattern I'd call out is deploying by copying a file out of a run directory: it works exactly once, and then you can't answer what's running, what produced it, or how to roll back, which is precisely the question you'll be asked during an incident.
options: They are three names for the same MLflow feature
Experiment tracking records runs and metrics for comparison, the artifact store holds the binary files, and the registry manages named versioned models with lifecycle stages
The registry stores training data; the artifact store stores code
Experiment tracking is for research and registries are for research too
cards.question: What is the difference between model registry, artifact store, and experiment tracking?

cards.explanation: Agents fail in the middle, so a single request log is nearly useless for debugging. You need distributed-tracing-style structured traces: one trace per user request with a span per LLM call, retrieval, and tool invocation, capturing the exact rendered prompt, the response, model and version, token counts, cost, latency, retries, errors, and the reasoning or decision that led to each action, all linked by trace ID so you can replay a session. Add derived metrics on top (steps per task, tool failure rate, loop detection, cost per task, groundedness on sampled traces) plus alerting on those. Practical constraints matter: prompts and outputs contain user data, so you need redaction, retention limits, and access control; volume is large, so sample non-error traces while keeping all failures; and you should be able to replay a captured trace against a new prompt or model version, which turns production incidents directly into regression tests.
cards.modelAnswer: Agents fail in the middle of a trajectory, so per-request logging tells you almost nothing. I'd model it as distributed tracing: one trace per user request, with a span for every LLM call, retrieval, and tool invocation, linked by trace ID so I can reconstruct an entire session in order. Each span captures the exact rendered prompt including everything the model actually saw, the raw response, model name and version, token counts in and out, cost, latency, retries, errors, and where applicable the decision or reasoning that produced the next action. The reason I insist on the fully rendered prompt is that most agent bugs become obvious the moment you read what the model was actually given, and reconstructing it from templates plus variables after the fact is unreliable. On top of the traces I'd derive metrics and alerts: steps per completed task, tool call failure rates by tool, loop and repetition detection, cost per task with per-tenant attribution, and sampled quality signals like groundedness and task success. Then the practical constraints. Prompts and outputs contain user data and often PII, so I need field-level redaction, retention limits, and access controls on the trace store, and that has to be designed in rather than retrofitted after legal asks. Volume is high and traces are large, so I'd sample successful traces while retaining all errors and all flagged-quality sessions. And the capability I'd most want is replay: being able to take a captured production trace and re-run it against a new prompt or model version, because that turns every incident into a permanent regression test instead of a one-off fix.
options: Log the final response and the total latency per request
Trace every step with linked spans: prompts, tool calls and results, token counts, costs, retries, and decisions, with sampling, privacy controls, and quality signals
Store all raw model outputs in a search index
Rely on the LLM provider's dashboard
cards.question: How would you design observability for an LLM agent in production?

cards.explanation: Start by defining what latency means to the user: for streaming interfaces, time-to-first-token usually matters far more than total completion time, and measuring p95/p99 rather than the mean is essential since tail latency drives complaints.
